talks.title: Exploiting Keyspace Reduction And Relay Attacks In 3Des And Aes Protected NFC Tags
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Exploiting Keyspace Reduction And Relay Attacks In 3Des And Aes Protected NFC Tags.
talks.summary:
Overview: Nathan Nye (True Anomaly) and Philip Toan (Ledger) present at Hardwear.io on exploiting keyspace reduction and relay attacks against 3DES and AES-protected NFC tags.

Key Topics: NFC authentication weaknesses in access control; relay attacks over sub-gigahertz links; keyspace reduction techniques; prior MIFARE Classic vulnerability research; and live card unlocking demonstration.

Technical Details: Researchers demonstrate authenticating with a locked NFC card via relay, then updating configuration to unlock memory pages from 10 of 48 to 44 of 48 accessible. The attack chains relay communication with an unlock-mode configuration write.

Takeaways: AES and 3DES-protected NFC implementations remain vulnerable to relay attacks. Physical access control deployments should not assume cryptographic protection alone prevents cloning.

talks.title: The IoT Longevity Crisis: Managing Obsolete Security and "Cloud Slop" with Yossi Oren
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of The IoT Longevity Crisis: Managing Obsolete Security and "Cloud Slop" with Yossi Oren.
talks.summary:
IoT Longevity Problem

Yossi Oren discusses how IoT product lifecycles diverge from vendor lifecycles. Devices may remain deployed for decades after companies, engineers, and smart features fade—illustrated by a fridge stuck in 2017. Sensors and actuators outlast the software and hardware supporting them.

Critical Infrastructure Exposure

Unlike home devices behind a perimeter, field-deployed IoT on bridges, traffic lights, and dams is physically accessible. Compromised devices can become network stepping stones, and upgrades on critical systems like dams carry operational risk when original designers are gone.

Separating Actuation from Cloud Slop

Oren advocates decoupling durable actuation from ephemeral "AI cloud slop" smart features so core functions survive when cloud services end. Sustainability demands planning for decades-long device lifetimes.

Documentation and AI

He urges writing imperfect documentation and teardown videos that future maintainers—and LLMs—can combine with binaries and product media to preserve working knowledge across generational hardware turnover.

talks.title: The Automation of Exploits: Will Eatherton on AI-Driven Security and the End of Obscurity
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning The Automation of Exploits: Will Eatherton on AI-Driven Security and the End of Obscurity.
talks.summary:
Attackers Without Silos

Cisco SVP Will Eatherton tells Hardwear.io that LLM-assisted testing is merging firmware, hardware, and software expertise. Specialized attackers once relied on niche obscurity; models now propose cross-domain exploits spanning FPGA designs, board components, and embedded code.

Automated Exploit Pipelines

Cisco experiments chain vulnerability hypothesis, lab device configuration, traffic generation, and result validation—work that once took days per creative tester. Similar AI coding experiments refactor legacy C into Rust at large scale, raising both development and offensive automation stakes.

Hardware Knowledge Gaps

Eatherton notes LLMs know common software frameworks well but lack training depth on proprietary schematics and Verilog compared to Python. Near-term gains come from better context retrieval—pulling firmware libraries, power-controller datasheets, and design artifacts into multi-step reasoning.

Open Source Still Wins

Despite AI risks, he does not expect a retreat from open-source hardware or software like SONiC. Shared components reduce unique attack surface, and AI may push teams to replace bespoke SSL libraries with maintained open alternatives.

talks.title: The "Last Mile" of Security: Roman Korkikikan on Hacking TPMs with Budget Hardware
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in The "Last Mile" of Security: Roman Korkikikan on Hacking TPMs with Budget Hardware.
talks.summary:
Attack cost

Roman Korkikian discusses hacking a TPM on budget edge-server hardware using custom sensing boards and used oscilloscopes, estimating total equipment under $2,000 rather than commercial lab gear.

Methodology

Side-channel and fault attacks are a last-mile option after software and protocol exploitation fail. He entered via cryptography/math, then specialized in power-analysis and voltage-fault techniques that break implementations, not algorithms.

TPM trust

The talk argues you cannot always trust TPMs; concrete device implementations may leak keys through physical analysis even when the crypto primitives remain sound.

Mitigation reality

Firmware updates can add masking, blinding, and randomization, but hardware-only flaws may require chip replacement, and certification cycles can delay fixes by years even after disclosure.

talks.title: The DIY Frontier of Autonomous Driving with John McMaster
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in The DIY Frontier of Autonomous Driving with John McMaster.
talks.summary:
## Overview
Hardware researcher John McMaster recounts a Hardwear.io networking-night experiment with George Hotz's comma.ai—a DIY driver-assistance stack that taps a car's CAN bus.

## How Comma.ai Works
Unlike commercial Waymo or Zoox vehicles, comma.ai intercepts CAN traffic after physical access to wiring. Code from GitHub plus a human "driver in the loop" enables semi-autonomous driving—McMaster dubs it "AI Jesus."

## Field Testing Reality
During qualification runs the system nearly steered into a pole on a left turn, requiring manual override. McMaster notes it is assistance, not full autonomy. A 12-volt reset left his infotainment dead—trade-offs of hacking production vehicles.

## Takeaways
Consumer self-driving hacks blur safety, liability, and hardware tinkering. Treat comma.ai as experimental ADAS requiring constant human supervision.

talks.title: Ethical Hacking for All Ages: Hardware Hacking with Script Kitty with Wolfgang Beck & Kody
talks.teaser: Shows how beginner soldering kits and a scripting USB device teach electronics, mesh networking and Wi-Fi security.
talks.summary:
Script Kitty, presented by Wolfgang Beck and Cody Kinsey, runs hands-on ethical hacking and electronics classes for beginners. The group started with kids camps in Montana and now brings the same approach to conferences, where adults are also drawn to the projects. In this short session, the presenters walked through several small hardware kits that double as learning tools.

The first item was a soldering badge with adjustable color dials, designed so that a first-time builder is unlikely to ruin it. It teaches circuits and two soldering styles in one kit, and it has sold more to adults than the kids' events did. The USB Nugget presents itself to a computer as a keyboard and runs scripts. Kids who had never programmed wrote prank payloads with it, and the same idea was later adapted for penetration testers, adding a screen, payload selection and a web interface for remote control. The Nibble board plugs into a Flipper Zero to add Wi-Fi and mesh networking through Meshtastic, MeshCore and Reticulum. Around 200 of these were soldered by a hackerspace group for the Chaos Communication Congress.

The final kit was a glowing, cat-shaped light that runs WLED and can be controlled over Wi-Fi. It is a beginner soldering project, and it also serves as a target in a Wi-Fi security segment. The overall takeaway is that inexpensive, approachable builds can teach circuits, scripting and wireless security together.

talks.title: Bridging the Glitch Gap: Hash Salehi on Making Professional Fault Injection Accessible
talks.teaser: Shows how a low-cost Pico EMP-based glitching board could make professional fault injection accessible to hobbyists.
talks.summary:
Hash Salehi explains why a 4:44 timestamp has stayed with him since last year, when he was trying to fault inject a car's computer. He recounts how an offer to break into a device paid about the same as a commercial chip shouter, so he chose a cheaper pulse tool instead. That decision cost months, because he had not pinned down exactly where the glitch needed to land.

The main lesson he draws is that buying the proper tool would have been the smarter move. He describes a board that uses a Pico EMP as its front-end driver, aimed at people who want higher voltage output, cleaner glitches and shorter recovery time between pulses without paying thousands of dollars. Paired with a cheap power supply from an online marketplace, it would give a user the setup he wished he had at the start.

He frames the project around accessibility, asking how a young person with limited means could get into this work, and expects that will help a new generation of researchers. Everything is published openly on his site, and he invites others to fill in any missing documentation through pull requests, possibly with AI coding assistants.

talks.title: Unmasking the Black Box: Eduardo Montovani on Wi-Fi Security, AI, and Affordable Hacking
talks.teaser: Explains why Wi-Fi chips get less research than Bluetooth, and how cheap off-the-shelf dongles support low-cost hardware research.
talks.summary:
The speaker explains why Wi-Fi was chosen as a research target: it receives far less attention than Bluetooth, yet it is more complex than Bluetooth and sits below the cellular baseband in difficulty. The appeal was treating the chip as a black box, where a request goes in and a radio message comes out without any visible view of the internals or the developer's choices. Early work often meant trying other components at random until something useful turned up.

On security posture, the speaker considers modern Wi-Fi fairly solid after about 20 years, with new flaws still appearing now and then, and even low-cost hardware usually carries some protective layers. 5G draws more researchers because its interfaces offer a much larger attack surface, which tends to expose overlooked bugs. The speaker says the Wi-Fi work was finished before AI tools were strong enough to help, and prefers human analysis for low-level hardware operations, though AI is seen as useful for general searching. For chip makers, the main advice is to remove unneeded features that widen exploitable paths and to keep doing regular code analysis.

The talk closes with a description of portable, inexpensive hardware, including a roughly $10 4G device from China. The speaker also built a web interface for an uncommon Wi-Fi USB dongle that can send and receive data, set the card to monitor mode and sniff traffic from the air. The session ends with an invitation to follow the research and to learn more about hardware security.

talks.title: Beyond the Hype: Guanxing on Exploiting Crypto Phones and the Evolution of Security Research
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Beyond the Hype: Guanxing on Exploiting Crypto Phones and the Evolution of Security Research.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this post-talk interview, security researcher Gwen Chen (referred to at the end as Guangcheng) from CertiK discusses his research into exploiting crypto phones and Ethereum wallets with interviewer Meltem Ozsoy (Intuitive Surgical) and a co-interviewer. The discussion covers his live demonstration of a USB-based exploit, the role of generative AI in reverse engineering, architectural flaws in crypto phones, and how researchers select emerging hardware and Web3 targets.

### Key Topics
- **Live Exploit Demos**: Chen reflected on delivering a live hardware exploit via USB to compromise an Ethereum wallet/phone. Because the attack utilized a physical USB connection rather than wireless vectors like Bluetooth or network connections, it was stable enough for a live stage demonstration.
- **Impact of AI on Security Research**: Chen broke down how tools like ChatGPT accelerated his reverse engineering workflow. Tasks like reverse engineering complex functions that previously took months were solved almost instantly by AI. However, he noted AI "took the fun" out of the research process, making the researcher feel like an agent being directed rather than an explorer, while stressing that domain knowledge in areas like TrustZone and boot ROMs is still mandatory to identify AI hallucinations and steer inquiries accurately.
- **Crypto Phone Architecture and Vendor Shortcuts**: The core premise of crypto phones is securing transactions and keys in trusted execution environments or hardware enclaves rather than regular userland Android space. While major manufacturers implement robust protections, smaller vendors often lack access to proprietary SDKs and relationships with chipset makers (e.g., Qualcomm, MediaTek) or Google, leading them to cut corners and downgrade security.
- **Target Selection in Web3**: Chen explained that the Web3 hardware ecosystem evolves so rapidly—ranging from hardware wallets and crypto POS terminals to DePIN devices and crypto phones—that new targets present themselves constantly without needing extensive searching.

### Technical Details
- **Exploit Vector**: Chen conducted a boot ROM exploitation delivered over USB to extract unencrypted keys from the crypto phone's Ethereum wallet in under a month.
- **Hardware Isolation vs. Boot ROM Flaws**: Chen highlighted that while a boot ROM exploit is severe, it does not automatically necessitate total system compromise if defense-in-depth is present. For example, Apple mitigated the "checkmate" boot ROM vulnerability using an isolated Secure Enclave Processor (SEP). Similarly, crypto phone vendors can utilize isolated secure chips or additional Android application-level obstacles to prevent access to keys even during low-level execution compromises.

### Takeaways
- Consumers and researchers should look beyond vendor marketing hype and white papers when evaluating crypto phones.
- Device trustworthiness should be judged by independent external evaluations, transparent bug bounty programs, responsible disclosure channels, and vendor reputation.
- Moving forward, Chen plans to shift focus toward more challenging hardware targets featuring newer technologies, such as hardware wallets incorporating iris biometric scanning.

talks.title: The F In Iot Stands For Future Proofing
talks.teaser: Argues that IoT devices must stay secure as long as they remain useful, and offers design ideas for longevity.
talks.summary:
The talk treats a standard garage door opener as a small IoT device and assesses it against confidentiality, integrity and availability. Adding a cloud-linked fingerbot to its manual release button makes the setup weaker, because it depends on a vendor cloud resting on a third-party platform and leaves unofficial interfaces exposed. The speaker also notes that when companies shut down, expired domains can let others take over devices that owners still rely on.

The speaker proposes three practices for longer-lived devices. First, separate long-lived functions from cloud-dependent features on the board, so the useful part survives. Second, enable local network control carefully, comparing unrestricted local access, access that needs physical presence and user consent, and short-lived tokens bound to the host hardware, which the speaker finds most promising. Third, publish as much documentation, firmware and code as possible, since future analysts, including AI tools, will need it.

For practical use, the talk points to Home Assistant and ESP Home running on cheap ESP32 boards. Recent ESP Home additions include infrared control, sub-GHz radio control for weakly protected devices, and serial proxying that brings older equipment onto a local system. The closing message urges hardware breakers to build useful, sustainable devices rather than discard working hardware.

talks.title: Reverse Engineering A Ledger Nano X Hardware Implant
talks.teaser: Traces how a tampered Ledger Nano X wallet hid a cellular-connected implant that captured recovery seeds.
talks.summary:
Joe Grand describes a case that began when a buyer in Thailand opened a cheap Ledger Nano X, purchased only for its battery, and found extra wiring and a smaller battery inside. He places this within hardware espionage, where legitimate devices are modified after they leave the factory and then resold. He compares it with earlier cases involving Treasure wallets, where swapped chips produced predictable keys, and with the 2020 Ledger customer data leak, which was followed by mailed devices carrying a USB drive that harvested seeds.

The middle of the talk covers his own investigation. He bought several units from third-party sellers on a marketplace, found that they also carried implants hidden under epoxy, and traced the added circuitry. The implant tapped the SPI lines between the secure element and the display, and it included a cellular module. Grand dumped the flash over SWD with OpenOCD, then read an embedded SIM with smart card tools, which showed a data-only subscription first registered in the Netherlands. Firmware analysis suggested the implant watched for the 26 letters shown during seed setup, stored them, and sent them over the cellular network.

He closes by covering follow-up work and coordination with Ledger, which recommends buying only from authorized resellers and comparing devices against known-good photos. His takeaway is that hardware provenance matters, and that attackers keep revising their implants as defenses change.

talks.title: Silicon Under Attack Physical Exploitation Of Modern Chips
talks.teaser: Panelists discuss fault injection, laser and EM attacks on modern chips, and why defenses rarely reach production silicon.
talks.summary:
The panel opens by noting that physical attacks on silicon have become far cheaper, with open frameworks and low-cost tools putting fault injection within reach of individuals. One panelist describes a single-person bench effort against an automotive-grade microcontroller, starting with voltage glitching, finding it unreliable, then moving to electromagnetic fault injection on a homemade scanning platform built from a CNC kit. He stresses that the real difficulty is learning how the chip reacts, logging resets and normal behavior to narrow down successful faults.

A laser-focused panelist explains that manufacturers need to know why a fault worked, since an unexplained success gives them nothing to fix. Smaller process nodes make precise faults harder, while package-on-package designs and chiplets force decapping, custom boards and more preparation. Chiplets widen the attack surface, embedded neural network weights become assets to protect, and AI tools help plan campaigns and analyze glitch data, though their output still needs checking.

Turning to defenses, the panelist working on polymorphic registers describes a design that destroys stored data locally when voltage or temperature crosses a set threshold, but says it has not been demonstrated in silicon yet. Panelists agree vendors add countermeasures mostly when buyers, regulators or insurers push, and one recounts a vendor that knew of a weakness yet suggested a pricier part. The closing advice is to question vendors, experiment with open tools, and push for security in purchasing decisions.

talks.title: Hardware At The Edge Reliability, Ai Infrastructure And Defensive Design
talks.teaser: Examines how AI data center growth raises hardware reliability stakes and how AI tools are used to probe network gear.
talks.summary:
This interview with Ethan, who leads an engineering organization building data center, web and service provider infrastructure, looks at why hardware reliability now carries strategic weight. Hyperscaler buying and AI data center buildouts put large volumes of devices into the field quickly, so faults that once surfaced slowly can spread widely. Examples included a capacitor whose orientation let airflow-borne dust cause intermittent shorts, and modular line cards whose weight rose to around 70 pounds, raising warping concerns.

Observability was named as the defensive design pillar teams most often struggle with, since adding diagnostics across chips, intermediate layers and telemetry reporting has become harder. That makes planning for misuse early in a product cycle more important. On AI, the speaker described internal experiments where models were given source code, design documents and schematics to suggest vulnerabilities, and then to chain lower-severity issues into exploit proposals. Results still contained many hallucinations, though some hardware-side ideas were judged interesting. Software release cadence is also shifting toward quarterly updates.

The discussion questioned whether hardware and software security remain separate disciplines, and suggested AI tools be used early in testing so easy issues are caught before human testers spend time on them. Greater open visibility into hardware designs was presented as helpful. The closing answers flagged co-packaged optics and management interfaces as areas where new exploit surfaces may emerge.

talks.title: Hacking 5G From Radio Security To The Apis
talks.teaser: Walks through testing 5G radio, core and API layers for misconfigurations, with demos of automated API pentesting tools.
talks.summary:
The talk, given by a radio security specialist, argues that 5G is not as opaque as many assume and still carries real weaknesses. It traces the evolution from 1G to 5G, showing how each generation changed the trust model, and argues that 5G swapped old telecom weaknesses for new ones rather than removing them. It separates non-standalone 5G, a 5G radio on a 4G core, from standalone 5G with a new core built on service-based interfaces.

On the radio side, the speaker described checking which ciphering and integrity settings a cell actually enforces, using a modem and a software-defined radio with an open-source 5G stack to act as a device or base station. Earlier engagements on the core network found isolation gaps that exposed management servers and subscriber secrets. A separate external test mapped exposed addresses to reach a gateway management console and export subscriber keys. A malformed GTP packet was also shown to crash a user plane function.

For service-based interfaces, the speaker presented an automated Burp Suite extension that discovers functions, dumps credentials and produces a report. Open RAN, which typically runs on Kubernetes, was shown to be exposed through misconfigured clusters where pods could be listed and commands run, and through an open chart repository where a malicious xApp could be planted. The talk closed with the Open Gateway network APIs developed with the GSMA and Linux Foundation, which expose data such as device location and SIM swap checks to developers. The takeaway is that 5G is not inherently secure, and its risk moves to new interfaces that deserve the same testing as web applications.

talks.title: Glitching Edge Ai Fault Injection On Npus, Automated By LLM Agents
talks.teaser: Shows how voltage glitching can fool an NPU running object detection, then how an LLM agent automates the fault campaign.
talks.summary:
The talk covers voltage fault injection against a neural processing unit on a Rockchip board, where a convolutional neural network performs object detection on camera frames. The speakers used a power glitcher, an oscilloscope and an EM probe to time glitches to the later stages of the network, aiming at its backbone and head. Across about 4,700 manual experiments, glitches shifted confidence scores, dropped or added objects, and in some runs produced a high-confidence detection of something absent from the image. The object tracker running on the CPU was also disrupted by the faulted output.

The second half asks how much of a fault injection campaign an LLM agent can handle. A supervisor model checks system health and decides when optimization may proceed, while an optimizer model proposes new glitch parameters. A Python layer controls the hardware, and an MCP server exposes instruments and returns structured summaries instead of raw data. The setup was first validated on a PIN-check target, where the agent narrowed the glitch window using a Welch's t-test over EM traces. A coding agent later sped up the rig five times by finding and patching a trigger signal in the target binary.

On the NPU, agent-driven campaigns reached the target outcome in an average of 1471 attempts, at about $3.95 per success and roughly 2.26 million prompt tokens, compared with 22,000 attempts for the manual run. The speakers' lessons were that more feedback is not automatically better, that domain context and right-sized evidence matter, and that soft goals tend to be ignored. They argue that AI can be used as a tool against hardware, and that hardware may become the next weak link as software flaws get patched.

talks.title: Supercharging The Picoemp With Surplus High Voltage Supplies
talks.teaser: Shows how a surplus high-voltage supply boosts a low-cost electromagnetic fault injection tool's pulse rate and voltage.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at the PicoEMP, a low-cost open-source electromagnetic fault injection tool, and asks how far it can be pushed. The speaker had used it on an automotive chip, where a rate of about one pulse per second and a coil voltage capped near 250 volts made the work very slow. Commercial chip shouters offer much better control but cost around $5,000, leaving little in between. The idea was to feed the coil from a used electrophoresis power supply, found for roughly $70, that reaches 3,000 volts at 400 watts.

Getting that supply to work came first. It entered an error state without a resistive load and had to be power-cycled, so the speaker bypassed the protection by connecting to a sensing board inside the unit. Using a function generator, a separate trigger board and an H-field probe on an oscilloscope, the modified PicoEMP produced clean pulses at 500 volts and 100 pulses per second. It then ran at 1,000 pulses per second for about 24 minutes with a fan, reaching around 140C. Voltage control was added by logging the supply's control protocol with a logic analyzer and writing a driver on a Pico board that builds an interpolated lookup table.

The speaker concluded that this setup does not replace a chip shouter, which has better pulse control, repeatability and thermal design. It is better seen as a second rig for hobbyists and for multi-pulse glitch chains, and the full build could be done for under $250 excluding a motion platform. The talk closed with a reminder to treat high voltage with respect and to check a supply's maximum voltage before buying one.

talks.title: Security Analysis Of Bluetooth Channel Sounding Protocol And Implementations
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding Security Analysis Of Bluetooth Channel Sounding Protocol And Implementations.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk, security consultant Sultan analyzes the Bluetooth Channel Sounding protocol, introduced in Bluetooth 6.0 to provide secure distance bounding and high-precision ranging. While traditionally distance bounding has leveraged Ultra-Wideband (UWB) or relied on insecure Bluetooth RSSI and Angle of Arrival (AoA) techniques, Channel Sounding aims to deliver secure distance estimates using existing 2.4 GHz radio hardware without substantial cost increases. The technology is primarily targeted at access control systems such as phone-as-a-key for automotive and building entry.

### Key Topics
- **Ranging Modes**: The core specification defines Mode 1 (packet-based round-trip time of flight), Mode 2 (multicarrier phase-based ranging across 72 channels), and Mode 3 (a combination of both). Mode 0 measures crystal frequency offsets between initiator and reflector.
- **Packet-Based Ranging (Mode 1)**: Employs CS sync packets with 32-bit access addresses and optional 32-to-128 bit sounding or random sequences generated by an AES-based pseudo-random number generator (PRNG). This gives 32 to 160 bits of pseudo-random data per packet, preventing simple early-response spoofing.
- **Phase-Based Ranging (Mode 2)**: Measures phase shift and amplitude variations across multiple frequencies in the 2.4 GHz band to infer time of flight via phase slope. Because unmodulated tones carry little entropy, it relies on a single-bit pseudo-random "extension slot" per step where a tone may or may not be transmitted.
- **Multipath Handling Algorithms**: To separate direct line-of-sight paths from multipath reflections, implementations analyze the sparse frequency response using Inverse Fast Fourier Transform (IFFT), the Multiple Signal Classification (MUSIC) algorithm, or trained neural networks.

### Technical Details & Implementation Flaws
Although Channel Sounding contains primitives intended for security, Sultan identifies critical architectural and implementation deficiencies across major vendor SDKs (TI, Nordic Semiconductor, NXP, and Silicon Labs):
1. **Lack of Specification Mandates**: The Bluetooth specification defines measurement primitives but leaves the method of combining data and calculating final distance to vendors. It also fails to mandate how security signals should be validated.
2. **Precision vs. Security Mismatch**: Packet-based ranging offers strong cryptographic protection against spoofing but suffers from extremely poor distance precision (~37.5 meters per sample period at common 4 MHz sampling rates) due to narrow channel bandwidth. Conversely, phase-based ranging delivers the necessary centimeter-level precision but has minimal entropy.
3. **Discarding Security Primitives**: In practice, vendor SDKs prioritize phase-based measurements and either omit, disable by default, or discard packet-based estimates. None of the examined implementations cross-validate phase measurements against packet time-of-flight.
4. **Ignored Extension Slots**: While hardware measures extension slots and reports their presence/absence over the Host Controller Interface (HCI), higher-layer SDK stacks completely discard extension slot data, leaving phase-based ranging vulnerable to tone-injection and phase-manipulation attacks.
5. **Absence of NATAM**: The Normalized Attack Detector Metric (NATAM), designed to detect Early Detect Late Commit (EDLC) attacks via cross-correlation or harmonic analysis, is optional in the specification and was not implemented by any evaluated vendor.

### Takeaways
Despite marketing claims promoting Channel Sounding as a secure ranging solution, current real-world implementations take the path of least resistance. Vendors default to unverified phase-based ranging for high precision while ignoring extension slots and omitting NATAM. Consequently, existing implementations fail to provide true secure distance bounding against active RF adversaries.

talks.title: Cross Talk Vulnerabilities In Cloud Based Quantum Computers
talks.teaser: Demonstrates how crosstalk from a co-located malicious circuit can corrupt results on superconducting quantum processors in the cloud.
talks.summary:
The talk examines security weaknesses in quantum computers accessed through the cloud, with the focus on the quantum processor rather than its classical control hardware. Once a user submits circuits, the speaker said, there are few security checks, and the analog pulses that drive the qubits cannot be protected with encryption the way network traffic can. Interest is rising as machines approach 100 to 200 qubits and companies build algorithms for them.

The core subject is crosstalk between circuits sharing one chip. Superconducting qubits sit in a fixed layout, and activity on one can leak noise into others, sometimes non-adjacent ones. Experiments on real IBM machines showed that an attacker circuit built from repeated controlled-NOT gates, with delays added so the compiler would not strip them out, lowered the chance of the correct answer for a victim running Grover's search, and nearly flipped the dominant output of a Bernstein-Vazirani run. Later work described a two-sided attack that flipped an idle victim qubit and a pulse-frequency attack in which 20 to 30 attacker qubits drove a victim from nearly all zeros to about 20 percent zeros.

The closing section covered proposed defenses such as isolation, scheduling and pattern detection, none yet built into commercial systems. Multi-tenancy is not publicly supported, so the experiments controlled both sides. The practical takeaway is that a single user loading a nonsense circuit can still corrupt another user's results, and that modular or chiplet designs may bring new crosstalk questions.

talks.title: NL 2025 | Breaking The Illusion Of Security: Rowhammer Is Back On DDR5 by Patrick Jattke
talks.teaser: Shows DDR5 memory is still open to Rowhammer bit flips, using custom bus-probing and fault-injection tools.
talks.summary:
This talk presents three projects from the speaker's PhD on Rowhammer, a bit-flip attack on DRAM, with a focus on DDR5. It starts by recalling how DDR4 mitigations were bypassed with more advanced hammering patterns. Random patterns tried on ten DDR5 modules produced bit flips on only one, raising the question of how well DDR5 is protected.

Maxi is an oscilloscope-based platform that captures and decodes DRAM commands on DDR4 and DDR5 buses. With it, the team found that the RFM feature was not used by the tested client CPUs, that Intel systems used fine granularity refresh, and that a new mitigation appeared on a Raptor Lake machine. Refold is a fault injection platform that alters command bits through a microcontroller and a custom interposer. On two modules from Micron and Samsung it measured an HCmin of about 16k, comparable to DDR4. Phoenix reverse engineered the mitigation on SK hynix DDR5 modules and found a state that repeats every 128 refresh intervals. Using longer patterns and a self-correcting refresh synchronisation method, it caused thousands of bit flips across 15 modules.

The main takeaway is that Rowhammer attacks on DDR5 became harder but remain possible. Mitigations now leave fewer blind spots, yet effective patterns span hundreds to thousands of refresh intervals rather than the dozens seen on DDR4. The speaker argues that these results depended on building custom measurement platforms and expertise, and that making such tools accessible would help other researchers enter the field.

talks.title: NL 2025: Modern memory error exploitation via speculative execution attacks: Anil Kurmus
talks.teaser: Shows how speculative execution can bypass stack canaries and kernel mutexes, turning memory bugs into data leaks.
talks.summary:
The talk explores combining memory error exploitation with speculative execution attacks. It contrasts the sequential view programmers expect with how a modern CPU predicts and runs instructions, then recaps how a mispredicted bounds check can expose data. A speculative write over a return address can also redirect control flow, but only within the speculation window.

The first case study defeats stack canaries. A stack overflow in libpng is normally caught by the canary check, yet that check is a conditional branch the CPU can mispredict. The attack needed an eviction set, a shared flush-and-reload channel, trained gadgets, and an overflow that corrupts the return path only speculatively. Go, LLVM CFI and GCC's vtable verification responded differently to similar bypass attempts.

The second case, Ghost Race, targets concurrent use-after-free in the Linux kernel. A mutex built on compare-exchange does not serialize speculation, so a null check after a free can be passed speculatively. A timer interrupt followed by a flood of extra interrupts widened the window, and the freed object was reclaimed to leak data at about 12 kilobytes per second. For attackers, speculation can supply a leak when memory-error routes are blocked, though it does not grant direct code execution. For defenders, the speaker weighed preventing speculation at a performance cost, blocking covert channels, which is hard, and segregating secrets across layers, which the speaker favours. Whether these attacks occur in the wild was left open.

talks.title: NL 2025: When Memory Lies: Breaching Processor Security via Rogue Memory Modules
talks.teaser: Shows how rogue memory modules and a cheap interposer can alias memory and undermine SEV attestation and scalable SGX enclaves.
talks.summary:
The talk shows how the memory subsystem can be manipulated to break trusted execution environments such as AMD SEV and Intel SGX and TDX. It explains why scalable designs lack memory freshness guarantees, which leaves room for replay attacks that a privileged attacker can exploit. The core idea is that a modified DIMM advertises an extra row bit in its SPD metadata, so the BIOS maps two physical addresses to the same memory cells. This aliasing lets an attacker read ciphertext and write it back later, and a live demo showed a VM's memory being rolled back.

The speakers applied this to SEV's launch measurement, capturing a hash and replaying it so attestation reports an expected value for a modified image. A cheap interposer on the SPD chip, costing about $10, is one way to do it, and a software route works on certain DIMMs whose SPD lock bit is unset, which do not fit server systems. Intel and AMD added boot-time alias checks and ECC-based metadata, but these run only once at boot. A runtime interposer that switches one DDR4 row address bit bypassed that check, enabling plaintext reads from scalable SGX enclaves that share one key, and extraction of the provisioning key used for quoting enclaves.

The takeaway is that boot-time checks are not enough, and robust protection needs strong integrity and freshness in memory encryption. In the Q&A, the speakers noted that DDR5 multicycle commands and parity checks make single-bit faults harder, and that soldered LPDDR is harder to interpose.

talks.title: NL 2025: Hacking to the Gate(way): Take Over Samsung SmartThings with a Single API Call
talks.teaser: Shows how a smart home hub was taken over through firmware extraction, a secure-boot bypass and a single crafted API request.
talks.summary:
The talk follows a DEVCORE research team as it attacks a Samsung SmartThings-family smart home hub, a device it targeted at Pwn2Own Ireland 2024. Initial port scanning revealed only one HTTPS port that returned 503 errors, so the team opened the hub, read its embedded storage chip after several attempts at desoldering it, and extracted the file system. Once that was decrypted, the key-protection chain led to a bootloader whose signature check did not tie the signed configuration to the image it loaded. Abusing that flaw let the researchers boot a modified ramdisk.

From there the focus shifted to a local API protected by token checks. A hidden debug command produced a valid token, and the device identifier could stand in for the user identifier, which let the team reset the hub with a single request and rebind it to their own account. The serial number needed for binding leaked through the Thread network name and mDNS, and later through a certificate field after the vendor changed those outputs. For code execution, they abused an edge driver that runs Lua, restored a removed os.execute function through debug.getupvalue, and then chained argument and command injection in a core dump handler.

The demo showed a reset, a rebind and a malicious edge driver serving a web page on the hub in about five minutes. The takeaway is that a security label means little until a product is examined directly, and that basic methods can still uncover serious flaws. The speaker noted the vendor had already fixed the issue by the time of a later retest.

talks.title: NL2025: Boot Vectors & Double Glitches: Bypassing RP2350s Secure Boot by Marius & Thomas
talks.teaser: Walks through how RP2350 secure boot was bypassed with vector-boot abuse and double glitches on a Pico 2 chip.
talks.summary:
Marius and Thomas Roth discuss their work on the RP2350 microcontroller used in the Raspberry Pi Pico 2. The chip pairs Arm Cortex-M33 and RISC-V cores with glitch detectors, a redundancy co-processor, one-time programmable (OTP) memory and secure boot. The speakers explain how a DEF CON hacking challenge offered a prize for reading 16 bytes of secret OTP data, and how ready-to-glitch boards were handed to attendees.

Marius describes a vector boot path reachable through power manager registers that runs before signature checks. A reboot type that the non-secure USB bootloader should not be able to request could be reached when a compiler layout let a single skipped compare or branch fall through into it. Running the boot ROM at a lower clock than the glitch detectors were tuned for opened a window for glitches. He reports that this path was never completed end to end. Thomas covers a double glitch against the OTP lock progression function, which runs twice and adds random delays of up to 256 cycles. After scanning the die with electromagnetic fault injection, he found a spot that bypassed the detector reliably, and long runs were needed to hit both timings.

The talk also reviews three other reported attacks: a voltage fault on the OTP power-on state machine, laser fault injection on a chip with its backside removed, and focused ion beam extraction of antifuse bits. Raspberry Pi fixed the issues in a later stepping. The speakers' lessons cover broad fault models that include external and internal IP, layered defenses, complex boot paths, inexpensive laser setups, and bounties that widen coverage. A second challenge targeting the AES side channel offers $20,000.

talks.title: NL 2025: Watch Out! A Security Case Study Of A COROS Sports Watch
talks.teaser: Shows how a popular COROS sports watch leaks data, exposes account tokens and crashes over Bluetooth Low Energy.
talks.summary:
The talk examines a widely worn COROS sports watch and asks what an attacker within Bluetooth range could do without physical access. The research found that the watch uses legacy Just Works pairing and adds no application-layer encryption, so its traffic can be eavesdropped on or altered. On Android, the companion app skips bonding entirely, which allowed an impersonated fake watch to capture the phone's account API token without any user interaction.

The presenter also showed that the watch accepts injected notifications while disconnected and can be made to reset or trigger a find-my-device alert. Blackbox fuzzing with Radamsa found two inputs that crash the watch. One came from a malformed notification structure, and the other came from a short message that caused an integer underflow and an out-of-bounds read. Firmware was obtained from the HTTP-based update process, and reversing the bootloader in Ghidra with SVD files revealed a second CPU and the firmware parsing logic.

Disclosure was slow, with fixes initially scheduled months away. After the advisories were published, a tech journalist's coverage added public pressure, and the vendor confirmed that all of its devices were affected and moved to prioritize the fixes. The takeaway for practitioners is that wearables with weak Bluetooth pairing can leak health and location data, and that vendor response timelines are worth scrutinising.

talks.title: NL 2025: Glitching Google's TV Streamer From Adb To Root
talks.teaser: Niek Timmers examines NL 2025: Glitching Google's TV Streamer From Adb To Root.
talks.summary:
### Overview

Nick Tmers from Railize presents a fault injection attack on Google's TV Streamer, demonstrating how electromagnetic glitches can corrupt CPU instructions to bypass kernel security checks and escalate privileges from an unprivileged ADB shell to root. Despite achieving a root shell, the attack is ultimately limited by SELinux enforcement.

### Key Topics

**Reconnaissance & Access**
- Google TV Streamer uses a quad-core ARM CPU at 1.8 GHz with DDR memory, eMMC storage, and external Wi-Fi/Ethernet chips
- Security posture similar to Pixel 9: secure boot, Android kernel hardening, and trusted execution environment (but no external Titan security chip)
- ADB debugging enabled via developer options; custom unprivileged code executable via Android Studio
- Firmware downloads obtained by interfacing with Google's OTA servers, yielding unencrypted boot and system partitions
- Kernel source and debug symbols publicly available from Google, including generic kernel image (GKI) with matching SHA-1 hash

**Fault Injection Setup**
- Electromagnetic fault injection (EMFI) technique using a Keysite glitch device to generate high-current pulses through a coil
- Setup: XYZ stage for probe positioning, USB control for power cycling resets, minimal wiring
- Target: corrupting CPU instructions during execution to bypass software security models

**Characterization Phase**
- Two-phase scanning of chip surface: coarse scan (10 power levels across 20×20 grid, ~40 minutes) identifies responsive locations; fine-grained scan targets those locations
- Custom test code runs in user-space loop, incrementing counter to 10,000; altered counter values written to disk indicate successful faults
- Fault models observed: instruction skipping, instruction corruption (changing operands or entire instruction), bit flips in instruction encoding
- Different sensitive locations per CPU core (quad-core dependency confirms CPU targeting)

**Privilege Escalation Attack**
- Target: setuid syscall's capability check for CAP_SETUID, which blocks unprivileged processes from changing UID to root
- Attack code continuously issues setuid(0,0,0) syscalls; glitch injection bypasses kernel capability check at random power levels
- Success indicated by process spawning root-owned Telnetd; attacker connects via Telnet for root shell
- Attack timeline: minutes to ~1 hour execution time despite Android boot overhead

**Results & Limitations**
- Successfully achieved root shell access with `id` command confirmation
- SELinux still enforced; cannot read /proc/kmem or flash memory (LSM hooks intact)
- Ability to read /proc/syslog by bypassing its permission checks suggests other syscall attacks possible
- Full device compromise not achieved; boot-level attacks identified as more powerful alternative

### Technical Details

- **Instruction Corruption Example**: Single bit flip in ARM64 instruction encoding (e.g., `0x21` → `0x20`) changes instruction semantics (operand or operation type)
- **Fault Parameters**: Power/current magnitude drives EM field strength; precise timing and location required for reproducibility
- **Kernel Protection Layers**: Capability checks, SELinux hooks, and Linux Security Modules; fault injection circumvents capability checks but not SELinux
- **Device Reset**: USB power cycling used for state recovery after error conditions

### Takeaways

- Google TV Streamer's CPU vulnerable to EM fault injection despite >1 GHz clock speeds
- Runtime privilege escalation via fault injection feasible on Android with ≤1 hour attack windows
- Software security architectures fail when executing on hardware lacking fault injection countermeasures
- SELinux provides secondary defense that withstood tested attack; full compromise likely requires kernel exploitation or alternative attack vectors
- Google and MediaTek acknowledged vulnerability as inherent to platform; not device-specific
- Boot-time attacks likely more efficient than runtime attacks for full compromise
- Demo available at Keysite booth showing live exploitation on unmodified Google TV Streamer running latest firmware

talks.title: NL'25: Exploitation Of Transient Execution Vulns To Leak Private Data From Public Clouds
talks.teaser: Shows how an attacker VM can leak a victim's TLS key through transient execution flaws on AWS and Google Cloud.
talks.summary:
The talk presents L1TF Reloaded, an attack that starts from an attacker virtual machine on dedicated cloud hosts and leaks the TLS private key of a neighbouring victim VM running an nginx web server. The speaker argues that critics often dismiss microarchitectural attacks as slow, noisy, or lab-only, and that this underestimates the risk. The exploit combines an L1 terminal fault primitive with a half-Spectre gadget in KVM, which lets the attacker read whatever data the hypervisor can see.

The team worked as a black-box attacker with no internal access, testing on a local Skylake server and on Google Cloud and AWS. Because the leak is slow and error-prone, the exploit walks host kernel structures by pointer chasing, checks each step for sanity, and backtracks after a mistake. A page table walker translates addresses so it can follow pointers inside the guest. Across 28 runs, 25 recovered the exact key, with an average runtime of 14 hours, of which about 11 hours went to initial setup. When every other core was filled with noisy VMs, all 10 runs still returned the correct key, averaging 15 hours. On AWS the attack reached host kernel memory but not guest data, while on Google it also read guest memory.

The speaker describes AWS's exclusive page frame ownership and Google's address space isolation as design-level defenses that remove guest memory from the hypervisor's view. The main takeaway is that individual microarchitectural leaks are unreliable, but robust end-to-end exploits can still be built on them, so spot mitigations may not be enough.

talks.title: NL 2025: [Keynote] Towards End-User Verifiable Silicon
talks.teaser: Presents infrared inspection of soldered chips as a way to verify silicon in finished products without destroying them.
talks.summary:
The talk argues for higher assurance silicon, borrowing the idea of structural correctness from projects such as Fiat Crypto, a formally proven compiler for elliptic curve code. It contrasts this with chip buyers today, who must rely on labels, certifications and designer claims. The speaker walks through supply chain risks, including gray markets, customs checkpoints and tampered products returned to distributors, and shows a decapped chip whose internals did not match its markings.

The central technique is IRIS, infrared in situ verification. It images a chip through its exposed backside after the chip is soldered to a board, so the device under inspection can still be used. It works on flip-chip and wafer-level packages with thinned, lightly doped substrates, but not on plastic-molded packages. Inexpensive microscope cameras with the infrared filter removed can do basic imaging, and a CNC-controlled rig can produce repeatable reference images. Example images show a touchscreen controller's converter channels and standard cells from a 130 nm design, and the speaker notes that electrical scan chain tests can be paired with optical checks.

The talk closes with open silicon. It argues that mature 28 nm nodes make open-source tape-outs economically viable, and describes adding an open RISC-V core and a software-defined I/O block to a commercial chip, along with RTL that allows simulation-based debugging. Practical takeaways include asking manufacturers for inspectable packaging, building shared databases of chip images, and helping find bugs in open designs.

talks.title: USA 2025: Extracting Protected Flash With STM32-TraceRip
talks.teaser: Shows how STM32 readout protection can be bypassed by reconstructing flash contents from CRC state held in SRAM.
talks.summary:
The speakers started with a low-cost STM32 G0 microcontroller found on a refrigerator control board and needed its flash contents, which were locked by level 1 readout protection. They reviewed published bypasses for older STM32 parts, such as glitching the readout protection, abusing the flash breakpoint unit, and abusing instruction fetches from the vector table. On this G0 those attacks no longer worked, but SRAM stayed readable even while the flash was locked.

Their approach relied on a CRC integrity check whose running state sat in SRAM. Reading that state at different delays after reset let them infer the bytes being processed. The published research code forced an SRAM copy that did not match typical CRC implementations, so they wrote a tool around OpenOCD on a Raspberry Pi Pico with a custom debug command to capture processor registers at varying delays. The captures were noisy and non-monotonic. Mark Omo and James Rowley then reconstructed the CRC16-XMODEM algorithm from register behaviour, pruned conflicting byte guesses, and recovered the application flash after recovering the program counter from the stack in SRAM.

The talk closed with limitations: clock drift during boot, a missing first portion of flash due to startup timing, and capture runs taking several days. The main takeaway is that ST's protection model assumes leaking processor state does not leak flash, but executed code reveals flash contents. The speakers said the same readout scheme appears across the STM32 range they tested, including the F0, F1, G0 and C0.

talks.title: USA 2025
talks.teaser: A short interview explores agentic AI, output validation, robotics, and an open-source home robot trained with depth cameras.
talks.summary:
The conversation opens with a forward-looking question about what artificial intelligence might produce next. The respondent points to science and research automation as a major direction, where models could help tackle larger problems and surface new ways to apply technology.

The discussion then turns to how large language models might evolve beyond single-shot answers. Agentic systems that plan and execute multiple steps are framed as both incremental and genuinely new compared with one-off responses. Parallel themes include validating model outputs before they are trusted, and robotics enabled by improved computer vision, speech interfaces, and depth sensing that can map physical spaces.

The close centers on a personal open-source robot inspired by the Mobile Aloha project, using depth cameras and repeated demonstration so the machine infers object relationships instead of blindly replaying motions. The presenter describes a wheeled, multi-arm unit used at home, experiments with hands-free training via a spatial computing headset, and lighthearted notes on keeping bedroom doors closed for safety.

talks.title: NL 2024: Rowhammer to GhostWrite Adv Exploitation & Discovery of HW Bugs, Fabian & Lukas
talks.teaser: Covers three CPU and memory hardware bugs that break isolation, and how differential fuzzing uncovered one of them.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a scenario: an app that looked safe quietly leaks passwords, which raises the question of whether the hardware underneath is at fault. The speakers cover three bugs: Rowhammer, a cache-discard attack on an AMD encrypted virtual machine, and GhostWrite, a flaw in a RISC-V processor.

Rowhammer repeatedly accesses neighbouring DRAM rows until bits flip. It is slow and limited to flipping bits, but it can be aimed at data structures, program code, page tables or cryptographic keys. The cache-discard attack abuses an instruction that drops modified cache lines without writing them back, which lets an attacker revert the protected machine's state. The speakers used it to bypass sudo's root check and an OpenSSH password check by manipulating return addresses. Microcode updates or hardware fixes mitigate it. GhostWrite is a vector store on a RISC-V chip that writes to physical memory regardless of isolation, enabling root access through sudo within cycles. The only mitigation disables the vector extension, costing up to 33% overhead and about half of the CPU's instruction features.

The team found GhostWrite with differential fuzzing: identical random instruction sequences were sent to several RISC-V cores and their results compared against the specification. The takeaway is that hardware is the root of trust, so quality control and configurable hardware matter, and security-critical code should default to an unauthenticated state.

talks.title: NL 2024: DramaQueen Revisiting Side Channels in DRAM Flipped by Ben Gras
talks.teaser: Shows how uncached crypto code can still leak its secret key through timing of DRAM row-buffer accesses.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at classic side channels, where a program's memory activity reveals secret data, such as the bit pattern of a scalar in elliptic-curve point multiplication. The speaker notes that CPU vendors often treat constant-time coding as the software's responsibility. The speaker then considers a shortcut: an existing cache-immunity framework that places security-sensitive code and data on uncached pages, combined with disabling hyper-threading, so the usual cache and sibling-thread channels disappear.

The speaker then shows that DRAM is itself a shared resource. Each access goes through a row buffer, so reads to a different row in the same bank are slower than reads to another bank. An attacker who repeatedly times one address in the same bank can see latency spikes caused by the victim's uncached accesses. Using ground-truth runs, the attacker trains a machine learning classifier to tell doubling steps from addition steps, then recovers the key bits from the noisy trace. In most experiments only very few guesses were needed to reach the real key, while the worst case ran into the millions.

The conclusion is that hiding from caches made the leak easier to read, not harder. Partitioning the memory controller per requester would weaken the signal, but contention on DRAM buses would probably remain. The takeaway for practitioners is that a proposed "safe mode" which turns off caches should not be trusted until DRAM is treated as a shared resource as well.

talks.title: NL 2024: Looking back in 10 Years of RowHammer
talks.teaser: Traces a decade of Rowhammer exploits, from early bit-flip papers to attacks on browsers, ECC memory and TRR defenses.
talks.summary:
The talk walks through a decade of Rowhammer research, year by year. It opens with the 2014 work showing that repeated accesses to neighbouring DRAM rows can flip bits, a result first dismissed as a reliability issue, and the 2015 follow-up that turned double-sided hammering into a route to browser sandbox exploits and page-table corruption. Early attacks depended on physical address information, which was later restricted, so later researchers used timing side channels and large pages in JavaScript to recover the row layout.

From 2016 onward the speaker follows exploits across new targets. These include a browser attack that combined page deduplication with bit flips, an Android exploit on ARM that produced a deterministic self-referencing page table, guest virtual machines, and SGX enclaves where flipped bits in a setuid binary could grant root. Other cases cover ECC memory, where flips could be made undetectable, the TRR mitigation defeated by decoy accesses, GPU-assisted hammering through WebGL, and network-driven hammering over RDMA. The later sections cover RowPress as a separate physical effect and 2024 work that extended the technique to RISC-V and other platforms.

The talk closes with a non-malicious use, binding a binary to a single device by deliberately flipping bits in its jump instructions. The main takeaway is that each mitigation has been bypassed with more complex access patterns, so Rowhammer should be treated as an ongoing risk rather than a solved problem.

talks.title: NL 2024: ARM MTE: The End Of Memory Corruption? Not Yet
talks.teaser: Shows how Arm's MTE memory tags can be leaked through speculative execution and cache timing, enabling bypasses in Chrome.
talks.summary:
Arm's Memory Tagging Extension (MTE) guards against memory corruption by attaching a 4-bit tag to pointers and memory, faulting when they disagree. This talk asks whether that ends the problem. Because tags are random, a blind attacker crashes on most attempts, so a reliable tag leak is the key. The researchers combine a cache timing side channel with speculative execution: a speculative access with a mismatched tag raises a fault that is discarded, yet the cache state it leaves can still be measured.

Two gadgets were identified. Tic Tac V1 uses several mismatched loads followed by a gap of about ten cycles, after which a test access slows down. Ablation experiments on the processor pointed to hardware data prefetching as the root cause, with speculative execution also contributing. A patent review suggested a "wrong path" mechanism could explain the periodic behavior. Tic Tac V2 instead relies on store-to-load forwarding being blocked after a tag fault.

Applied to Google Chrome, the same idea used a V8 array access that speculatively passed its bounds check, leaking tags from the renderer. With the leaked tags, a heap overflow could be carried out without a crash. Vendor responses differed: Arm did not treat tags as secrets, Google's Android team called it a hardware flaw while still seeing MTE as strong, and the V8 team placed it outside its sandbox model. Possible fixes trade performance against leakage, and software can scan binaries for gadgets. The takeaway is that MTE tags should not be relied on as secrets yet.

talks.title: NL 2024: Byepervisor: How We Broke The PS5 Hypervisor
talks.teaser: Walks through two hypervisor flaws that yield the first public full break on PS5 firmware 2.70 and lower, with live homebrew demo.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with how PlayStation 5 hardening exceeds the prior console generation: execute-only memory for user and kernel text, nested paging under AMD virtualization, and hypervisor interception of sensitive control and machine state registers. Prior community techniques—direct platform security processor mailbox traffic, interrupt descriptor table hijacking for soft hooks, and a disclosed user-mutex kernel bug—extended research reach but stopped short of dissolving hypervisor enforcement.

The core work targets early hypervisor revisions where the monitor still lives inside the kernel image. Guest-reachable VM exit handler jump tables can be made writable through page-table mirroring, enabling hypervisor entry hijack and register-oriented programming chains that zero nested-paging and guest execute-trap bits in the virtual machine control block. A separate initialization flaw ties shared QA debug flags to nested page table builds; after suspend and resume those flags reload from hibernation data while hypervisor setup runs again, leaving kernel text readable and writable without fighting nested permissions—reducing offset hunting from dozens of values to a handful.

A live rest-mode cycle demonstrates patched kernel hooks loading homebrew. The speaker contrasts firmware 3.0’s separated hypervisor with these embedded designs, notes that public code and tooling will ship under a PS5 development organization, and argues that readable kernel text unlocks API-level reversing, easier exploit iteration, and paths resembling post–kernel-exploit PlayStation 4 research.

talks.title: NL 2024: EL3XIR: Fuzzing COTS Secure Monitors
talks.teaser: Marcel Busch analyzes NL 2024: EL3XIR: Fuzzing COTS Secure Monitors.
talks.summary:
Overview: ARM TrustZone forms the security backbone of mobile devices. TrustZone-based Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs) facilitate security-sensitive tasks like user authentication and disk encryption. As such, bugs in the TEE software stack may compromise the entire system’s integrity. Unfortunately, modern dynamic analysis techniques (like fuzzing) typically used to identify and eliminate those bugs cannot be effectively applied to TEE components. In this talk, we introduce EL3XIR, a framework to effectively rehost and fuzz the secure monitor firmware layer of proprietary TrustZone-based TEEs. Wh
Details: ile other approaches have focused on naively rehosting or fuzzing Trusted Applications or the TEE OS, EL3XIR targets the highly-privileged but underexplored secure monitor and its unique challenges. Secure monitors expose complex functionality through diverse secure monitor calls that may depend on multiple peripherals. In this talk, we share how we overcame these challenges regarding input injection and peripheral emulation for several targets to find a total of 34 bugs, out of which 17 were classified as security critical. Affected vendors confirmed 14 of these bugs, and as a result, EL3XIR was assigned six CVEs.

talks.title: NL 2023 | Understanding Physics To Break AES With Side-channel Hardware -Stephan & Roman
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for NL 2023 | Understanding Physics To Break AES With Side-channel Hardware -Stephan & Roman.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation, embedded systems/electronics designer Matthew and security researcher Roman examine side-channel hardware setups from an electronic design perspective. Originating from Matthew's critique of Roman's test setup while repeating a side-channel attack on a Jade crypto wallet, the talk bridges physical electronics engineering with cryptographic side-channel analysis. The speakers demonstrate how wiring, decoupling capacitors, probe noise, and power supplies directly impact correlation power analysis (CPA) on hardware AES implementations, targeting an ESP32 microcontroller with a built-in cryptographic engine.

### Key Topics
- **Impact of Wires and Inductance**: Evaluating how wire length and loop area introduce parasitic inductance, which attenuates high-frequency current content and degrades correlation quality.
- **Decoupling Capacitors**: Investigating the common practice of removing decoupling capacitors to prevent high-frequency operational currents from bypassing external current-measurement instrumentation.
- **Target Clock vs. Leakage Bandwidth**: Analyzing filtering cutoffs to discover the optimal frequency band for recovering AES keys, contrasting system clock speed with cryptographic leakage frequencies.
- **Measurement Hardware and Ground Loops**: Comparing measurement instruments (differential probes, current probes, LISNs, shunt resistors) and solving ground loops and oscilloscope input noise.
- **Low-Cost Custom Hardware Solutions**: Designing accessible, budget-friendly low-side and inline side-channel acquisition hardware.

### Technical Details
- **Wiring and Parasitic Inductance**: Testing signal transmission from 1 MHz to 500 MHz confirmed that larger wiring loops increase inductance and introduce up to 10 dB of high-frequency attenuation. In time-domain AES measurements on the ESP32, connecting the target directly via solder joints preserved high-frequency spikes and allowed key recovery at 50,000 traces. Introducing just 2 cm wires significantly damped these transients and forced the Pearson correlation to require far more traces for successful key recovery.
- **Decoupling Capacitors**: Because decoupling capacitors sit near the microcontroller to supply transient switching currents locally, leaving them populated shunts the high frequencies away from the power supply sensing path. While slow operations like ciphertext transfers remained detectable with capacitors present, the actual AES key could not be recovered within 300,000 traces without removing them. However, removing decoupling capacitors means long supply wires can cause severe voltage dips, potentially causing target reboots.
- **Bandwidth and Filtering**: Even though the ESP32 CPU runs at 160 MHz, low-pass filtering experiments revealed that the highest Pearson correlation coefficient and clearest key separation occurred when low-pass filtering from DC to 95 MHz. Adding content between 95 MHz and 100 MHz degraded correlation, proving that high-cost gigahertz measurement equipment is unnecessary.
- **Noise Optimization and Instrumentation**: Environmental noise, power supply ripple, and probe self-noise hinder trace quality. Standard bench power supplies performed poorly compared to clean battery setups or power supplies conditioned with low-dropout (LDO) regulators. Current probes (limited to ~100 MHz and introducing ~75 µA RMS noise) and differential probes (flat response dominated by ~28 µA RMS noise) performed worse in correlation attacks than custom pre-amplified boards.
- **Custom Acquisition Hardware**: To eliminate ground loops and drown out the oscilloscope's internal noise floor without requiring averaging across acquisitions, Matthew developed two low-cost hardware platforms:
  1. *Low-side board ($125)*: Integrates target power delivery, an on-board shunt resistor, and a two-stage op-amp amplifier with potentiometers for variable gain, achieving up to 1 GHz bandwidth.
  2. *Inline/high-side board ($25)*: Designed to connect in-line across power traces using a balun transformer to isolate DC from high-frequency components, paired with RF amplifiers, avoiding ground loops.
- **EM Side-Channel Applicability**: Addressing an audience question, Matthew explained that removing decoupling capacitors also benefits electromagnetic (EM) side-channel attacks by enlarging the high-frequency current loop path, effectively turning it into a larger loop antenna that radiates stronger EM signals.

### Takeaways
To achieve fast, reliable, and low-cost side-channel key recovery, practitioners should eliminate jumper wires by soldering directly, desolder local decoupling capacitors, power targets via batteries or LDO-filtered supplies, and amplify signals prior to the oscilloscope. Hardware AES on chips like the ESP32 can be broken efficiently using inexpensive secondhand oscilloscopes and custom front-end boards without spending thousands of dollars on high-end differential probes.

talks.title: HW.io NL 03 | Panel: A New Future For IoT Security: Better Solutions And What Did Not Work So Far
talks.teaser: Panelists explain why cost and complexity keep hardware security out of IoT devices, and weigh newer alternatives.
talks.summary:
The panel focuses on what has not worked for IoT security, starting with cost as the main barrier to adding hardware roots of trust to embedded and edge devices used in hospitals, traffic control and smart city infrastructure. Panelists say security is often the first budget item cut, while backward compatibility concerns and the scarcity of skilled engineers slow adoption. One anecdote describes a carmaker still relying on a deprecated TPM 1.2 for provisioning. Software-only protection was described as a false sense of security, with firmware-based trusted modules offered as a cheaper middle ground.

Discussion then turned to newer options: a small secure element built into the main chip to reduce cost and board size, and vendor-managed security stacks that simplify use but require more trust in the supplier. Machine learning was discussed both as a way to harden implementations and as a source of attacks such as adversarial inputs and side-channel leakage. Post-quantum cryptography drew attention because of store-now-decrypt-later risk for long-lived devices such as cars, although larger keys and slower operations raise cost. An audience question on managing keys across hundreds of vehicle controllers led to remarks on key hierarchies and revocation.

The panel closed on updatability, device recovery and ownership after resale, with consumer security labels proposed as a way to reward secure products. The practical takeaway: match protection to the attacker and the device's value, and plan for updates and keys from the start.

talks.title: NL 2023 | Automated Fault Injection Attacks On Embedded Devices
talks.teaser: Details how electromagnetic fault injection can hijack automotive microcontroller firmware without prior knowledge of the code.
talks.summary:
The talk covers automated electromagnetic fault injection against automotive electronic control units. The team first tried voltage glitching, but it required heavy board modification and temperature control, so they switched to EMFI, which needs no changes to the board. Their main target was a gateway ECU built on an automotive-grade NXP microcontroller. Published attacks on similar chips did not work on the real device, and program counter corruption tricks that suit ARM were much harder on PowerPC.

The attack used the standard diagnostic flashing process. Its unlock step relies on repair shop secrets that have leaked publicly, and the erase step happens before the new image is verified, so an attacker could reach about 4 MB of flash with a jump. Exception handlers on this device printed register dumps over UART, which gave the team feedback on each injection. A genetic search algorithm used that feedback to tune coil position, pulse duration, voltage, timing and memory state. It found a working program counter corruption after roughly 10,000 injections on average, at about five per second. The resulting code execution could read the bootloader and re-enable JTAG through configuration records.

The setup cost about 5,000 and worked on five targets from three manufacturers across three architectures. The lesson for practitioners is that fault injection can be cheaper and more automatable than expected when a target emits useful feedback. Suggested mitigations include memory protection unit write or execute rules, running the bootloader inside the HSM, and authenticating every firmware write rather than relying on a single validity flag.

talks.title: NL 2023 | Hacking A Smart Doorbell: An IoT Hacking Guide
talks.teaser: Shows how a smart doorbell's Bluetooth Low Energy setup traffic and unencrypted video stream can be sniffed and abused.
talks.summary:
The talk walks through hacking a cheap smart doorbell that offers Wi-Fi and Bluetooth Low Energy, using a neighbour on the home network as the threat model. It begins with the companion Android app: decompiling it and using Frida to bypass SSL pinning showed encrypted API traffic, and certificate validation held for the main domain. Attention then turns to Bluetooth Low Energy, covering the stack from HCI through ATT and GATT, and how services are enumerated with nRF Connect and Bettercap.

Sniffing the setup session is the core of the attack. Android HCI snoop logs serve as a reference, and a Sniffle receiver on low-cost TI boards captures the pairing traffic over the air. Filtering the ATT write requests exposes the Wi-Fi network name, password and an account name, sent as JSON split across packets because pairing used no link-layer encryption. The camera's Wi-Fi traffic is also unencrypted: ring notifications go over HTTP and the video stream over UDP as JPEG frames, which a short Python script can extract and which can be replaced with other images.

The closing advice is to place the doorbell on a separate Wi-Fi network and set it up somewhere trusted, since its proprietary firmware is hard to change. In Q&A, the speaker noted that the Bluetooth service shuts down after setup, and an audience member said similar devices also send credentials in plain text.

talks.title: NL 2023 | Attacking Vehicle Fleet Management Systems
talks.teaser: Shows how exposed telematics boxes and an unauthenticated MQTT fleet backend let attackers track and control vehicles.
talks.summary:
Two researchers describe a side project that began in 2020 to examine internet-connected automotive embedded devices for flaws that could be exploited remotely at scale. Most of the roughly 18 devices they tested had serious, easy-to-find issues. The talk focuses on two telematics control units used for fleet management, which the speakers said could affect tens of thousands of vehicles.

The first unit, a box sold by a Chinese vendor and installed in heavy machinery such as cranes and trucks, could be rooted physically through an exposed USB connector. Its firmware had no binary protections. The bundled MQTT client pointed to a broker with no authentication, where a binary protocol carried GPS, fuel, and engine data tied to SIM identifiers. Anyone could publish to any vehicle's topic, impersonating vehicles or the backend. The speakers described possible CAN injection and malicious firmware updates but did not test them. Vendor responses were slow, and the flaw was reportedly still present at the last check.

The second case started from exposed brokers found with Shodan and Censys. Documentation and domain names helped identify one fleet-management vendor. Firmware was pulled from an update URL seen in traffic, revealing a command handler that ran without a token check. An ID derived from epoch time let the team achieve code execution on thousands of devices, with access to live video, tire pressure monitoring, and engine immobilization. Disclosure was still open when the talk was given, so the vendor's name was withheld. The takeaway is that fleet backends should require authentication and that exposed IoT services deserve regular external checks.

talks.title: NL2023 | Protect Your Screen From Eavesdropping: Don’t Forget Its Power Supply-Emmanuel
talks.teaser: Shows how screen video can leak through cables, the air and power lines, and what reduces that exposure.
talks.summary:
The talk, given by a presenter from France's national cybersecurity agency, introduces TEMPEST, the risk that electronic equipment leaks data through electromagnetic emissions. It explains the basics of electromagnetic compatibility and how a signal on a data bus can be rebuilt from the emissions a circuit gives off. Leakage can travel over the air, along power lines and along attached conductors. Video is the most exposed because its repetition lets an attacker average captures, and poorly shielded connectors make it worse.

Protection combines equipment grading with building measures. A typical shielded enclosure gives around 100 dB between 10 MHz and 1 GHz, but only while its door stays closed, and higher-performance designs reach 140 dB up to 40 GHz. Pairing strongly shielded equipment with weakly shielded rooms, and the reverse, is presented as a cost-effective trade-off.

Two demonstrations followed. A monitor linked by an unshielded cable was captured over the air with a cheap antenna at short range, and swapping in a shielded cable removed the signal. A clamp on the monitor's power line then recovered its video. In the Q&A, unprotected power lines were said to leak over several hundred metres and air interception to work at tens of metres, while phones need very close range. The takeaway: power supply lines need the same attention as cables, especially in shared buildings.
