talks.title: NL 2023 | Basebanheimer: Now I Am Become Death, The Destroyer Of Chains -Daniel Komaromy
talks.teaser: Walks through cellular baseband exploitation on Samsung and MediaTek modems, from a heap overflow to a Linux kernel pivot.
talks.summary:
The talk covers cellular baseband research aimed at building complete exploit chains, from a zero-click trigger in the modem through to the application processor, on newer Samsung Shannon and MediaTek Dimensity chipsets. For Samsung, the speaker described a heap overflow in LTE session management, where traffic flow template packet filter components were limited only by a formula while a fixed-size array could hold fewer entries. A hidden debug mode that records heap events and produces RAM dumps helped with debugging, and network-controlled filter allocation served as heap shaping. The usual unlinking technique did not fit, because the overflow writes pointers rather than chosen values.

Samsung's user-space radio interface daemon also produced stack and heap overflows quickly, though hardened allocators make them hard to weaponize. On MediaTek Dimensity, the move to a new instruction set required a decompiler plugin and QEMU support before bug hunting. A layer 2 GPRS radio link control bug came from unlimited reassembly of containers across messages, and the vendor advisory described it inaccurately. The talk also explored a direct route into the Linux kernel through shared-memory ring buffers, where an integer wrap and attacker-controlled offsets allowed arbitrary reads and writes. That is effectively full coverage on 32-bit kernels, and on 64-bit kernels scanning for targets was practical. A demo closed the talk.

Several chains remained under embargo or unfinished, so the speaker presented them as work in progress. The main takeaway is that baseband bugs are often reachable through specification gaps and shared-memory bookkeeping, and that public tooling and debugging aids have made these modems far easier to study.

talks.title: NL 2023 | Blue2thprinting: Answering The Question Of 'WTF Am I Even Looking At?!'
talks.teaser: A researcher maps passive and active techniques to identify Bluetooth silicon and firmware from over-the-air signals.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames a practical problem for over-the-air Bluetooth exploitation: when a device is seen on the air, defenders and researchers often cannot tell which controller, module, or firmware revision is inside, so known chip flaws cannot be scoped to real-world products. The speaker outlines a hierarchy from silicon vendors and part numbers through module integrators to thousands of registered product makers, and argues that a single observable field rarely reaches the firmware version that mattered in prior attacks on Texas Instruments, Broadcom, and related stacks.

The core method is “tooth printing,” combining many weak signals rather than one fingerprint. Approaches range from passive advertisement sniffing and everyday inquiry behavior to semi-active link-layer version queries and deliberately malformed classic link management packets crafted with tools such as Spinooth and Bratooth. Large captures show that Bluetooth device address OUIs help only a few percent of low-energy devices, while version responses expose vendor company IDs more often in classic than low energy. Subversion numbers may reflect silicon stepping rather than firmware builds. Manufacturer data, GATT reads, and advertised 128-bit service UUIDs each add partial teeth, though many paths are slow or sparse for firmware strings.

Practitioners should expect incomplete answers per device, prioritize high-signal fields where responses exist, and validate prints against ground truth before tying observations to exploitability. The speaker shares collection code, a literature timeline, and a call for collaborators to widen measurement so wireless assessment can move from guessing chips to evidence-backed targeting.

talks.title: USA 2023 | Building A Modern Bluetooth Sniffer
talks.teaser: Shows how to sniff all Bluetooth channels at once with software-defined radio and feed the decoded packets into Wireshark.
talks.summary:
The talk addresses a practical limit of Bluetooth sniffing. Narrowband software-defined radios hop between channels and miss traffic, while wideband capture hardware is expensive. The speaker presents a multi-channel approach using a Blade RF device, whose newer firmware covers enough spectrum to watch all Bluetooth channels at the same time. He also introduces a tool that integrates with Wireshark, so captured packets appear directly under the interface list.

Much of the talk explains the signal processing behind the tool. Raw IQ samples are split into individual channels with a polyphase channelizer, bursts are detected by amplitude, and frequency demodulation with offset correction turns each burst into bits. Without a connection's access address, the decoder finds packet starts by checking whether the length field in the BLE header matches the burst length. To keep up with the sample rate, the channelizer uses SIMD fixed-point arithmetic and a GPU-accelerated FFT library. The speaker said this let a modern laptop decode all 80 classic channels and all 40 BLE channels in real time. He also noted that per-radio physical characteristics can be plotted to track individual devices.

The live demo showed Bluetooth advertising packets, including some unencrypted BLE traffic. The speaker closed by describing unfinished work: classic Bluetooth support, Windows builds, and channel hopping for cheaper radios that cannot cover the full band. A practitioner who wants to try this today can install the tool with a supported radio, though its limits on narrower radios matter for planning.

talks.title: Securing The Unseen: Vulnerability Research In Confidential Computing by Josh Eads and Cfir Cohen
talks.teaser: Shares audit findings across AMD SNP and Intel TDX confidential computing, including firmware crypto and interrupt-handling flaws.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces confidential computing, which isolates guest memory and state from the hypervisor, host firmware and peripherals, with remote attestation proving what was loaded. Its threat model treats the host as an adversary, while physical attacks are out of scope. The speakers describe white-box audits of AMD's SNP and Intel's TDX, carried out with vendor documentation, source code and engineers, which found dozens of vulnerabilities, some fixed before launch.

On AMD's side, a firmware bug encrypted persistent state with a fixed IV in counter mode, so identical data produced identical keystream. Combined with an earlier invalid-curve flaw, this could expose private keys. Another issue let a firmware API update page ownership without invalidating the IOTLB, allowing DMA writes into private pages, shown with a PCIe interposer. For Intel TDX, a module loader disabled interrupts by nulling the IDT, but a non-canonical LGDT address still triggered a fault that could be steered, tested in a simulator. Row hammer against logical integrity depended on ECC that was not verified and has since been fixed, and several access oracles leaked host-visible activity.

The main takeaways are to define the threat model and check security invariants across the whole system rather than per component, to review crypto at the implementation, algorithm and protocol layers, and to look closely wherever performance was traded for security. Side channels matter more when guests are meant to be opaque, and the speakers encourage public audits and open specifications so users can verify these systems.

talks.title: Red Team Vs. Blue Team by Endres Puschner & Steffen Becker | hardwear.io USA 2023
talks.teaser: Shows how a red team versus blue team exercise tested detection of hardware Trojans in four digital chips.
talks.summary:
The talk presents a hardware Trojan detection case study in which one group of researchers played red team and another played blue team. Hardware Trojans are malicious changes to an integrated circuit made by a party other than the original designer, and the risk sits in outsourced fabrication and shipping. Instead of altering silicon before manufacture, the red team edited the design files of chips that were already made, adding four cells and replacing six per chip. The blue team then had to find those changes.

The blue team imaged each chip from the back with a scanning electron microscope, which took one or two days and produced about 300 gigabytes of grayscale tiles. They matched design cell coordinates from the GDS2 file to the images, cut out every cell, and compared it against a reference using template matching and a wire detector. Added cells were found almost perfectly. Replaced cells on the 90, 65 and 40 nanometer chips were detectable, but three on the 28 nanometer chip looked too similar to reference cells, and catching them would have meant tolerating more than 70k false positives. Dust and debris also produced false positives. A live demo showed the algorithms running on a laptop in hours.

The takeaway is that added cells are straightforward to spot with classical image processing, while replacements get harder as feature sizes shrink. The team released its images, anonymized design files and algorithms on GitHub. The speakers closed by arguing that realistic Trojan insertion studies are still needed to test countermeasures from the literature.

talks.title: Exploring chip decaping techniques for silicon die inspection and reverse engineering
talks.teaser: Shows how hot air can soften a chip's plastic package so its silicon die can be exposed for inspection.
talks.summary:
Chip secrets are often locked inside their packages, so the silicon die and the circuits on it cannot be seen directly. The talk focuses on removing the die from plastic packages, a step needed before the silicon can be examined closely.

Two approaches are compared. Very strong acid works but is dangerous to handle. Heating the package with a hot air tool is far cheaper and simpler, and it is the method demonstrated. The plastic casing is heated until it is hot enough to weaken, then the package is cracked open by hand to reveal the die.

Once the die is exposed, the speaker cleans off the remaining material and shows the silicon sitting in the opened package. The takeaway for practitioners is that a basic heat source can expose a die for visual inspection and reverse engineering without resorting to acid.

talks.title: Affordable EMFI Attacks Against Modern IoT Chips by Davide Toldo
talks.teaser: Shows how a low-cost electromagnetic fault injection rig can skip instructions on a modern IoT chip with secure boot.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that modern IoT chips with closed debug ports, secure boot and flash encryption still have a gap. Electromagnetic fault injection (EMFI) can disrupt a chip from outside and skip checks even when the code itself is sound. The speaker presents it as an introductory walkthrough for newcomers who want a reproducible EMFI setup on a budget, and explains why a pulse must be placed accurately in both time and space.

The build starts with a cheap XY positioning stage, where a belt-driven 3D printer or drawing robot is preferred over lead-screw designs because of backlash. An inexpensive FPGA board handles the delay generator, with a Raspberry Pi Pico or ChipWhisperer as alternatives. Pulsers range from a commercial unit that reaches higher voltage to the open-source PicoEMP. Custom hardware reset and SMB-connected breakouts, plus a control script that logs results to CSV for 2D mapping, complete the rig. On a recent chip, a test loop showed instruction skips in specific die regions, while brownout detection and USB polling noise complicated the work.

The takeaway is that the entry cost is modest and that deployed devices may be exposed if an attacker has physical access and time. Practitioners should check whether this attack fits their threat model. If glitches do not appear, a higher-voltage pulser may be needed, and even well-written code cannot fully defend against this class of attack.

talks.title: How To Hack Shannon Baseband (from A Phone) by Natalie Silvanovich | hardwear
talks.teaser: Shows how a Shannon baseband on a Pixel 7 can be attacked remotely through a VoLTE call, from bug finding to code execution.
talks.summary:
Natalie Silvanovich, a team lead on Google's Project Zero, describes a two-month baseband hackathon in which about five people tried to find and exploit a bug in the Shannon modem used in the Pixel 7. The team wanted to know how long it takes to find such a bug and what an exploit could then reach. Instead of the usual proximity attack with a fake base station, they looked at an attacker who simply calls the victim over VoLTE, where session setup and media negotiation (SIP and SDP) pass through carrier servers that filter traffic in varying ways.

Testing a unicorn emulator against individual functions, together with fuzzing, surfaced several overflows in SDP and SIP parsing. One accept-types array overflowed once more than twelve entries were supplied, and a configuration-type bug allowed an overflow with arbitrary byte values. Trying these on a rooted Galaxy S9 showed that the caller's carrier mattered most for getting payloads through. The modem had no ASLR and a fixed stack cookie, so the team used a heap allocator with unsafe unlinking to overwrite a free function pointer. An ARM gadget then removed memory access restrictions, allowing shellcode to run from the heap. The demo swapped an incoming text message for another one.

The main lesson was that missing tooling, especially logging and debugging, was the biggest barrier, and that baseband bugs are hard to research without code execution. The speaker argues that ASLR and heap hardening would have substantially slowed the work, and that fully remote baseband attacks that need no physical proximity are feasible.

talks.title: BreakMi: Reversing, Exploiting & Fixing Fitness Tracking Ecosystems by M. Casagrande & D. Antonioli
talks.teaser: Reverse engineers Xiaomi and Fitbit tracker Bluetooth protocols and shows how pairing and session flaws enable device takeover.
talks.summary:
Fitness trackers pair with a phone companion app over Bluetooth Low Energy, and the app relays their data to a vendor backend over Wi-Fi. This talk assesses the Xiaomi and Fitbit ecosystems, whose application-layer protocols are proprietary and undocumented. The researchers captured Bluetooth traffic with HCI snoop logs and Wireshark, decompiled the Android companion apps, used dynamic instrumentation to match captured packets with values in memory, and intercepted the app's Wi-Fi traffic to map backend endpoints.

In the Xiaomi devices tested, link-layer encryption was disabled and the application layer offered no confidentiality or integrity. The older pairing version sent the pairing key in clear text behind a weak button confirmation. The newer version relied on a public key shared across the whole ecosystem, and its authentication challenge could be replayed, with only the app authenticating to the tracker. The speakers demonstrated dropping, impersonation and man-in-the-middle attacks from nearby, plus a remote attack from a malicious Android app that shares the phone's BLE channel and can trigger an unauthenticated factory reset, enabling device takeover. The Fitbit Charge 2 fared better, with link-layer security enabled and MAC-based authentication, but its real-time mode was unencrypted and its pairing was replayable, which still allowed impersonation.

The toolkit is open source, and the authors reported the issues to both vendors. Xiaomi classified the problem as a lack of encryption and reportedly shipped new firmware, while Google acknowledged the findings and released a fix. The proposed countermeasures are user-indicated pairing, authenticated encryption keyed with the pairing key, and enabling BLE link-layer security. The takeaway is that vendor-specific app-layer protocols should not be trusted to protect wearable data on their own.

talks.title: Inside Apple's Lightning: JTAGging The IPhone For Fuzzing And Profit by Thomas Roth
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Inside Apple's Lightning: JTAGging The IPhone For Fuzzing And Profit by Thomas Roth.

talks.title: Cryo-Mechanical RAM Content Extraction: A DIY Cold Boot Robot For A Thousand Bucks by Ang Cui
talks.teaser: Shows a low-cost CNC robot that freezes and removes DRAM chips to extract decrypted memory from a Siemens PLC.
talks.summary:
The talk tackles a practical barrier in embedded reverse engineering: vendors disable JTAG and UART, and encrypted firmware leaves little to inspect. The speaker's motivating case was a Siemens S7-1500 PLC CPU with a missing root of trust, where the only official workaround was restricting physical access. Instead of glitching the board, the team aimed to pull decrypted contents straight out of DDR memory.

The method builds on cold boot attacks: chilling memory so its contents survive power loss, then moving the chips to a reader. Obstacles included no DIMM slot, five soldered chips with scrambled bit mapping, and the risk of cracking boards. The robot used inexpensive CNC hardware fitted with closed-loop stepper motors to correct lead screw error and backlash, elastomer test sockets to seat chips without shorts, and modeling clay to hold the board flat, keeping chips near -50 Celsius. A closed-loop cooling system later replaced the dry-ice bath, and a near-field probe located windows where the CPU was busy and not writing memory.

The talk closed with open questions about targeting application-level code, slowing DDR4 clocks for affordable FPGAs, and returning memory to the system. The main takeaway is that a physical extraction rig can be built for under a thousand dollars, with precision coming from careful mechanical calibration rather than expensive equipment.

talks.title: Next-Gen Exploitation: Exploring The PS5 Security Landscape by Specter | hardwear.io USA 2023
talks.teaser: Compares PS4 and PS5 attack surface and mitigations, then reverses the PS5 hypervisor and its kernel code integrity model.
talks.summary:
The talk compares the PS4 and PS5 from an attack-surface and mitigation standpoint. On the PS4, the FreeBSD-derived kernel shipped with custom system calls, no syscall filtering, and weak mitigations, and some privileged interfaces such as eBPF and raw sockets were reachable from the browser sandbox. A USB filesystem integer truncation bug serves as a case study of how a single out-of-bounds write in the kernel heap could be chained into a jailbreak.

For the PS5, the speaker describes much stronger defenses: SMAP and ASLR enforced, software control flow integrity, execute-only kernel text, and a proprietary hypervisor built on AMD SVM that uses guest mode execute trap. Working from a kernel dump, the speaker walks through the hypervisor's boot checks, its nested paging setup, and the filtering of control register and MSR writes, and notes roughly 14 hypercalls up to firmware 3.0. A packet options race use-after-free that was reintroduced in firmware 3.0 is shown to give a kernel info leak and a read/write primitive, which made a blind kernel exploit from WebKit possible on firmware 3.0 through 4.51. The talk also covers the secure processors, including the MP0 and MP3 components and an on-die dual-core A53.

The takeaway is that the hypervisor pushes attackers toward data-only attacks. The speaker argues that console exploitation remains possible but now needs more steps, more time, and carries greater risk of a patch breaking the chain.

talks.title: Benchmarking The Static Power Vulnerability Of Four CMOS Generations by Thorben Moos | hardwear.io
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Benchmarking The Static Power Vulnerability Of Four CMOS Generations by Thorben Moos | hardwear.io.

talks.title: The Misuse Of Secure Components In Hardware Wallets by Michael Mouchous & Karim Abdellatif
talks.teaser: Shows how misusing a secure memory chip's access controls and provisioning undermined a hardware wallet's key protection.
talks.summary:
The talk shows how a hardware wallet can lose its protections through misuse of a secure component, not a single hardware flaw. The device pairs a microcontroller with an authentication chip that holds the user's seed and PIN-related secrets. The speakers first explain the chip's slot-based access control, where each slot is public, protected by another key, or private.

The first problem came from reading the microcontroller's one-time-programmable memory. By disturbing the boot process, the researchers reached that memory and dumped a key protecting the secure chip. On one unit the key showed a fixed, predictable pattern. The cause traced back to provisioning: a random-number command ran before the configuration was locked and returned a fixed value, so affected units shared a key, and a later unit showed random values after a change to the initialization order. The second problem was PIN handling. The chip's password-checking feature was tied to the wrong slot, so the PIN check could be bypassed and the seed read directly.

For the third issue, the team built a laser fault-injection bench and tested two revisions of the chip. Glitching a read let them bypass slot protection and retrieve protected data. The older revision mostly zeroed bits, while the newer one corrupted critical slots more often, which could break the device. The talk concludes that the root causes were misunderstood commands, misconfiguration and continued use of an older chip revision. Units made before the change should be assumed to share a key, and fixing them requires hardware changes, since nothing in the field can be patched.

talks.title: Back To The Future With Platform Security by Enrique Nissim, Joseph Tartaro and Krzysztof Okupski
talks.teaser: Traces AMD platform security features and SMM flaws that let attackers reach ring -2 and persist across reboots.
talks.summary:
The talk examines AMD platform security, focusing on System Management Mode (SMM), the privileged ring -2 environment, and how AMD configures protection for SMRAM and flash. The speakers say the research began when a gaming laptop rejected a firmware dump, and they describe a missing SMM lock setting that let them modify SMRAM and run code there. They then show that on several systems the flash protection registers could be reprogrammed from the operating system, and that a Lenovo ThinkPad allowed direct flash access.

The middle section covers firmware modules that expose flash read, write and erase functions without proper parameter checks. The speakers chained these into arbitrary read and write primitives inside SMM. They explain AMD's PSP ROM Armor as a mitigation that routes flash writes through the Platform Security Processor, then describe how they reached the PSP mailbox and, using a modified firmware volume, disabled the SMM protections to gain persistence across reboots. They also cover AMD's SMM supervisor, its OEM policy blobs, and gaps such as unrestricted PSP mailbox access.

The closing part says more than 20 issues were reported across OEMs and BIOS vendors, and that many could be fixed with simple configuration changes. The speakers urge attendees with AMD machines to run their utility and share results. An AMD PSP engineer in the question period disputed some points and suggested a joint talk later.

talks.title: "Un-fare Advantage” - Hacking The MBTA CharlieCard From 2008 To Present by Bobby Rauch | hardwear.io
talks.teaser: Traces how Boston's transit fare card was read and abused with a Flipper Zero and an Android phone, then disclosed to the operator.
talks.summary:
The talk examines the CharlieCard, the contactless fare card used on Boston's MBTA transit system. It traces the card's history from a 2008 court filing over MIT students' research, through a 2016 warning from MIT's security office that led the operator to add checksums, a ride counter and monitoring for clone-style commands. A 2019 NCC Group researcher described a key-recovery attack without proving it.

In 2022 the speaker used a Flipper Zero to read all 32 sector keys from his own card. Tracing them showed they had been committed to a public GitHub repository in 2018, then copied into an Android app for MIFARE Classic, so any phone could read the cards. He showed the balance lived on the card rather than in a central database, and that the online reload service trusted card contents. Restoring an earlier snapshot let him regain value after riding. He also described lost-card replacement and Gen 2 clone cards as further attack paths, and showed a recorded free ride.

Disclosure went through the general contact page, as the MBTA had no vulnerability disclosure program. Terms with a 90-day window were negotiated with help from Harvard's Cyber Law Clinic, whose memo judged the email agreements not binding. Suggested fixes included server-side validation of value changes, regular key rotation and a move to newer fare technology; the MBTA said it improved fraud monitoring. The takeaway is that likelihood and impact shift as technology changes, so organizations should watch open-source sources for early signals.

talks.title: Keynote |The Microarchitectures That I Saw And The Ones That I Hope To One Day See by Rodrigo Branco
talks.teaser: Recounts CPU side-channel disclosures and vendor responses, drawing lessons on hidden assumptions and system composition.
talks.summary:
In this keynote, Rodrigo Branco looks back on about fifteen years of CPU security work, with more attention to failures and frustrations than to wins. He argues that most serious flaws come from two sources: assumptions that abstraction layers make about the components beneath them, and the mistaken belief that individually secure parts remain secure when combined. For unfamiliar systems, he suggests listing what you don't know, then building tooling to answer those questions.

The middle of the talk recounts how side-channel concerns were handled inside a major chip vendor. A casual answer given to students in 2007, that cache leaks were a software problem, hardened into internal policy and resisted later challenges. He describes pushing for a clear position on kernel address randomization after a TSX-based bypass, the 2017 research that used cache side channels against browser ASLR, and an early public disclosure in 2018 triggered by a competitor's patch. Other cases include a report on the management engine dismissed as unexploitable until the research team was reorganized, and cloud mitigations that had been broken for years without anyone noticing.

He closes by urging basic checks, such as re-running published proofs of concept, and by noting that bugs in hardware that cannot be patched tend to persist. He criticizes marketing-driven vendor responses and legal pressure around disclosure, and encourages researchers to keep probing complex systems, since skills carry across targets.

talks.title: An Overview Of The Security Of Some Hardware FIDO(2) Tokens by Victor Lomne
talks.teaser: Surveys hardware FIDO2 security keys, covering protocol basics, certification levels, and teardowns of several token families.
talks.summary:
The talk gives an overview of FIDO(2) and the hardware tokens that implement it, aiming to reduce reliance on passwords and resist phishing. It explains the registration and authentication flows, in which a token holds a per-service credential key and an attestation key used to prove authenticity. Optional layers such as shared attestation keys and signature counters are described, along with the newer passwordless mode and the broader set of signature algorithms.

The attack surface is then reviewed, from a compromised host sending requests that skip user presence to physical attacks like side-channel or fault injection, with the note that credential keys cannot be exported. Certification schemes are compared, including FIDO levels, Common Criteria and a French scheme, and the speaker criticises their unclear process and weak product traceability. Teardowns of several token families follow, covering Ubico keys, Google Titan keys, and many cheaper white-label devices built on different microcontrollers and secure elements, some easy to open and others hard.

The Titan case is revisited: a 2019 Bluetooth issue was patched, while a side-channel attack on the secure element could not be fixed because its ROM cannot be updated. The speaker concludes that buyers should favour tamper-resistant casings, common-criteria-certified secure elements and, if possible, two-chip designs. Future work suggested includes fuzzing USB stacks combined with fault injection and differential analysis of ECDSA signatures.

talks.title: Security Pitfall Of Hand-geometry recognition-based Access Control Systems by Luca Bongiorni
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Security Pitfall Of Hand-geometry recognition-based Access Control Systems by Luca Bongiorni.

talks.title: Blackbox Fuzzing With Side Channels by Sergei Volokitin | hardwear.io NL 2022
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Blackbox Fuzzing With Side Channels by Sergei Volokitin | hardwear.io NL 2022.

talks.title: Bypass NXP LPC-Family Debug Check with Voltage Fault Injection by Waleed AlZamil and Bandar Alharbi
talks.teaser: Shows how a voltage glitch during power-on defeats the debug lock on an NXP LPC1343 microcontroller.
talks.summary:
The talk examines the code read protection (CRP) mechanism in NXP LPC microcontrollers, which decides at boot whether the debug interface stays enabled. The speakers walk through the protection levels, the configuration word that sets them, and where the boot code checks that word. They note that earlier 2017 research used voltage fault injection to reach flash through the ISP bootloader, which led them to target the debug lock instead.

Their test setup used an LPC1343 driven by a glitch generator and a probe, with the decoupling capacitor on the core supply removed to make the glitch easier to deliver. Attempts that timed the glitch from a reset trigger did not work. Moving the trigger to a power-on cycle produced a successful glitch. The team used it to re-enable the debug interface, read back the stored CRP3 value, and showed the attack against the CRP1, CRP2 and CRP3 levels. They also compared the boot code across other LPC families, found a similar mechanism, and assumed comparable checks exist there.

The practical takeaway is that a debug lock enforced by a boot-time check can be undone by a well-timed voltage glitch, so hardware read protection has to account for fault injection. The speakers said they contacted NXP, which discussed the findings with them and was professional in its response. The session closed with audience questions about how the glitch was triggered and whether the vendor planned mitigations.

talks.title: Hardware Attacks Against SM4 In Practice by Sylvain Pelissier and Nicolas Oberli
talks.teaser: Shows how power analysis and fault injection recover SM4 keys from software and a RISC-V hardware accelerator.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at SM4, a block cipher from China's national standards that is becoming mandatory for some products and has dedicated instructions in ARMv8.4 and RISC-V. The speakers walk through its structure, including the key schedule that produces round keys, the 32-bit word operations, and the S-box-based round function. They note that a firmware image can be checked for its constants and S-box to spot SM4, and that a key schedule in memory can be searched for.

For side-channel work, they captured power traces from a software SM4 implementation running on an ESP32, averaging many encryptions per trace. Correlation power analysis against the first-round S-box output recovered round keys one at a time, and the master key was then obtained by reversing the key schedule. Attacking from the ciphertext side was harder and needed a backwards approach before it produced correlation. For faults, they applied differential fault analysis to simulated and real faulted outputs, moving from a static lookup table to an improved fold attack that needs fewer faults. In simulation the full key was recovered quickly.

On a RISC-V microcontroller with a hardware SM4 accelerator, power and electromagnetic side-channel attempts gave no usable leakage with their equipment. Electromagnetic fault injection did produce faulted ciphertexts, and about 300 unique ones out of roughly 1400 collected were enough for the analysis to recover the key, showing the accelerator was vulnerable. The speakers said they would release their tools, including a key schedule finder and an analysis library, so practitioners can test their own SM4 implementations.

talks.title: Practical Invasive Attacks, How Hardware is Hacked For Compatible Product Creation by Thomas Olivier
talks.teaser: Shows how an invasive reverse engineering team probes a secure chip's ROM to clone printer cartridge electronics.
talks.summary:
Compatible printer cartridge makers need to understand the secure chips inside original cartridges. The speaker framed this as a threat model in which the main barrier is how long an attacker needs to clone a device. These chips are packaged black boxes with no datasheet, pinout or architecture reference, so the work starts from zero. The target had analog blocks, a digital CPU, flash, ROM and RAM spread across five metal layers.

The team delayered the die by mechanical polishing, imaged each layer with a scanning microscope, stitched the images and rebuilt the standard cell library to read the netlist. An angled polish exposed the ROM bits, and the extracted dump looked unencrypted, yet it still did not yield readable strings or recognisable code. The shield over the chip blocked direct probing, so the team used focused ion beam rewiring to reach internal signals, then microprobed them and found that the ROM boots before the flash. Netlist tracing exposed memory select logic, a control path into the instruction register, and a shield sensor whose input could be tied to supply voltage, disabling the shield and two other countermeasures.

Full analysis stayed out of reach because the ROM address scrambling and an apparently custom instruction set remained unresolved. Next steps were to simulate the fetch circuitry and rebuild the datasheet. The speaker's takeaway is that a shield is only one layer, that no chip resists unlimited invasive effort, and that certification schemes need better ways to assess reverse engineering attacks.

talks.title: How To Tame Your Robot by Jiska Classen & Fabian Freyer | hardwear.io NL 2022
talks.teaser: Shows how firmware analysis unlocks hidden service commands on a cloud-tethered vacuum robot for local control and repair.
talks.summary:
The presentation follows premium Neato vacuum robots from factory provisioning through app pairing, dual-cloud operation, and vendor-only repair channels. A serial console exposes limited user commands while authorized diagnostics stay behind per-robot security keys that throttle guessing after five failures.

Starting from firmware obtained via an earlier bootloader RAM-retention trick, the speakers trace the invalid-key error in a disassembler, map five 24-byte command categories, and follow memory writes into an encryption routine. Inputs reduce to static firmware data and each unit’s MAC-based serial; re-hosted assembly and Python finally match live behavior once the scheme is identified as RC4 XORed with the MAC, enabling a key generator for factory service commands.

Live experiments cover backups, risky setting resets, Wi-Fi disablement, log filtering, turbo tuning, and sensor recalibration pitfalls. Closing themes stress client-only authorization in IoT, safety when changing calibration, coordinated vendor disclosure, and why rotating keys at repair sites matters once firmware secrets leak.

talks.title: Bluetooth LE Link Layer Relay Attacks by Sultan Qasim Khan | hardwear.io NL 2022
talks.teaser: Explains how Bluetooth LE link-layer relay attacks defeat proximity-based keyless entry, and how to mitigate them.
talks.summary:
Proximity-based keyless systems, including car key fobs, smart locks, building access controls and some laptops and phones, unlock when a trusted token is nearby. They estimate distance from signal strength, time of flight or phase measurements. Signal-strength checks are easy to fool, and ranging schemes without a cryptographic distance check can also be beaten. Relaying traffic between a token and a lock makes both devices believe they are close together, even when they are far apart.

The talk reviews earlier relay approaches against Bluetooth Low Energy. GAP-layer relays used standard host APIs, HCI-level relays bypassed the host stack, and analog relays carried the whole 2.4 GHz band but added latency and range limits. The focus is a link-layer relay, in which one device acts as a master toward the real peripheral and as a slave toward the real central, forwarding link-layer packets. Added latency can be hidden by choosing a shorter connection interval on one side. Encryption is the main obstacle, because control packets are encrypted and both sides must keep matching counters. The attacker must therefore find when connection updates take effect, using traffic analysis and empty packets to probe timing. A live demonstration relayed an unlock request over distance to a Tesla Model Y at short range.

The main mitigations are requiring user interaction before an unlock, and using secure ranging standards that verify distance cryptographically, which limits how far a relay can stretch the apparent distance. The practical takeaway is that signal-strength or unauthenticated timing checks alone should not protect valuable assets, since BLE relay attacks are practical.

talks.title: Using EMC Equipment As A Side Channel Acquisition Technique by Nicolas Oberli & Benjamin Vernoux
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding Using EMC Equipment As A Side Channel Acquisition Technique by Nicolas Oberli & Benjamin Vernoux.

talks.title: Keynote | Reverse Engineering Is Good For Soul by Travis Goodspeed | hardwear.io NL 2022
talks.teaser: Shares personal stories of reverse engineering, from smart card firmware dumps to a DIY wristwatch that doubles as a radio.
talks.summary:
The keynote argues that reverse engineering is the work the speaker enjoys most, more than security itself, and that it is worth protecting from jobs that crowd it out. Travis Goodspeed recounts his career, including a stint in New York taking apart products and a factory line, and time working with Windows reverse engineer Jeff Chapel, whose publishing dropped off once he lacked the quiet to work. A nuclear engineer friend serves as a contrast: he stopped enjoying his job because he could not take on small, self-contained problems.

The technical examples come next. A 1998 report on Nagravision smart cards, released during litigation, described reading firmware through instruction fetches by placing needles on the chip, along with a buffer overflow in the card's input buffer. Goodspeed adapted that overflow to a modern USB smart card reader and published a Go client that dumps the reader's firmware. He also built a home chemistry setup for decapping and delayering chips, and wrote a ROM annotation tool called Mastermind. Separately, he described the 1997 dispute between AOL and MSN Messenger, in which an overflow in AOL's Oscar protocol client was used to survey which messenger users were running.

He closes with his own wristwatch project: a TI MSP430-based board that fits an original watch case, with amateur radio transmit, a frequency counter, and an on-watch disassembler. He urges listeners to keep reverse engineering in their lives and to protect the time needed to do it.

talks.title: Grinding Tractors To A Halt Growing Pains In Agricultural HardwareSecurity by Sick Codes hardwear.io
talks.teaser: Follows chip-off extraction of John Deere tractor firmware and exposed keys, showing how unencrypted embedded devices leak secrets.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with recent ransomware and extortion incidents hitting agriculture and food companies, including Colonial Pipeline, JBS Foods, a farmer cooperative and AGCO. From there it asks what happens to a manufacturer's embedded code once hardware leaves the factory, since used units circulate on resale sites and can be taken apart at home.

The research centres on a secondhand John Deere telematics gateway. Its NAND flash was removed with a hot air gun and read through a socket, then the file system was rebuilt in a Docker container. Findings included an engineering mode that could be switched on before login, a temporary folder not held in RAM, and plaintext databases holding a Wi-Fi password. A key pair for an MQTT setup was identical across devices; the vendor confirmed it was a development key left in production, though it was not in active use. A hardcoded repository login let the speaker download about 4,000 RPM packages before directory listing was disabled, and a leftover trash folder on one unit revealed the packages needed to rebuild the operating system on a Raspberry Pi.

The speaker closes by arguing that the minimal kit is cheap, that very few researchers examine agricultural equipment, and that secondhand chips may still hold customer data. The Q&A touched on right-to-repair, the vendor's response to the disclosures, and the later launch of a bug bounty program.

talks.title: Exploiting AMBA AXI Protocol For DoS Attacks Of Shared Resources | Francesco Restuccia | hardwear.io
talks.teaser: Shows how legitimate AXI bus behaviors let one manager starve shared FPGA SoC resources, and which fixes were proposed.
talks.summary:
This talk examines how the AMBA AXI on-chip bus, a common interconnect standard in modern system-on-chips, can be abused by an untrusted manager, such as buggy or third-party IP. The experiments ran on two commercial Xilinx FPGA SoC platforms, the Zynq 7000 and Zynq UltraScale+, using fully compliant managers and the vendor's standard interconnect.

The first problem is unfair bandwidth sharing. One accelerator's share fell from an expected 33 percent to about 3 percent when interfering managers issued greedy traffic, and a simple calculation showed that a single interferer with longer bursts could cut it by 88 percent. The second is a bus stall. AXI requires write data to follow address order, so a manager that issues a write and delays its data blocks every other manager's writes to all peripherals. Examples included a Xilinx deep learning processing unit that held the bus for hundreds of cycles, and a DMA that issued its write alongside its read. In a mixed-critical automotive-style setup, a critical accelerator's response time became unbounded and the neural network could not finish frames.

For mitigation, the speaker proposed an AXI burst equalizer that splits and merges transactions to a nominal size, restoring fair data sharing, and an access stall monitor that reclaims the bus when a stall threatens schedulability. The monitor needs knowledge of the bus workload, which limits it for mixed-critical systems. The takeaway is to verify bus-level interactions when integrating third-party IP, since the protocol permits these behaviours.

talks.title: Perimeter Breached! Hacking An Access Control System by Steve Povolny & Sam Quinn | hardwear.io USA
talks.teaser: Shows how a building access control panel was taken over through its serial, JTAG and web interface flaws to gain root and unlock doors.
talks.summary:
Trellix researchers Steve Povolny and Sam Quinn explain why they targeted access control systems, which they see as a single point of failure bridging physical and digital security. They bought a used Mercury-made panel whose marketing said it was approved for government facilities, then started with its circuit board. A four-pin port carried serial output that stopped during boot, and a 20-pin port looked like JTAG.

Using a J-Link debugger, they halted the processor, dumped the U-Boot bootloader and found a hard-coded boot delay of zero that blocked interrupting boot. Patching it gave them a bootloader shell and then a root shell over serial. A hardware watchdog that rebooted the board about every 15 seconds was disabled by flipping one bit in its mode register. The web interface ran CGI pages as root, and a hostname field reached a system call. Character filters were bypassed with tabs and curl, and that payload only ran at boot. A firmware upload diagnostic page skipped authentication and had a buffer overflow in signature-size parsing, which chained with the injection into unauthenticated remote code execution.

The team reported eight zero-days to the vendor. The two covered in the talk scored 9.0 and 10.0, and the vendor said other OEM partners using the boards are affected too. For the demo, they wrote a small program that called a kernel driver to hold door relays open. The takeaway is that certification claims say little about device security, and debug ports and default settings deserve close scrutiny.

talks.title: Breaking A Recent SoC’s Hardware AES Accelerator Using Body Biasing Injection by Karim M. Abdellatif
talks.teaser: Shows a low-cost body biasing injector faulting a recent SoC's hardware AES accelerator and recovering its key.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at body biasing injection, a fault injection technique that applies a high voltage through a needle touching the substrate of a decapped chip. The speaker notes it is rarely covered in the literature and is cheaper than laser attacks, though it still requires decapping. The earlier low-cost design was extended with a programmable voltage near 250 volts, both pulse polarities, microcontroller control and USB power.

A glitchable counter loop first confirmed that positive and negative pulses altered results at different spots on the surface. The target was a low-power SoC with Wi-Fi and Bluetooth, built on 40 nm and used in hardware wallets. Power traces and a signal-to-noise leakage check identified the window where the AES accelerator ran. Early faults at 250 volts only corrupted the output communication. An external supply raised the effective voltage to about 500 volts, and tuning let the speaker fault AES in round nine with roughly 60 percent success.

With faulty ciphertexts from round nine, the speaker ran differential fault analysis and recovered the full AES key using about 10,000 trials. Practical notes covered damage risk: three chips were damaged, so the needle should be lifted before moving across the surface, and front-side decapping is harder. The main takeaway is that a cheap homemade injector can break a hardware AES accelerator. Future work includes testing more devices and checking how the technique affects unsecured elements and glitch detectors.

talks.title: Armed To Boot: A Novel Enhancement To Arm's Secure Boot Chain by Derek & Ryan | hardwear.io USA
talks.teaser: Presents a single-domain secure boot design for Arm servers that lets several parties share one eFuse root of trust.
talks.summary:
The talk examines why standard Arm secure boot designs, which assume one entity signs all firmware, fit poorly with datacenter server supply chains where several vendors contribute silicon, firmware, software and hardware. The presenters recount their earlier approach, which anchored trust in UEFI key variables and TPM measurements, and explain why they found that protection incomplete against firmware persistence.

They then describe the design they moved toward, adapted from an AMD hardware trust model and implemented on Ampere processors. In it, a customer public key hash is burned into processor eFuses during a one-time provisioning step run by the server vendor, and the boot firmware is authenticated against that hash at each boot. The manufacturing and validation sequence was walked through, and a live demo showed a modified BIOS flash being rejected during boot. The presenters also covered the BMC as a weak point, since it has privileged host access and an older firmware security record, and suggested a CPU-agnostic identity-key approach as a next step.

In the Q&A, they noted that a compromised private key would force rework of affected hardware, and that each processor generation gets its own root key. The main takeaway is that a per-customer root of trust can give a consistent, repeatable procedure across many device types, though the design depends on careful key management.

talks.title: Leveraging Electromagnetic Emanations For IoT Malware Classification by Damien Marion, Pham, Annelie
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Leveraging Electromagnetic Emanations For IoT Malware Classification by Damien Marion, Pham, Annelie.

talks.title: Optimization And Amplification Of Cache Side Channel Signals by David Kaplan | hardwear.io USA 2022
talks.teaser: Shows how speculative execution turns cache state into amplified timing signals, even without a precise timer.
talks.summary:
Cache side channel attacks have a setup phase, a victim execution phase and a recovery phase. This talk concentrates on recovery, where an attacker must determine whether a cache line is present, usually by timing an access with a high-precision timer. The speaker asks whether that timer is really needed and whether every line must be checked one by one. The approach relies on speculative execution: a mispredicted branch briefly fetches a second cache line whose final state depends on the first. Chaining these effects creates inverter, replicator and NAND-style gadgets that copy or combine cache line states without timing each line directly. The talk was demonstrated on x86 hardware.

To make weak timers workable, the speaker presents amplification. A single-stage amplifier raised the timing difference to about 700 cycles. A self-reinforcing amplifier restores the signal after each pass and repeats the process, with results degrading after roughly 700,000 iterations due to system noise. With a 100,000-iteration amplifier, a 100 millisecond timer recovered the state over 80 percent of the time, and a 10 millisecond timer reached about 95 percent. Two further constructions were shown: a binary search over an array of cache lines and a counter whose state is stored in cache lines, each needing fewer timing measurements.

The takeaways are that disabling or monitoring high-precision timers is a weak mitigation, because these gadgets avoid timer calls, and that repeated victim invocations can sharpen results. Defenders should instead focus on the execution phase, for example by making code touch the same cache lines on every path or by limiting speculation over secret-dependent values.

talks.title: Self-labeling Electronic Shelf Labels by Steffen Robertz | hardwear.io USA 2022
talks.teaser: Shows how electronic shelf labels can be torn down, decoded over their 433 MHz radio link, and forged or replayed.
talks.summary:
The talk examines electronic shelf labels, the e-ink price tags used in supermarkets and increasingly in hospitals and document storage. The speaker outlines the market growth and possible abuse, including blocking price updates, luring shoppers to malicious QR codes, and reusing cheap displays. The target was a tag from a common Chinese supplier, paired with a base station that converts Ethernet into a proprietary 433 MHz protocol.

The teardown covered the external flash, which held the image data, and an unlabelled microcontroller. Acid decapping exposed a die marking, and a unique-ID lookup pointed to an STM8 low-power part. Its SWIM debug header, found on the board, allowed flash readout, although protection was enabled. The FCC filings did not match the observed signal, which was FSK slightly off the stated frequency. Replaying a captured price update with an SDR restored an old price, so no replay protection existed. The speaker decoded the frame types and their run-length image compression, then rebuilt the protocol in GNU Radio to push a custom image onto a tag.

The main lesson is that the protocol had no authentication, integrity checks or real error correction, and that a custom radio protocol offers little protection when a cheap transceiver chip can capture it. Because tags do not reply to the sender, an attacker's range is mainly limited by transmit power. The speaker recommends encryption, authentication and error correction, and plans to publish the tools and firmware dumps.

talks.title: Breaking SoC Security By Glitching OTP Data Transfers by Cristofaro Mune | hardwear.io USA 2022
talks.teaser: Shows how electromagnetic fault injection on OTP config transfers in an ESP32 bypasses boot and flash encryption protections.
talks.summary:
Modern system-on-chip devices store security settings in one-time programmable fuse memory and copy those bits into shadow registers during boot, where hardware and software then consume them. The talk asks what happens if that transfer itself is disturbed. Fault injection is usually aimed at software control flow, but the speakers argue it can also corrupt purely hardware paths that move this configuration data.

The target was the ESP32, a low-cost IoT chip with secure boot, flash encryption and JTAG disabling. Using electromagnetic fault injection with commercially available equipment, the team scanned the chip surface during reset and classified each run by what a fuse dump returned. They narrowed the location, power and timing until single configuration bits flipped mid-transfer. Targeting the read-protection bit let them recover the protected secure boot key, with a success rate of about one percent and no brute force. Glitching the JTAG-disable bit then allowed a live demo in which plaintext firmware was read from flash despite encryption being enabled.

The core lesson is that data being safe while stored says nothing about its safety in transit between components. The speakers pointed to countermeasures across the stack, including shielding and clock-based protections against injection, detection of glitches and bus-level error checks, and repeated transfers. They suggested that design-level mitigations for OTP data movement are possible, and that such attacks are often overlooked because fault injection research tends to focus on software.

talks.title: Physical Side Channel Attacks On PCs by Daniel Genkin & Roei Schuster | hardwear.io USA 2022
talks.teaser: Acoustic and built-in microphone leakage on laptops enables remote RSA and ECDSA key recovery over VoIP.
talks.summary:
The presenters contrast software microarchitectural side channels with physical ones on laptops and desktops, focusing on acoustic emissions from voltage regulators and capacitors on the motherboard. Using spectrograms and sensitive microphones, they distinguish CPU operation types up to hundreds of kilohertz and show RSA decryptions produce distinct spectral signatures. Liquid self-amplification exploits conditional branches in Karatsuba multiplication during modular exponentiation, enabling bit-by-bit extraction of RSA primes; demonstrations use nearby microphones, parabolic reflectors, a volunteer’s body as a conductor, and commodity phone microphones at short range.

The second half challenges the need for physical proximity. Built-in laptop microphones coupled to the sound card pick up electromagnetic leakage from the CPU, and lossy VoIP codecs preserve that signal across Mumble and similar apps. Attackers can classify browsing activity (reported 94% accuracy on 14 sites in their paper) and recover ECDSA signing keys by timing leading-zero skips in scalar multiplication, averaging RFC 6979 deterministic nonces across thousands of signed messages, and applying a lattice attack. A Counter-Strike scenario shows inferring opponent position from rendering load while on voice chat.

Practitioners should treat analog sensors as coupled to the processor, favor constant-time and constant-EM implementations, and recognize that algorithmically amplified chosen-input attacks can dominate background system noise on Linux laptops.

talks.title: Unwanted Features: Finding & Exploiting An In ROM Buffer Overflow On The LPC55S69 by Laura Abbott
talks.teaser: Details a buffer overflow in an NXP boot ROM on a microcontroller and how it leads to code execution despite protections.
talks.summary:
The talk begins with why a company building servers chose the NXP LPC55S69 microcontroller as a hardware root of trust for measuring its software. Because the chip's boot ROM includes a firmware update parser for the SB2 format, the team had to decide whether that code could be trusted.

The core finding is that the ROM parser treats SB2 header fields as untrusted input. An integer underflow and a conditionally updated callback let a copy run past a global buffer, and an adjacent heap allocator variable gives the attacker control of the callback pointer. That redirects execution into ROM code, which the memory protection unit restricts, but an executable ROM patch area in SRAM sits at the end of the overflowed region. A stack canary, checked only during ISP mode, was bypassed by a single 512-byte write that overwrote it. The payload then disables the MPU and SAU. An attacker could read flash and roll back signed images, but keys and secure boot settings on a sealed device stayed protected. The unique device secret had not yet been locked at the time, which threatens DICE-based device identity.

NXP agreed to fix the issue in new silicon, but that takes time, so interim mitigations such as validating the header in code on the chip and checking signatures were weighed, with the caveat that signatures prove only authenticity. The team decided to write its own update mechanism instead. Takeaways include validating input at every boundary, recognizing that ROM bugs are hard to fix, and publishing ROM source so customers can audit it.

talks.title: bd-jb: Blu-ray Disc Java Sandbox Escape by Andy Nguyen | hardwear.io USA 2022
talks.teaser: Walks through a Blu-ray Java sandbox escape on PlayStation consoles, chaining privilege escalation into native code execution.
talks.summary:
The talk covers a sandbox escape in Blu-ray Disc Java (BD-J), the runtime that runs interactive content on Blu-ray players and PlayStation consoles. The presenter explains why the PS5's execute-only memory makes browser-based entry points harder, and why a disc, which needs no remote access, became the target. The Java security model is then outlined, including the access controller and privileged execution.

Several bugs are shown. A deserialization flaw in a user preferences file let a crafted object load code in privileged context, a route since fixed upstream. A second flaw allowed privileged methods to be called by name through a proxy by inheriting a trusted method in an attacker subclass. On PS4, a further gadget enabled privileged constructor calls, and a path-prefix check in the security policy granted full permissions to a crafted path. With full permissions, the payload disabled the security manager and obtained sun.misc.Unsafe, which provided native memory access, function lookup and function calls. A JIT optimisation crash on PS4 was worked around by training a loop.

For arbitrary code execution, the presenter targeted the separate JIT compiler process, whose protocol let an untrusted pointer write payloads into a page shared with the runtime process. The talk ends with a live demo on a PS5 where a disc launched a notification, followed by a kernel stage that depended on a race condition. The user-land chain was presented as reliable and firmware-agnostic, with the PS4 limit noted at firmware below 9.5.

talks.title: Keynote | Adventures Of Wallet Hacking by Joe Grand | hardwear.io USA 2022
talks.teaser: Recounts hardware hacks on a hardware wallet, an Android phone and a faulty Ledger, from voltage glitching to soldered bypasses.
talks.summary:
This keynote is a tour of hardware hacking jobs the speaker took on for customers who had lost access to cryptocurrency. The first case was a Trezor One whose recovery seed was locked behind a forgotten PIN. The speaker explained that the STM32 microcontroller has read-protection levels, and that a voltage glitch during boot ROM execution could downgrade the chip so its debug interface and RAM became readable. He removed bypass capacitors from the core voltage and reset lines to sharpen the glitch, and used a J-Link and a ChipWhisperer, cutting the timing search from hours to minutes.

The middle of the talk covered other methods. Electromagnetic fault injection had been used by another researcher to dump flash over USB, but the speaker's test device ran older firmware that was not affected. A bootloader-level approach using UART reads was also described, where timing jitter of about 10 microseconds meant a glitch could sometimes erase flash instead of reading it. For a Ledger Nano S with a failed button, he bypassed the switch by soldering his own button, a fix that took about 20 minutes. For a Samsung Galaxy S3 whose swipe password was needed, he reached JTAG through micro-soldered wires, with a backup plan of reading the eMMC chip directly.

The closing message was that the simplest effective attack is often the right one, and that older, unpatched hardware stays in use for years, so many devices remain exposed. The speaker stressed patience and persistence, and said slides would be posted on his website.

talks.title: Deep Learning-based Side-channel Analysis: Challenges & Perspectives | Stjepan | hardwear.io Webinar
talks.teaser: Explains where deep learning side-channel analysis stands and lists the open challenges researchers still need to solve.
talks.summary:
Stjepan Picek introduces side-channel attacks, which observe physical leakage such as power or electromagnetic measurements rather than weaknesses in an algorithm. He explains profiling attacks as two stages: a profiling phase that models leakage on a copy of the device, then an attack phase that uses the model. He links this directly to supervised machine learning, and notes that template attacks from 2002 remain a strong baseline when their assumptions hold.

Recent results from his group follow. Feeding raw traces to very deep networks has been shown to work, but his experiments found that wider feature inputs let networks with only two or three hidden layers break a target from a single trace. He also showed triplet-learning-based feature selection, which lets a template attack approach deep learning performance. He presented an open-source framework for deep learning side-channel analysis that supports hyperparameter tuning, data augmentation and reproducible experiments.

He closed with open challenges: unsupervised learning, the gap between academic benchmarks and industrial hardware with stronger countermeasures, data augmentation, feature engineering, design guidelines for networks, universal models and explainability. In his countermeasure tests, hiding looked weaker than masking, and first-order Boolean masking seemed easier to defeat than multiplicative masking. The takeaway is that deep learning is powerful for side-channel work, but whether current methods scale to realistic targets is still unclear.

talks.title: Can you park a car in a classroom? | Phillippe Azalbert | hardwear.io Webinar
talks.teaser: Describes how a portable automotive test bench was built from scavenged ECUs, with sensor emulation and lessons for car security training.
talks.summary:
This talk from Quarks Lab explains why automotive security training benefits from a portable test bench, and how one was built. Modern cars run dozens of electronic control units over networks such as CAN and LIN, with a growing wireless attack surface. Bringing a real car to a training room is impractical, since few attendees can touch it at once and a triggered crash frame can lock the powertrain module until a manufacturer tool resets it.

The Car in a Box is a case sized to fit aboard a plane, holding ECUs from a scrapped vehicle wired to several networks, an infotainment unit with Bluetooth and cellular, and a control panel. The builders learned that some modules are immobilizer-enrolled and need a matching working car, that wake-up frames must be present, and that pin documentation should be located before wiring straight to pins instead of untangling harnesses. Sensors were emulated with an Arduino Mega using relays to ground, digital potentiometers for variable resistance, and a timer-driven clock for square signals, while a tyre pressure sensor was replayed with a software-defined radio. A Raspberry Pi touchscreen controls the simulation over serial.

Takeaways include that the same ECU weaknesses can span models and manufacturers, that some signals such as fuel level are averaged over about a minute, and that most microcontrollers are protected, so firmware recovery may need vendor hardware. Third-party diagnostic apps can reveal hidden manufacturer commands. The speaker also answered questions on costs, a build time of three to four weeks, and the role of UDS diagnostics.

talks.title: PP0117 Secure Sub-System in System-on-Chip (3S IN SOC) Protection Profile Overview | hardwear.io
talks.teaser: Describes the PP117 protection profile for secure subsystems in SoCs, covering external memory threats and certification reuse.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces PP117, a Common Criteria protection profile for a secure subsystem integrated into a system-on-chip. The presenters explain that secure elements are increasingly being built into SoCs and that existing guidance, written for standalone secure elements, does not cover the risks of this integration. The profile keeps strict conformance to PP084 and adds support for external memory, with optional packages for software loading, update, recovery and provisioning planned as later additions.

The middle of the talk covers the threats added for external memory, including clone, replacement, replay and rollback attacks. The speakers show how encryption, authentication and an irreversibility counter address them. They then describe a reuse methodology: a secure subsystem paired with a certified secure flash can be evaluated as a composite and carried into later SoC generations with limited re-evaluation. If the flash interface changes between generations, the existing certification may need to be evaluated again.

The closing point is that a designer integrating a secure subsystem into an SoC needs to review PP117 rather than rely on PP084 alone. The secure flash option is presented as a way to simplify both reuse and certification effort.

talks.title: The AMD Branch (Mis)predictor: New Types & Methods of Straight-Line Speculation(SLS) Vulnerabilities
talks.teaser: Explains a newly found straight-line speculation flaw in certain AMD Zen CPUs and why some mitigations are hard to apply.
talks.summary:
The talk examines branch prediction on AMD x86 processors and straight-line speculation (SLS), where the core keeps executing the instructions that follow an unconditional branch before the misprediction is resolved. It starts with the split between the front end, which fetches and decodes, and the out-of-order back end, then walks through static, dynamic and two-level predictors and the branch target buffer that supplies targets for jumps and calls.

Earlier work had seen SLS on Arm and on some x86 parts, but only for indirect jumps, calls and returns. The new finding is that on Zen 1 and Zen 2 cores, direct unconditional jumps and calls also allow speculation past them, whatever the branch direction, and this can even happen between two hyper-threads sharing a core. The speaker reports that the Zen 3 branch predictor redesign does not show this for direct branches. Forcing a miss by filling the target buffer opens the window. Only a handful of short instructions run inside it. Loads can leave cache traces, so a full Spectre v1 style gadget does not fit, but data already held in registers, or fed by store-to-load forwarding, can be used.

For mitigation, a software breakpoint instruction placed after a jump or return stops the speculation cleanly. Calls are harder: a serializing fence hurts performance, and zeroing the return register before a call depends on compiler behaviour and calling conventions that may not always hold. The speaker's hardening product uses the register-zeroing approach because it performs better, and the talk closes with pointers to the speaker's write-ups.

talks.title: Disarming TrustZone with TEE Privilege Reduction | David Cerdeira & Sandro Pinto | hardwear.io
talks.teaser: Presents ReZone, a design that limits a compromised trusted OS using SoC bus controllers instead of TrustZone's own controls.
talks.summary:
The talk examines Arm TrustZone, where trusted execution environments run a trusted OS with far more privilege than it needs. Earlier vulnerability studies traced many flaws to this excess trust, since a compromised trusted OS can reach the normal-world OS and the secure monitor. Prior work that restricted privilege through the address space controller did not hold up on real silicon, because all cores in a cluster share one bus master ID.

The speakers present ReZone, which adds a platform partitioning controller on the system bus. An auxiliary microcontroller configures it through a gatekeeper, while a trampoline in the secure monitor coordinates each world switch. A survey of 17 SoCs from nine vendors found 13 able to support the design, and a prototype ran on an NXP i.MX 8 MQ board. Building it required flushing caches, suspending sibling cores during reconfiguration, and disabling the EL3 MMU to prevent crashes and cache injection. Short calls suffered the most overhead, with one internal API test about four times slower, while a DRM decryption step slowed by about 1.5 times.

The authors estimate the design mitigates 87 percent of critical trusted OS and application vulnerabilities in their review, but not poorly implemented trusted applications, hardware attacks or cryptographic flaws. They also argue it remains relevant on newer Arm architectures, because secure-world components can still reach the normal world. Practitioners get a case for enforcing privilege separation with commodity bus controllers.

talks.title: MoonBounce: Internals of the 3rd publicly known UEFI firmware implant | Mark Lechtik | hardwear.io
talks.teaser: Traces how the MoonBounce UEFI implant hooks boot services to reach Windows user mode and links it to APT41.
talks.summary:
The talk presents Kaspersky's analysis of MoonBounce, a UEFI firmware implant found in the wild by the company's firmware scanning technology. The speaker explains the boot process the implant abuses, focusing on the DXE dispatcher stored in SPI flash, where the attackers patched the first bytes of several boot services functions with inline hooks. Each hook restores the original bytes after its first run and passes control on, so normal boot continues.

The infection chain is walked through in stages. An AllocatePool hook places shellcode in physical memory, and a CreateEventEx hook registers a callback for legacy boot so the payload can be mapped in that case as well. An ExitBootServices hook lets the implant survive into the Windows loader, where it hooks OslArchTransferToKernel and then ExAllocatePool in the kernel. A driver then watches for svchost processes running with the netsvcs argument and injects a user-mode stager via APC to reach a command-and-control server. The second-stage payload was not recovered.

Attribution rests on shared infrastructure: a Scrambled Cross implant reached command servers that resolved to the same IPs as the MoonBounce domain, and some used a certificate tied to APT41. Compilation timestamps and other backdoors on the network suggest long-term remote access. The closing advice covers firmware updates, TPM and Boot Guard where supported, firmware scanning, and training analysts to act on firmware alerts.

talks.title: CPU Fuzzing for Discovering Hardware caused Information Leakage Michael
talks.teaser: Shows how CPU fuzzing finds new microarchitectural side channels and attacks that leak data across cores and virtual machines.
talks.summary:
The talk covers how microarchitectural side channels and transient execution attacks can be found automatically rather than through slow manual analysis. Because this research depends on expertise and luck, the speaker applies fuzzing, a software testing technique, to CPUs. Each test uses a reset sequence, a trigger sequence and a measurement sequence of instructions, and compares cold and hot paths to reveal timing differences. This model rediscovers flush and reload on its own.

Running the approach on five AMD and Intel CPUs for about four days each rediscovered two known side channels and uncovered four new ones. Two attacks were built on them. One abuses the RDRAND instruction, whose latency rises across cores and virtual machines, enabling a covert channel between AWS instances without memory sharing or networking. Another shows that the non-temporal MOV can replace CLFLUSH, leaking more bytes per Meltdown access and breaking KASLR. A mutation-based fuzzer for data sampling attacks then ran for 26 hours, finding a new zombie load variant, Medusa, that leaked an OpenSSL RSA key, and a regression on Ice Lake.

The speaker concludes that these fuzzers are still simple and lack guidance, so progress needs feedback from performance counters, debug interfaces or other side channels. The tools and accompanying papers are open source on GitHub.

talks.title: TII at Hardwear.io NL 2021
talks.teaser: Covers defending post-quantum cryptography from physical, injection, and side-channel attacks through new hardware designs.
talks.summary:
The segment outlines dual research threads at a hardware-focused institute: one group pursues defensive architectures meant to make post-quantum algorithms efficient on hardware, while another probes hardware security through side-channel scrutiny of cryptographic software stacks.

Post-quantum deployment is framed as an active concern because physical threats—especially side-channel and injection classes highlighted at the event—could undermine algorithms once they ship. The speakers describe conference participation as a way to surface lesser-known risks such as supply-chain compromise and to widen awareness beyond narrow crypto circles.

Practitioners hear little step-by-step methodology; the emphasis is strategic. Organizations should plan for physical attack surfaces on future post-quantum stacks, pair architecture work with side-channel validation, and treat supply-chain exposure as a first-class hardware security problem rather than an afterthought.

talks.title: Smartek at Hardwear.io NL 2021
talks.teaser: A maker showcases magnetic building blocks inspired by LEGO, including conference-themed models and plans for larger kid-safe versions.
talks.summary:
The segment introduces a long-running personal project to improve on familiar plastic building bricks by using magnets instead of stud-and-tube coupling. The creator describes an early name tied to “magnetic LEGO,” then a rebranded product line sold alongside day-job work, aimed at older teens rather than young children because swallowed magnets are dangerous.

On display are several finished models, including aircraft and colorful sets that apparently sell well, plus figurines remixed from existing brick designs. Licensed characters such as Mario cannot be resold as-is; at hacker-oriented events, people instead hack or extend community builds. The site is used to show how one figurine design can be reworked into another, with a joking note about cost and weight.

Looking ahead six months, the focus is shapes beyond simple cubes, larger formats, and elements that rotate. The biggest toy fair in the world in February is the main commercial milestone, while a rainbow fidget product is intended as something safer to market toward kids.

talks.title: NL 2021: Blackboxing Diebold-Nixdorf ATMs by Vladimir Kononovich
talks.teaser: Explains how researchers decrypted, re-signed and uploaded custom firmware to an ATM cash dispenser over USB.
talks.summary:
The talk covers research into a cash dispenser module from a well-known ATM vendor, started after the speaker's team obtained a pair of firmware files from a bank project. The files were encrypted. The speaker explains that the decryption routine is a modified XTEA cipher with a non-standard delta constant, and that its key material is read from a dedicated region of the controller board. The firmware header also checks for a special block that can point to alternate key offsets, which made it possible to work with keys the team did not hold.

The firmware signature was self-signed, so the team could re-sign modified images with a shorter RSA key, since the signature field size is set by the format. The modified image was then uploaded to the dispenser over USB, using the device identifiers to trigger the upgrade path. The smart card that protects USB traffic also had a denial-of-service issue. Requesting a session key for the maximum counter value blocked further key generation, although the speaker notes that reinitializing the applet restores it when vendor keys are available.

To complete the attack, the team patched the firmware so it no longer requested session keys from the smart card, adjusted the vendor Java software, and synchronized session counters. They then configured cassette contents, ran a cash-out, and opened the shutter to collect the banknotes. The speaker presents this as a black-box method that needs only a USB connection inside the dispenser and leaves no logs. The practical lesson is that self-signed firmware and weak key handling undermine otherwise strong transport protection. At the time of the talk, the related CVEs were still in the registration and confirmation process.
