talks.title: NL 2021: Flippin‘ Fake Flops For Fun, Fame And Fortune by Jasper Van Woudenberg
talks.teaser: Pre-silicon fault injection models single-bit glitches in RTL to expose bypass paths and test fixes before chips are fabricated.
talks.summary:
The presentation argues for finding fault-injection weaknesses while a design still exists only as RTL, when changes remain cheap. It surveys real-world injectors—from inexpensive electromagnetic pulses through ChipWhisperer-style voltage glitching, body-bias and laser attacks, down to microprobing—and frames every method as disturbing the die so security-relevant bits flip at the wrong time.

Simulation adds a controllable glitch bus in Verilog, compiles netlists with Verilator, and exploits single-bit storage to explore many flip locations per clock cycle in parallel. On the open-source PicoRV32 core, a short UART branch test that should always report failure yields hundreds of distinct single-bit flip-flop faults that print success, clustered around the conditional branch; duplicating the check cuts the count but leaves exotic paths such as corrupted return addresses. The same pipeline targets OpenTitan’s AES block, matching truncated-round outputs to glitches; redundant round counters meant to harden the design can be partly removed by synthesis, and in one comparison slightly increased observable faults.

Practitioners should treat redundancy, volatile reads, and synthesis “optimization” as part of the threat model, validate countermeasures in simulation, and expect RTL results to diverge somewhat from post-synthesis gate-level runs. Scale, fault models beyond single-bit flips, and correlation with silicon remain open engineering questions.

talks.title: How to perform electromagnetic side channel analysis by simulation by Davide | hardwear.io Webinar
talks.teaser: Shows how simulated electromagnetic traces of a chip can reveal leakage hotspots before the silicon is fabricated.
talks.summary:
Electromagnetic side-channel attacks need only one leaky position over a chip's surface to compromise a device, yet existing power analysis tools cannot show where that position is or how the physical layout affects it. The talk presents a simulation flow that models the magnetic field of a whole chip. Current flowing in the upper metal layers is extracted with a commercial tool, the Biot-Savart law turns each current segment into a magnetic field, and the flux through a probe's surface is differentiated over time to produce the voltage an oscilloscope would record.

Simulated traces are noise-free, so a standard correlation attack lights up almost the entire die, unlike measured maps. To address this, the speaker computes how much noise would have to be added to a simulated trace to push a correlation below significance, and reports a correlation only when the correct key guess stands out from the others. Validation on a test chip compared simulated and measured correlation maps across different probe heights and diameters, vertical and horizontal probes, and front-side versus back-side analysis, finding close agreement in the leaking areas and their intensities.

The flow was then applied at the design stage to locate leaky standard cells and to compare two chip variants with different power routing. The variant whose supply and ground rails carry current in opposing directions showed fewer and weaker leaking areas, matching the measurements. The speaker noted that simulation time did not visibly grow with circuit complexity. The takeaway for designers is that such a flow can assess electromagnetic robustness and guide layout changes before fabrication.

talks.title: NL 2021: A Side Journey To Titan by Victor Lomné
talks.teaser: Shows how electromagnetic emissions from a Google Titan security key's secure element can leak ECDSA nonces, enabling key cloning.
talks.summary:
This FIDO U2F token from Google acts as a second factor for logins such as a Google account. The talk presents a side-channel attack on the key's secure element, an NXP A700x chip, using the local electromagnetic radiation it emits while producing ECDSA signatures. The work begins by identifying the chip and its Java Card operating system, then opens the package to expose the die so probes and an oscilloscope can capture measurements close to the silicon.

The middle of the talk covers the analysis. Traces from many signing operations are grouped with clustering and expectation maximisation to classify the bits of an intermediate value, then matched across signatures. The speaker shows how the multiplication step in the signature computation leaks partial information. That leakage is then fed into a lattice-based attack to recover the full private key, and the team checked the approach with simulations before running it on real measurements.

The closing part discusses limits and impact. The attack needs physical access to the key and is not trivial to perform. A signature counter checked by the server can flag a cloned key, and the team reported the findings to Google and NXP. The speaker also notes a side observation: a correlation between the elliptic curve group order and the success rate of the lattice attack. Practitioners should take away that hardware tokens can leak secrets through electromagnetic emanations, so physical threat models matter even for security keys.

talks.title: NL 2021: Teardown And Feasibility Study Of IronKey by Sergei Skorobogatov
talks.teaser: Nine IronKey generations join fifteen rival encrypted USB models in a teardown that probes epoxy, chips, and password-counter bypasses.
talks.summary:
The presentation motivates scrutiny of IronKey, a FIPS-certified encrypted USB flash drive marketed to military and government users, because public teardown data was scarce and a legitimate user reportedly lost access to cryptocurrency. The speaker reverse-engineered twenty-six drives across nine IronKey families and fifteen competing products, comparing certification claims and internal architectures.

Opening cases required cutting metal shells and dissolving epoxy via thermal, chemical, or related methods. Across generations the designs shifted from custom IronKey-labeled controllers and Atmel secure authentication parts to Phison USB microcontrollers, eMMC storage, Renesas SATA bridges, and in some lines no dedicated secure element at all. Kingston IronKey D300 hardware matched the DataTraveler 4000 G2 board and firmware. Remarketed “IronKey” chips often proved standard Atmel dies with factory debug wiring visible on the silicon.

Practical testing targeted bypassing password-attempt limits by imaging and restoring external memory. IronKey F150, D80, and D300 succumbed when serial flash, microSD, standard NAND, or eMMC contents were copied back after lockout. Polishing eMMC packages exposed test pads reaching the internal NAND. The speaker argues FIPS level three does not ensure a secure chip is present, vendors ignored eMMC replay-protected features, and cryptocurrency hardware wallets appear to use substantially stronger silicon than these drives.

talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning NL 2021: Divide & Conquer Revisited: FI As A SW EXP Primitive by Rafael and Federico.

talks.title: NL 2021 : Breaking The Security Barrier Of A B.Braun Infusion Pump by Douglas & Philippe
talks.teaser: Chains network flaws and firmware reversing to alter a B. Braun infusion pump's dosing calculations remotely.
talks.summary:
The talk walks through a security assessment of a B. Braun infusion pump from 2017 and the docking station it sits in. The researchers picked the device after checking with industry contacts that it was still widely used in hospitals. The system has three processors: a pump microcontroller running the critical firmware, an embedded Linux station, and a Wi-Fi card with its own ARM CPU. The team desoldered the pump's flash chip to dump its firmware, then worked out the load address from the datasheet's memory map so it could be analysed in IDA.

On the station, a years-old commit message in an open-source JSON bridge pointed to a format string bug. The team confirmed it on the device and used it for user-level access. A configuration export and import feature kept file permissions inside its tar archive, so a setuid binary and a replaced script gave root. Instead of hunting for another zero day to reach the pump's CAN bus, they used debug strings and function names in the pcs binary to map the command path, then attached gdb server to reuse an existing CAN operator.

With that access, they changed the tube head volume in the pump's internal database, which the pump uses to calculate how much drug it delivers. In a test run of 100 ml per hour with a 1000 VTBI target, the pump reported about five milliliters dispensed, while visibly about twice that was delivered. The attack only works while the pump is in standby or off, not while connected to a patient. The researchers reported five CVEs and stressed that patching these devices is costly for hospitals, so root access on a connected device is where a realistic medical attack begins.

talks.title: NL 2021: Automated Vulnerability Hunting In SMM Using Brick by Assaf & Itai
talks.teaser: Shows how SMM handlers in UEFI firmware can be checked for memory corruption bugs using an automated IDA-based tool.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces System Management Mode, the highly privileged x86 CPU mode that firmware uses for tasks such as power management and legacy device emulation. It explains how SMM memory (SMRAM) is isolated from the operating system, and how software triggers system management interrupts through a communication buffer that lives outside protected memory. That buffer is the attack surface the rest of the talk focuses on.

The speaker then covers common bug classes in SMM handlers. A missing size check on the communication buffer can let writes spill into SMRAM. Unvalidated nested pointers can give an attacker an arbitrary write target. Double fetches of a value can be exploited by a DMA device that changes the buffer between the validation check and its later use. Each class is illustrated with a small example and its mitigation, such as explicit size checks and copying sensitive fields into SMRAM local variables.

The talk then presents Brick, an open-source static analysis tool built on IDA. It extracts SMM images from firmware, runs heuristic detection modules for each bug class, and writes an HTML report. A live demo scans several modules and highlights suspicious handlers, while code from the EDK2 reference implementation comes out clean. The speaker reports a few CVEs found with the tool, notes that the heuristics produce false positives and negatives so human review remains necessary, and invites contributions to improve detection accuracy and speed.

talks.title: NL 2021 : When Threat Models Meet by Herbert Bos
talks.teaser: Shows how mixing separate threat models, such as memory corruption and speculative execution, defeats kernel defenses.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the idea that a threat model decides what an attacker tries to achieve, what they can do, and therefore what defenders should guard against. The speaker argues that teams often get these wrong by assuming attackers cannot do something that later research shows they can. Layered abstractions are presented as necessary but leaky, since shared hardware resources such as the cache let processes that appear isolated influence each other. A cache timing example shows how a secret key can be recovered by a neighbouring process.

The middle section covers ways attack classes can be combined. In a sequential chain, one technique is used first, such as a transient execution flaw that leaks randomized addresses before a buffer overflow is turned into code execution. A memory deduplication side channel is shown to leak pointers, which are then paired with a rowhammer bit flip to redirect control to a planted object. The most interesting case is a symbiotic combination, where speculative execution and conventional memory corruption strengthen each other. Corrupting a function pointer that is only used during speculation avoids crashes, so the attacker can probe kernel code and data pages and break kernel address layout randomization.

A live demonstration follows the same steps: locating the kernel base, finding a suitable data page, locating gadgets and reaching root. The takeaway is that isolated partitions and single-layer knowledge are not enough, because attackers combine threat models freely and defences must account for the layers beneath the code.

talks.title: Breaking chips with undetectable hardware trojans | Matt Venn | hardwear.io webinars 2021
talks.teaser: Shows how a change to a chip's doping layers can add a hidden trojan that alters logic without visible changes.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a short primer on how transistors work and how they combine into logic cells, using an inverter from the open SkyWater 130 nanometre design kit as the example. The speaker explains that layout files can be turned back into a netlist and simulated, even without the original design files, and demonstrates this on that small inverter.

The main demonstration uses a simple padlock chip built with the open-source OpenLane flow. The extracted circuit opens only with the correct button combination. The speaker then shows how changing just the diffusion layers, swapping the doping type in one transistor and cutting a connection in another, can force a flip-flop output high. Editing the layout in KLayout creates the altered mask data, and the simulation shows the lock opening on a wrong combination, one clock cycle sooner.

The talk closes on the limits of the attack. Inserting such a change requires access to the foundry's files, and mask sets are expensive, so the modification is framed as a proof of concept. Recovering the logic from a raw die is much harder without the process design kit. A large customer could counter it by requesting masks back for inspection, while shared shuttle runs make that impractical. The practical takeaway is that layout-level edits can change behaviour while looking identical under a microscope.

talks.title: Securing Your Microcontroller with Arm TrustZone Technology | Oren Hollander | hardwear_io Webinar
talks.teaser: Explains how Arm TrustZone for ARMv8-M isolates secure and non-secure code on microcontrollers.
talks.summary:
The session opens with why embedded software needs stronger isolation. The speaker walks through three real attacks: Stuxnet, which spread through Windows workstations and reached PLCs at an Iranian nuclear plant; LoJax, a UEFI firmware rootkit that survives operating system reinstalls; and a dynamic voltage and frequency scaling attack that can leak cryptographic keys from the secure area on Arm CPUs.

The core of the talk covers Arm TrustZone for ARMv8-M, the security extension aimed at Cortex-M microcontrollers. It explains how the address space is split into secure and non-secure regions using a Security Attribution Unit and an optional implementation-defined attribution unit, and how the two combine so that the stricter setting wins. It describes secure gateway veneers as the only controlled entry points from non-secure to secure code, how interrupts can be assigned to either world, and how registers are stacked and cleared on world switches. Toolchain support is covered too, including the CMSE extensions in GCC and Arm Compiler and SAU setup through CMSIS.

The closing section weighs what TrustZone does and does not stop. It protects software against software attacks, as long as the secure code itself has no bugs, and can block bus masters such as DMA when the silicon vendor uses the extra security signal. It does not stop glitching or power side-channel attacks, which need hardware countermeasures. Debug access to the secure world is governed by vendor-specific secure debug authentication, so practitioners should check what their chip provides.

talks.title: PCIe device security-The evolution of DMA attacks | Maggie & Cuauhtemoc | hardwear.io webinars 2021
talks.teaser: Traces the history of PCIe direct memory access attacks and the Intel features, like VT-d and SR-IOV, that defend against them.
talks.summary:
PCIe is a long-lived interconnect used in everything from small IoT boards to data center servers. The talk focuses on direct memory access (DMA), which lets a device read and write system memory without the CPU's involvement. That efficiency is also what makes it an attack path. The speakers argue that limiting physical access to expansion slots does not remove the risk, because integrated DMA engines and add-in cards with their own firmware can start memory transactions without the host's knowledge.

The presenters survey roughly two decades of DMA research and tooling, from early Windows kernel subversion and Thunderbolt work to FPGA-based implants and wireless DMA devices. They then cover defenses. Intel VT-d remaps device memory access so a device can only reach regions explicitly mapped to it, while SR-IOV splits one physical device into virtual functions that can be assigned to separate guests. For each, they outline benefits and tradeoffs, including the need to define DMAR tables correctly and the fact that VT-d does not isolate devices sharing an external PCIe bridge.

The closing section looks at emerging standards, including SPDM for device attestation and CXL for cache-coherent and memory-semantic links. The practical takeaways are to keep VT-d enabled for both pre-boot and runtime, review DMAR tables, keep devices behind the same bridge at the same trust level, and keep firmware and drivers current. A short Q&A covered how virtual functions are assigned and whether DMA can be used to capture memory for forensics.

talks.title: SpecFuzz: Bringing Spectre-type vulnerabilities to the surface | Oleksii Oleksenko | hardwear.io
talks.teaser: Explains how simulated branch mispredictions let fuzzing expose Spectre v1 bugs, so only vulnerable branches get costly patches.
talks.summary:
Oleksii Oleksenko presents SpecFuzz, a tool for finding Spectre v1 (bounds check bypass) vulnerabilities in software. Spectre is hard to find with ordinary testing because speculative execution leaves no visible trace to the program, and the usual mitigations slow applications by about 50 percent, so few projects adopt them. The approach is to simulate branch mispredictions inside the program itself. An LLVM compiler pass duplicates the branch entry with a flipped condition, checkpoints the program state, and rolls back after a bounded window of about 250 instructions. AddressSanitizer then flags invalid memory accesses made during this simulated speculation.

Because real programs produce very long lists of violations, the approach adds an analyzer that turns raw fuzzing results into readable reports, plus an automated patching step. The patcher hardens only the branches where violations were found, along with branches the fuzzer never reached, using either LFENCE or speculative load hardening. To keep the search manageable, the tool prioritizes single mispredictions and tests nested ones less often. On several libraries, including OpenSSL and a JSON parser, partial hardening ran noticeably faster than full hardening, with the gain depending on how much code the fuzzer covered.

The speaker noted that the method finds instances of known hardware-level Spectre flaws in software but cannot uncover new hardware bugs. On the tested libraries most violations appeared within the first hour, while large libraries kept yielding new ones for longer. The takeaway for developers is that fuzzing combined with targeted patching can make Spectre defenses affordable, and the tool's source code is publicly available.

talks.title: ICHSA 2021: Security & Safety: How can two walk together, except they be agreed by Aviv Barkai
talks.teaser: Compares functional safety and cyber security, showing where their goals, methods and standards overlap and where they diverge.
talks.summary:
Aviv Barkai, a hardware and systems engineer who spent years on functional safety before moving into cyber security, argues that the two fields share more ground than their separate practices suggest. He starts by defining functional safety as freedom from unacceptable risk, with the focus on physical injury and damage to health rather than financial loss. Reliability is framed through statistical error rates per hour, caused by factors such as cosmic radiation and electromigration, alongside systematic errors that are essentially design bugs.

Barkai then compares the two disciplines. Both aim to keep a system running correctly, both rely on defense in depth and layered mechanisms, and both care about integrity and availability. Security, however, deals with malicious rather than random failures, and its threat landscape is growing with more attackers and attacks, while safety's trend is toward fewer errors per hour. To illustrate availability demands, he notes that a tier 4 data center at 99.995% availability allows about 26.30 minutes of downtime per year. Confidentiality falls outside the core of safety.

On alignment, he points to IEEE 2851, which seeks a shared language for safety and security analysis, and ISO 21434 for road vehicle cyber security, which treats safety violations as attack outcomes. He sees academic proposals for unified frameworks but says no unified approach has emerged, with work in industry still running in parallel. His call to action is for security specialists to learn from safety techniques such as diverse mechanisms, and for safety engineers to learn from security monitoring, so that the disciplines work jointly.

talks.title: ICHSA 2021: IoT PUF or: How I Learned to Stop Worrying and Love Security Research by Kang Wang
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning ICHSA 2021: IoT PUF or: How I Learned to Stop Worrying and Love Security Research by Kang Wang.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation, Kang Wang of Alibaba Group shares insights on IoT device identity threats, physically unclonable functions (PUF), and broader methodologies for security researchers. Framing device unclonability through historical precedents—such as ancient Chinese tiger tallies and secret society paper tokens—Wang illustrates how modern IoT security faces severe cloning challenges across fragmented and resource-constrained environments. Beyond hardware identification and SRAM PUF challenges, Wang presents practical security research case studies covering drone frequency hopping, click farms, microphone circuit behavior, and productivity methodologies for hackers.

### Key Topics
- **Unclonability and Historical Context:** Using historical artifacts such as the ancient bronze tiger tally and paper tokens from late 19th-century secret societies to illustrate challenge-response pairs, token verification, and the economics of cloning.
- **IoT Identification Challenges:** Limitations of standard identification methods including IP addresses (easily masked by VPNs/proxies), MAC addresses (easily modified via command-line tools like dd in OpenWrt flash partitions), LAN scanning, browser fingerprinting, and MEMS sensor defects.
- **Physically Unclonable Functions (PUF):** Utilizing startup state unpredictability in SRAM cells, where roughly 80–84% of cells are constantly biased to 0 or 1 while ~20% exhibit usable randomness.
- **Economics and Supply Chain Realities in Research:** Reverse engineering commercial off-the-shelf hardware (such as DJI Phantom 2 controllers) to discover that design decisions are driven by cost and off-the-shelf chip availability rather than bespoke engineering.
- **Privacy and Practical Hacking:** Examining privacy trade-offs, click farm economics, hardware mute circuits (such as capacitor discharge in the Amazon Echo), policy hacking, and hacker productivity tools.

### Technical Details
- **SRAM PUF Characteristics and Deployment:** An SRAM cell operates like a 1-bit latch with a balanced architecture. On power-up, while ~84% of cells stabilize consistently across multiple boots, the remainder provide entropy. However, practical engineering deployments face common-mode noise from temperature and magnetic interference, aging degradation, and strict engineering constraints—specifically that firmware engineers resist modifying bootloader code due to the risk of bricking production batches of 10,000 to 100,000 devices. Fast search algorithms are also required to manage weak PUFs with limited challenge-response pairs.
- **RF Reverse Engineering:** In an investigation of a DJI Phantom 2 drone remote controller utilizing an RFMD ML2730 radio chip, Wang captured channel sequences across the 10 kHz to 100 MHz spread using a real-time signal analyzer (after encountering bandwidth limitations with a 20 MHz HackRF). The frequency hopping pattern simplified to a basic formula: `(channel - 14) mod 36`, matching legacy designs used by Japanese radio brand Futaba.
- **Sensor and Hardware Audits:** Accelerometer angles (cosine theta) can reveal automated click farms where racks of phones share the exact same physical tilt. Hardware privacy audits on the Amazon Echo mute button showed that due to the slow discharge of the microphone's RLC equivalent circuit, ADC data could still capture microphone signals for up to 60 seconds after activation.

### Takeaways
Wang emphasizes that security researchers should "follow the money," recognizing that real-world engineering teams face commercial and cost constraints. Furthermore, the talk advocates for adopting diverse hacker mindsets: low-cost hardware hacking (e.g., RTL-SDR), policy hacking (such as Project Zero's strict 90-day disclosure rule to eliminate internal negotiation), and personal productivity hacks (leveraging Makefiles, Unix mailboxes, RSS-to-email pipelines, and open-source workflows) with the ultimate objective of using security skills to protect others.

talks.teaser: Traces the design of the open source CANtact Pro, a two-channel CAN FD and single-wire CAN adapter, and lessons from building it.
talks.summary:
Eric Evenchick introduces Controller Area Network (CAN), a multi-master bus common in cars, industrial control and avionics, and explains why it is often trusted by default: any node that can send frames is believed by everyone else on the bus. He describes higher-layer protocols built on it, such as ISO-TP for longer payloads and diagnostic services, and calibration protocols that can expose memory access if left enabled in production.

He then traces the history of the open source CANtact line, from the first low-cost USB adapter built on an STM32 microcontroller to the goal of a two-channel CANtact Pro supporting CAN FD and single-wire CAN. Design choices covered include an NXP Cortex-M4 part with a USB bootloader, discrete isolation for the signal and power paths, and a case built from a prefab enclosure customized by a manufacturer. On the software side, he covers Linux SocketCAN support, a cross-platform driver written in Rust over libusb, and Python bindings published to PyPI through automated GitHub builds.

The talk closes with practical lessons from hardware production: plan enclosures and mechanical fit from the start, expect bill-of-materials costs to multiply through wholesale and retail pricing, get feedback from pre-release testers, and account for component shortages. Next steps include improving the Rust command-line interface, upstreaming CAN FD support into the Linux kernel, and building a breakout board for OBD-II connectors.

talks.title: Secure Builds for Secure Software | Chris Frantz | hardwear.io USA Conference 2021
talks.teaser: Explains how hermetic, reproducible builds let auditors verify firmware for an open source silicon root of trust.
talks.summary:
Chris Frantz, software lead for the OpenTitan project, explained why the open source silicon root of trust needs a build that outside auditors can verify. Its boot code, the mask ROM and ROM extension, is built only from public repository code, so anyone should get identical binaries from a given version. He framed the problem as the hidden choices in a plain make invocation: which tools run, where dependencies come from, whether host details leak in, and whether builds reproduce.

To show the stakes, he described a real failure where an unlisted generated header made a build converge only after repeated runs. He then listed requirements: an acyclic dependency graph, queryable relationships, multi-language support, sandboxed tools, managed third-party dependencies, and reproducible outputs. The project chose Bazel, with rules written in Starlark, pinned dependencies verified by SHA-256 hash, and a demonstration of querying the UART driver's dependency graph. He also noted test-only rules and selecting tests affected by a changed file list for presubmit.

Near the end he covered air-gapped builds, where dependencies are fetched and verified ahead of time for transfer into a secure environment. He also listed open work, including Verilog builds, Rust firmware, and bringing Cargo dependencies under Bazel. His takeaway was to treat build configuration as configuration management, since reproducible artifacts let outside parties confirm what ships.

talks.title: Proving the efficacy of software countermeasures for fault injection | Joshua Beaker | hardwear.io
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Proving the efficacy of software countermeasures for fault injection | Joshua Beaker | hardwear.io.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this hardwear.io conference presentation, Joshua Baker (also referred to as Joshua Beaker), a security analyst at Riscure, explains how to design, test, and combine software-only countermeasures to protect embedded software against hardware fault injection (FI) attacks. While hardware security research often focuses heavily on offensive attacks, this talk demonstrates practical defensive techniques implemented entirely in software (primarily C and ARM assembly) without requiring dedicated hardware modifications.

### Key Topics
- **Fault Injection Mechanics & Fault Model**: Fault injection involves using external disturbances (such as electrical or electromagnetic glitching) to alter a chip's internal electrical state, changing stored data or instruction opcodes. Baker uses a fault model assuming an attacker who can induce a single bit flip or skip an instruction.
- **Simulation with `fi_sim`**: To evaluate code resilience, Baker utilizes `fi_sim`, an open-source tool developed by Mark te Stroet (referred to as Mark Time). It simulates every possible fault against a target binary—specifically pineboot, an image verification bootloader—and tracks which injected faults successfully bypass security checks.
- **Seven Software Countermeasures**:
  1. *Minimal Branches*: Inlining functions using C attributes to eliminate branch instructions, preventing attackers from glitching branch target addresses or skipping function calls.
  2. *Flow Control*: Maintaining a rolling tally/counter of unique, non-trivial constants (such as prime values) added across each executed function, and verifying the cumulative tally before critical operations.
  3. *Assign Values / Non-arbitrary Values & Trapdoors*: Avoiding naive zero/one or boolean indicators for success/failure in favor of complex values (e.g., specific hex constants) and periodically verifying sensitive stored values via checksums or encryption.
  4. *Decision Check*: Performing duplicate checks on critical decisions while using `volatile` variables to prevent the compiler from optimizing out redundant conditional logic.
  5. *Aggregate Check*: Avoiding the premature combination of multiple checks into a single boolean state, which otherwise creates a single point of failure for an attacker.
  6. *Loop Check*: Verifying that loop iteration counters reached their expected final value or range, protecting against early loop termination or skipped iterations.
  7. *Crypto Check*: Mitigating fault-based key recovery attacks by re-encrypting or decrypting immediately after encryption and verifying the outcome against the original value.

### Technical Details & Evaluation
Baker emphasizes that isolated countermeasures often add code that inadvertently increases the attack surface. In an evaluation against pineboot:
- The baseline code had 327 exploitable fault locations.
- Adding initial countermeasures initially increased the fault count (at one point adding 222 possible faults), as newly introduced branch or arithmetic instructions were not yet hardened.
- Progressing through the defensive pipeline brought the counts down from 340 to 250, then 268, and finally down to just 8 exploitable faults once all countermeasures were combined.
- The 8 remaining faults were entirely bit flips (no instruction skips/NOPs), consisting of 4 load faults in raw assembly (`entry.S`), 3 subfaults related to an un-inlined function call, and 1 branch fault inside encryption routines.

### Takeaways
- Software countermeasures must be combined comprehensively; like patching a leaky pipe, securing only one part of the code shifts vulnerability pressure to unprotected areas.
- Developers must thoroughly test implementations in simulators like `fi_sim` rather than guessing, because compiler optimizations can strip away redundant defensive code.
- Defenses introduce measurable overhead: in the pineboot demonstration, code size roughly doubled and execution time doubled or tripled, meaning teams must carefully evaluate runtime tradeoffs when protecting critical assets.

talks.title: ICHSA 2021: Inspectre Gadget Connecting the Dots b/w Prefetch, Meltdown & Foreshadow by Daniel Gruss
talks.teaser: The session links prefetch-era findings to kernel Spectre gadgets that still enable Foreshadow-style leakage from virtual machines.
talks.summary:
The talk revisits a prefetch-based address-translation attack from 2016 and asks why it still succeeded after KPTI and KAISER-style kernel hardening. Through controlled experiments—omitting prefetch, varying loop counts, swapping instructions, and testing across patched and unpatched kernels—the presenter shows that documented prefetch behavior is not what drives the leak. The real mechanism is speculative dereference inside the kernel: attacker-chosen virtual addresses sit in registers when a syscall or interrupt mispredicts into a gadget that touches those values, loading cache lines without a user-space prefetch.

That model reframes Meltdown, Spectre, and Foreshadow as connected microarchitectural effects. Foreshadow’s reliance on the present bit and L1-centric mitigations is challenged by hypervisor gadgets that fetch host-aligned data while a guest runs; a recorded demo recovers host physical bytes from inside a VM. The same primitive can hunt register contents, including scenarios where direct register readout is blocked, by treating values as addresses and binary-searching a mapped space.

Practitioners should treat root-cause claims about side channels as fragile: mitigations that blocked an older binary may fail when compiler register layout or kernel gadgets change. Full Spectre v2 protections matter even when partial features such as IBRS exist, and cross-vendor CPUs that are Spectre-susceptible appear vulnerable to this class of speculative dereferencing.

talks.title: ICHSA 2021: Secure Hardware Design: Starting from the Roots of Trust by Ingrid Verbauwhede
talks.teaser: Outlines how to build secure hardware from the root of trust upward, using PIN checks and device attacks as examples.
talks.summary:
The talk takes a design-first view of secure hardware, starting from the roots of trust that the rest of a system depends on. It frames the work across levels of abstraction, from high-level architecture and security policy down to individual components and their implementations, and argues that security has to be considered at each level rather than added at the end.

The middle section works through concrete examples. A PIN verification scheme is used to show how an attacker can exploit differences in execution time and repeated guessing, and how measurable device behaviour can leak information. The talk also touches on random number generation, where statistical testing of the output is presented as part of checking an implementation. A connected camera that links to cloud services is discussed as another case where the surrounding system matters.

The closing part returns to design practice. The takeaway is that secure hardware needs trust anchored at the bottom of the stack, careful choice of components and countermeasures, and verification of each implementation, because a sound design can still be broken by how it is built and used.

talks.title: ICHSA 2021: Timeless Timing Attacks by Christina Pöpper
talks.teaser: Shows how ordering network responses instead of timing them lets attackers leak server secrets with far fewer requests.
talks.summary:
Timing side channels appear when a program's running time depends on secret data, so an attacker can learn about the secret without reading it directly. Classic remote timing attacks time network round trips, but jitter is far larger than the server's processing differences, so they need very many requests and statistics to cope with the noise.

The talk's timeless variant drops absolute timing and instead sends two requests at once, either bundled into one HTTP/2 packet via multiplexing or, for HTTP/1.x, wrapped through Tor, so the server handles both concurrently. The attacker only records which response returns first. Both requests share the same network path, so the order reflects the processing-time difference whenever that difference exceeds the combined jitter. Measured timing differences as small as about 100 nanoseconds were reported, versus roughly 10 microseconds for classical attacks, with far fewer measurements. The gain over networks was considerable, while the gain on a local system was small.

Defenses discussed include constant-time execution, which is hard for many applications, adding random delays, and avoiding packet combining, which can cost performance. The attack depends on responses being produced concurrently and immediately, so sequential cryptographic operations limit it. Open work covers other potentially vulnerable protocols and countermeasures. The takeaway is that response ordering alone can leak server secrets, so concurrency belongs in remote timing assessments.

talks.title: Artificial Intelligence for Fault Injection Parameter Selection | Marina Krček | hardwear.io webinar
talks.teaser: Shows how memetic and sampling-based search can pick laser fault injection settings far more efficiently than random testing.
talks.summary:
Marina Krček, a PhD candidate at TU Delft who works with STMicroelectronics, addresses how to choose settings for fault injection attacks on hardware. These attacks disturb a device's environment, through voltage or clock glitching, electromagnetic pulses or lasers, to provoke faulty behaviour that an analyst can exploit. The main obstacle is that each technique has several parameters, so the search space grows too large for exhaustive testing. The talk cites an electromagnetic example where an exhaustive search would take roughly 29,000 years, and a five-parameter laser setup that still needed about 59 days even with narrowed intervals.

The first method builds a sensitivity curve from a fast characterization approach for semi-invasive attacks. Measurements across a scan area, varying laser power and pulse width, are classified by device response and scored by impact. A multilayer perceptron then predicts the level of influence at unmeasured settings, and the predictions closely matched an exhaustive search on the encryption target. The authors reported that results transfer between samples of the same target.

The second method applies a memetic algorithm, which combines a genetic algorithm with a local search, to laser fault injection on a chip from ST while register data was being loaded. Fitness rewards fault responses, and candidate points are sorted by coordinates to limit slow motor stage movement. On average, random search found 0.9 fail results while the memetic approach found 31. Comparing initial population sampling methods, Latin hypercube and Taguchi arrays gave more stable outcomes than random initialisation, so well-distributed starting samples are suggested where overhead allows. Future work includes larger populations and neural networks to predict unmeasured parameter sets.

talks.title: Call for Papers | Pro Tips by Cristofaro Mune | hardwear.io 2021
talks.teaser: Offers conference submission advice: prior-art research, valuing negative results, and clear impact and methodology in proposals.
talks.summary:
A veteran presenter reflects on submitting and speaking at a hardware-focused security conference, from early European editions through the first U.S. event. Earlier stage work included Linux privilege escalation via voltage fault injection and remote timing attacks using hardware timestamping on networked devices, alongside recurring trainings on secure boot and trusted execution environments.

The program is framed as welcoming research that spans silicon-level fault injection, devices, IoT, embedded software, and side-channel or microarchitectural analysis on CPUs. With the call for papers open, the speaker encourages researchers whose daily work sits at the hardware–software boundary to consider submitting.

The core of the session is practical CFP guidance applicable beyond a single venue. Speakers should map existing work before claiming novelty, since duplicate “first ever” claims waste everyone’s time. Failed or inconclusive experiments remain worth presenting when the process and conclusions advance the field. Submissions should spell out impact and methodology in detail so reviewers grasp both results and why the work matters to the broader ecosystem.

talks.title: Hunting for the keys of the SAMA5 castle | Dmitry Janushkevich | hardwear.io Webinar 2021
talks.teaser: Shows how power analysis and a CBC weakness let the speaker extract customer keys from a SAMA5 boot ROM.
talks.summary:
This talk walks through a security review of the SAMA5 family of Microchip (formerly Atmel) system-on-chip devices, which are used in human machine interfaces, security gateways, scanners, printers and point-of-sale terminals. Starting from public material, the researcher used the vendor's open-source Samba tool, whose source documented how applets are loaded and how the secure-mode protocol works. Applets are privileged code that runs with access to the whole system, so compromising one could affect every device. The datasheet also pointed to ROM behaviour kept under NDA, which made the boot code a natural target.

The researcher then chained two weaknesses. Using a ChipWhisperer Lite, timing and power measurements showed that the CMAC check on an applet leaked information through its comparison, and a bit-by-bit attack on the power trace recovered a valid tag in a little over twenty minutes. Because the applet is encrypted with CBC, tampering with one ciphertext block lets an attacker flip chosen bits in the next plaintext block. A forged applet could therefore dump the ROM, and from there the customer keys. The issues were reported to the vendor and affect most devices in the series, and the mitigation was limited because the secure monitor had to stay enabled.

The closing lessons are that the design, implementation and verification of a system-on-chip must all be correct, and that getting cryptography right in software is hard even when the hardware is sound. Power analysis turned out to be cheaper and less specialised than expected. The talk also argues for keeping boot ROM code small and for relying on keys rather than secrecy of the design.

talks.title: Practical Hardware Attacks on Deep Learning | Sanghyun Hong | Hardwear.io Webinar 2021
talks.teaser: Shows how Rowhammer bit flips and cache side channels can degrade or reverse-engineer deep learning models running on shared hardware.
talks.summary:
The talk treats deep learning models as software running on physical hardware, a view the speaker argues adversarial machine learning research has largely ignored. Most prior work studies models in isolation, so fault-injection and side-channel threats to the underlying platform, especially in cloud deployments, get little attention.

The first case study covers Rowhammer, a fault-injection technique that flips bits in DRAM. Flipping one high exponent bit in a weight can sharply reduce a network's accuracy. Across eight convolutional models, each contained at least one bit whose flip caused an accuracy drop above 98 percent, and dropout and batch normalization did not remove the weakness. In a cloud virtual machine setup, a weak attacker who flipped bits at random still caused an accuracy drop over 10 percent in 62 percent of attacks, usually within a few minutes, with only six program crashes observed.

The second case uses a Flush+Reload cache side channel to observe a single inference and reconstruct the architecture of a victim's neural network. The method relies on regularities in how layers execute in sequence and how matrix multiplication loops reveal layer sizes. On two custom architectures the reconstruction had zero error and took 12 CPU hours, compared with 40k GPU hours for an architecture search. The speaker concludes that system-level defenses may not be enough and that hardware and software need co-designed protections for deep learning systems.

talks.title: Automotive product security (or the same old story but on wheels) | Rafael Boix Carpi | Hardwear.io
talks.teaser: Shows why automotive ECU security keeps repeating old embedded-device mistakes, and what developers can do about it.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that automotive security is repeating a pattern seen earlier in pay-TV smart cards and other embedded devices: products are first broken through software, then hardened, then attacked through hardware. Rafael Boix Carpi traces that history and points to the 2015 remote Jeep attack, which drew wide press coverage and pushed carmakers and governments to act. Recent standards and UN regulations now make cyber security a condition for selling new vehicles in Europe, though much of today's car software was designed before that shift.

The middle of the talk looks at why automotive projects still struggle. Developers and security engineers often read the same requirement differently, and vague wording leaves gaps. Threat analysis should weigh attacker cost against profit, and a scalable attack changes that balance: a 2018 European study estimated odometer-tampering fraud at 1.31 billion euros, with a fraud scenario of 8.77 billion. Other examples included a pseudo-random generator used where a cryptographic one was needed, safety-certified chips that could be glitched when tested from an attacker's view, and a hard-coded password that safety reasoning had accepted.

The closing advice is to treat safety and security as separate goals, validate every assumption, and train the whole development chain. Teams should build threat models that include physical access and scale, and they should understand why something breaks, not only how to break it.

talks.title: Security Property-driven Fault Injection Assessment in Modern SoCs by Farimah Farahmandi
talks.teaser: Shows a property-driven framework that pinpoints critical SoC locations vulnerable to fault injection attacks.
talks.summary:
IoT devices are built on system-on-chips that store keys and sensitive data, and hardware flaws are hard to patch once silicon is produced. The talk surveyed fault injection methods, including clock and voltage glitching, laser-based attacks on SRAM, and focused ion beam edits. Such faults can force a chip to store wrong values or skip critical instructions. Existing countermeasures are limited: active shielding and sensors are costly, while parity and redundancy schemes give partial coverage. Designers rarely know which parts of a chip to protect.

The speaker presented a framework that takes security properties written by the designer, builds a fault model covering the spatial and temporal control of a given injection technique, and simulates faults at gate level. Locations whose faults violate a property are reported, and the search is narrowed using cone-of-influence and feasibility checks. In an AES case study, a fault during a state transition could make the done signal assert after the first round, exposing key and plaintext information. Another case showed that don't-care states, once synthesis connects them to protected states, can bypass protection without appearing in standard verification.

Benchmark results identified a small set of critical locations that could be protected locally, aiming for stronger protection at manageable overhead. The analysis was simulation-based, with FPGA validation underway for one property. Planned work includes extending the framework to RTL and physical layers, adding fault models, and extracting properties automatically.

talks.title: The Practical Design & Implementation of Zero-Trust Supply Chains for Electronic Products
talks.teaser: Explains how a hardware maker can reduce supply chain risk by verifying components and shrinking its trusted base.
talks.summary:
Two security architects from Bloomberg, Phil Vashon and Joel, explain how their company builds trust into electronic products such as the biometric authentication devices used to log in to its services. They begin with the older model used by the IBM 4758, where a trusted factory and an anti-tamper canister protected off-the-shelf parts, and contrast it with a modern security token that keeps its trust inside a single secure microcontroller. They then walk through the threats they consider: counterfeit, recycled, cloned or tampered chips, interdiction in transit, and contract assembly lines whose workers cannot be vetted.

The middle of the talk covers how they choose what to defend. They accept that attacks on silicon fabrication and insiders are very costly, so they focus on downstream stages such as packaging, logistics and board assembly. Their trusted base is limited to the biometric sensor and the secure microcontroller, which must prove their identity and communicate over encrypted, authenticated channels. Flash, RAM and the surrounding circuit board are treated as reliability problems rather than security risks. They also describe working with vendors early, co-designing features, checking that delivered parts match the specification, and auditing manufacturing steps.

The closing part stresses that the threat model and usability, budget and time to market set the limits of what is practical. Attestation and telemetry let them watch devices in the field, since the user may hold a device indefinitely. The Q&A adds that vendor test modes and debug ports are a persistent concern, and that the speakers could not share any public examples of supply chain attacks on their own products.

talks.title: A Look Into (Few) SCA & Fault attack vulnerabilities in lattice based PQC schemes & Countermeasures
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning A Look Into (Few) SCA & Fault attack vulnerabilities in lattice based PQC schemes & Countermeasures.
talks.summary:
### Overview
This talk explores practical implementation security in post-quantum cryptography (PQC), with a particular focus on lattice-based schemes. As classical public-key cryptography faces threats from quantum algorithms, NIST initiated a standardization process for quantum-resistant alternatives, many of which rely on lattice problems such as Learning With Errors (LWE) and Module-LWE. While these mathematical constructions offer theoretical security against quantum computers, their physical implementations on embedded devices and microcontrollers remain susceptible to physical attacks, specifically fault injection attacks and side-channel analysis (SCA).

### Key Topics
- **Post-Quantum Cryptography & Lattices:** Background on NIST PQC standardization and underlying hardness problems such as LWE, where public matrix operations and noise terms are used to protect secret keys.
- **Fault Injection Attacks:** Examination of physical attack techniques—ranging from low-cost clock or voltage glitching to high-cost localized laser or electromagnetic pulse injections—aimed at disrupting computations.
- **Side-Channel Analysis (SCA):** Exploiting incidental physical leakage (power consumption, electromagnetic emissions, or timing) during sensitive operations such as polynomial multiplication, NTT (Number Theoretic Transform), and message decoding.
- **Countermeasures:** Implementation defenses including algorithmic verification steps, masking techniques, and constant-time execution.

### Technical Details
- **Fault Attacks on Lattice Schemes:** The speaker illustrates how injecting faults into intermediate variables can drastically reduce scheme security. For instance, altering a single bit or skipping a specific loop condition allows attackers to establish a simplified system of linear equations, enabling key recovery through mathematical solvers without needing to solve the full underlying lattice problem. Faults during signature generation (such as bypassing rejection sampling or corrupting polynomial addition operations) can similarly leak sensitive secret key information.
- **Side-Channel Leakage in Decryption and NTT:** Side-channel leakage is evaluated across critical components such as the Number Theoretic Transform (NTT) and decryption routines. When implementations perform secret-dependent operations without constant-time behavior or proper masking, power and EM traces (even down to single-trace template attacks) can reveal intermediate values. 
- **Combined Threats & Verification:** The talk notes that verifying ciphertext integrity or public-key validity before completing decryption can mitigate certain oracle-style chosen-ciphertext side-channel attacks, though verification itself must be implemented securely to prevent timing or fault-based bypasses.

### Takeaways
- Mathematical quantum resistance does not automatically guarantee implementation security; physical microcontrollers running PQC schemes require dedicated hardening.
- Even single-bit faults or slight timing/power leakages during polynomial operations can completely compromise secret keys.
- Designers and developers must apply comprehensive protections—combining masking, constant-time primitives, and fault detection/redundancy—rather than relying solely on the theoretical hardness of lattice problems.

talks.title: CANanalyze: a python framework for automotive protocols | Erwan Le Disez | Etienne Charron
talks.teaser: Shows a Python framework that emulates and validates automotive CAN gateways and probes UDS diagnostic services.
talks.summary:
Automotive electronic control units exchange data over CAN buses, and the multimedia network is a likely entry point for an attacker because it connects to Bluetooth and Wi-Fi. A central gateway is meant to filter what crosses into the vehicle network, which matters because UDS debug services can expose memory read and write functions. The speakers said these debug services must be confirmed closed in the field, and that the gateway must be verified to block sensitive UDS frames.

The talk then covered the physical side of CAN testing: a daisy-chain bus with termination resistors, OBD-II access, and interface hardware, with Linux SocketCAN support for software access. They presented CANanalyze, a Python framework developed by Renault and Antares from an internal collection of scripts. It offers a simple API layered over UDS, ISO-TP and CAN abstractions, and can use several hardware interfaces at once. Its scripts emulate a gateway driven by a JSON calibration file of routing and filtering rules keyed on CAN ID and payload mask, validate a physical gateway against that file, find UDS addresses, and list supported services from negative responses.

A live demo ran a virtual gateway with a whitelist configuration alongside a validation script that sweeps CAN IDs. A second calibration with one extra ID was flagged as an error. The takeaway is that the tool targets quick penetration-test validation with a deliberately small set of UDS services, is available on GitHub, and the speakers invited contributions.

talks.title: Looking at Silicon | Ken Shirriff
talks.teaser: Shows how microscope photos of vintage chip dies reveal transistors, logic gates, microcode ROMs and FPGA configuration bits.
talks.summary:
The talk shows how to read the structure of old silicon chips from microscope photos of their dies. It starts with the Intel 8008, showing how individual transistors look as switches and how they combine into inverters, NAND and NOR gates, bit-storage loops and registers. The speaker then covers the HP nanoprocessor, where each chip needed its own bias voltage, and the FPGA, where repeated tiles hold configuration memory, lookup tables and routing switches that map onto a bitstream format.

The middle section focuses on reading ROM contents directly from the die. For the Sinclair scientific calculator, the speaker recovered a 320-word program and built a simulator to show how trig and logarithm functions were approximated with slow, repeated decimal shifts. In the Intel 8086, a 10-kilobit microcode ROM was read out and checked against die photos, which revealed a couple of undocumented instructions. The 8087 constant ROM was shown to hold the binary value of pi. Counterfeit cases followed: a memory chip that was really a touch-tone generator, and an 8086 that turned out to be a semi-custom logic array.

The closing part gives practical advice for newcomers. Ceramic and metal-can packages can be opened with a saw or chisel instead of harsh acids. A metallurgical microscope, many overlapping photos stitched into one high-resolution image, and household chemicals for stripping oxide and metal layers make the work feasible at home. Online die photos also allow practice. The speaker notes that analysis becomes much harder after about 1980, when two metal layers and tiny features call for electron microscopy.

talks.title: JackHammer: Rowhammer and Cache Attacks on Heterogeneous FPGA-CPU Platforms | Daniel | Thore | Zane
talks.teaser: Shows how an FPGA on a shared CPU platform can run faster Rowhammer and cache attacks against host memory.
talks.summary:
Cloud providers increasingly rent FPGAs alongside CPUs, and this talk asks what hardware sharing means when an accelerator and a processor use the same memory system. The speakers compared two Intel Arria 10 setups: an FPGA integrated on the CPU die and linked over UPI and PCIe, and a discrete PCIe accelerator card. They explained the differing address spaces, the DMA paths between the two chips, and the cache hints the FPGA can set.

Timing measurements from the FPGA could distinguish last-level cache hits from DRAM accesses, and the integrated version also had a cache of its own with a constant response time. Writes with cache hints did not behave as documented, which the team traced to Intel's DDIO feature. That limits eviction-based attacks to a subset of cache ways. As a proof of concept, they built a covert channel from the FPGA to the CPU that reached 94.98 kilobits per second using repetition encoding.

The main result is Jackhammer, a Rowhammer implementation that runs from the FPGA against host memory and bypasses the CPU caches. In the tests it sent more memory accesses per second than a CPU-based Rowhammer attack and flipped about four times as many bits per second in many cases. A fault injection against an RSA-CRT signature in wolfSSL, reported and fixed in December 2019, showed the bit flips could be used in practice. At the standard 64 millisecond refresh interval Jackhammer caused faults 25 percent faster than the CPU attack, rising to 185 percent when the refresh rate was doubled. The takeaway for practitioners is that accelerators sharing memory with other tenants belong in the hardware threat model.

talks.title: Things not to do when using an IOMMU | Ilja van Sprundel & Joseph Tartaro
talks.teaser: Catalogs how kernel drivers misuse IOMMU mappings, from leaked and late unmaps to information leaks reachable over DMA.
talks.summary:
An IOMMU lets a host limit which memory a device can reach through DMA, acting like a firewall between peripherals and system RAM. The talk takes the IOMMU and platform as working correctly and focuses on driver code, where mappings are set up and where mistakes happen. It traces how DMA went from a trusted path to an attack surface, and why external ports, secure devices and virtual machines depend on IOMMU protection.

The speakers grouped recurring driver mistakes and illustrated each with examples from Linux and FreeBSD. Mapping errors include leaked mappings that outlive their buffers, device-controlled unmaps driven by pointers in shared memory, and unmapping only after freeing. Race conditions arise when drivers validate data in memory the device can still change. Information leaks come from buffers that are never cleared, or from structure padding and unused fields. Because mappings are page-granular, small buffers can expose neighbouring stack or heap data, and a demonstration against an emulated network card recovered credentials from kernel heap memory.

Their conclusion is that enabling an IOMMU only stops trivial DMA attacks. Stronger protection requires drivers to unmap as soon as possible, keep pointers private, validate every device-supplied value, clear buffers and keep function pointers out of shared memory. They called for simpler, granularity-aware APIs, consistent IOMMU deployment and better documentation, noting that they were not aware of any secure-coding standard for driver DMA.

talks.teaser: Walks through black-box reverse engineering of car ECUs, from locating debug headers to CAN scans and firmware extraction.
talks.summary:
Nils Weiss and Enrico Pozzobon, automotive security researchers at the University of Applied Sciences in Regensburg, present a step-by-step approach to black-box reverse engineering of ECUs without the vehicle they belong to. The opening part covers hardware analysis: identifying interfaces on a board, finding debug headers and locating external memory chips. It also looks at the practical difficulties of operating an ECU on a bench rather than in a car.

The middle of the talk moves to the CAN bus. The speakers explain transport layer scans, which examine how messages are split into frames and how flow control frames govern the exchange, followed by application layer scans that probe the services the unit responds to. Both are presented as stages in working out how the ECU communicates.

The later sections show an example exploitation of an ECU and an example firmware extraction, then move into exploit development built on those results. For practitioners, the useful takeaway is an ordered workflow: map the hardware, reach the bus, enumerate the protocol layers, then extract firmware and build an exploit from what was found.

talks.title: Toasting MCUs: A Firmware Extraction by EMFI | Karim & Olivier | Hardwear.io Conference Netherlands
talks.teaser: Shows a low-cost programmable electromagnetic fault injector and its use to bypass firmware protections on an IoT microcontroller.
talks.summary:
A security team from Ledger presents a low-cost electromagnetic fault injection (EMFI) platform they built because commercial tools were expensive and earlier homemade designs used a fixed voltage and an external power supply. The board runs from USB at 3.3 V. A step-up stage feeds a voltage multiplier that reaches about 1.2 kV, charging a ceramic capacitor bank that discharges quickly through an IGBT. An STM32 microcontroller sets the output voltage via PWM and reads it back through an ADC, so pulse strength can be tuned in software.

The design choices are explained: ceramic capacitors for fast discharge despite limited energy storage, a dedicated gate driver for the IGBT, and two SMA outputs that let the pulse polarity be flipped without building another coil. The presenter then tested the tool on an IoT chip with three protection levels. By scanning the die surface and changing the voltage per location, he found that low voltages had little effect while higher ones crashed the chip, with roughly 300 to 500 V being the useful range. At 400 V, a fault against the level-bypass command succeeded in about 60 percent of attempts. A later fault during a read-memory command, checked through power traces, succeeded about 30 percent of the time.

The closing comparison points to portable USB power, programmable voltage and a total build cost near 200 dollars. In the Q&A, the team said probe distance was not varied because voltage served as the tuning knob, that some packages needed decapsulation while others did not, and that closely spaced pulses were possible because the capacitors keep residual charge. The takeaway is that a cheap, programmable EMFI board can support repeated fault attempts against real microcontroller protections.

talks.title: Look mum, no key! Bypassing Encrypted Secure Boot | Cristofaro Mune & Niek Timmers
talks.teaser: Shows how electromagnetic fault injection bypasses ESP32 encrypted secure boot and reads plaintext flash without the key.
talks.summary:
The talk shows how electromagnetic fault injection can defeat encrypted secure boot on the ESP32, an Xtensa-based IoT chip, without the encryption key. The team first checked their probe and setup by reproducing earlier voltage-glitching results and using a simple counting loop to confirm the chip responded to the technique. They then mapped a sensitive spot on the die and tuned timing and pulse strength against a trigger tied to the end of bootloader loading, reaching a signature-check bypass at about two successful glitches per minute.

Next they glitched the memory copy loop that moves the bootloader into RAM, so that copied pointer values reached the program counter and gave control of execution. Flash encryption blocked this route because decryption is transparent to the CPU. Instead they used the ROM download mode, which cannot be disabled, to place code in SRAM, and found that SRAM survives a watchdog warm reset. Glitching the reboot redirected execution into leftover data, and from there they reached the normal-mode command handler and read plaintext flash, checking each attempt with a liveness command.

A single EM glitch thus bypassed secure boot and flash encryption and extracted plaintext flash. The disclosure produced CVEs, and revision 3 of the chip adds fault-injection checks and permanently disables the bootloader function. The speakers advised starting with low pulse strength, since strong pulses can damage nearby components. Their takeaway is that fault injection should not be limited to skipping instructions, because combining it with other techniques makes attacks far more effective.

talks.title: Beyond Root: Custom Firmware for Embedded Mobile Chipsets | Christopher Wade | Hardwear.io Webinar
talks.teaser: Shows how a phone's proprietary NFC chip was reverse engineered, its firmware checks bypassed, and custom firmware loaded.
talks.summary:
This talk looks at the proprietary NFC controllers inside smartphones, which stay closed off even when the phone is rooted. The speaker starts with a Samsung NFC chip in an older Galaxy S6, rebuilds its firmware update protocol from logcat traces, and maps the command set. Analysing the update flow, the speaker finds a bootloader that accepts oversized hash and signature sizes. That overflows the stack and allows a jump past the signature check into custom code.

To work without debugging access, the speaker emulates the bootloader with the Unicorn CPU emulator, supplying the I2C registers it reads so that update commands can be replayed and fuzzed. On a newer Galaxy S9 chip the protocol had changed, with SHA-256 replacing SHA-1 and an earlier memory-read command removed. The speaker recovers the stack size from crash behaviour, overwrites return addresses to reach the same bypass, and places C code compiled without a linker into unused flash space, patching it over existing functions.

With that custom firmware running, the speaker hooks the NCI response path and the tag discovery state machine. The phone then acts as a MIFARE Classic tag with chosen ATQA, SAK and UID values, and can passively sniff traffic from a reader. Samsung patched the bootloader issues on newer chips but not older ones. The main takeaway is that phones contain exploitable embedded processors that deserve the same scrutiny as other embedded devices.

talks.title: Side-channel analysis on SoC devices: a Graal's quest | Hugues Thiebeauld | Hardwear.io Webinar
talks.teaser: Walks through locating and exploiting AES side-channel leakage on system-on-chip devices, from die mapping to key recovery.
talks.summary:
This talk looks at side-channel analysis against system-on-chip (SoC) devices, drawing on practical cases gathered over several years. It starts from the basic idea: an algorithm such as AES can resist logical attacks yet leak intermediate values through power consumption or electromagnetic emanations. Statistical processing of many traces can then recover the key. On an SoC the hard part is finding the small region that performs the cryptographic operation, since an integrated AES may occupy only about one percent of a die holding roughly 168 million gates.

To locate the target, the speaker described cartography: scanning a grid over the die, collecting a few thousand traces per point, and building heat maps of statistical tests, with executions that skip AES kept as controls against false positives. Other problems were triggering on a hardware-accelerated AES that ran in 11 cycles, or 55 nanoseconds, which demanded a suitable sampling rate, and background activity such as DRAM fetches and clock governor settings. On an eight-core chip, the same code leaked more strongly on core 0 than on core 1. On one device the leakage sat at an intermediate point between rounds, so a monobit model with linear regression recovered the full key.

The speaker concluded that finding the recipe can take an expert several weeks, while exploitation once the leakage point and conditions are known may take only a few hours with relatively simple equipment. Sample preparation for package-on-package devices can add further work. Deep learning attacks without profiling were described as very computationally heavy, so classic techniques were presented as more efficient. Practitioners should weigh this threat when choosing a design, and when testing, aim for the best-controlled conditions, such as bare metal with privileges.

talks.title: Sinking U-Boots with Depthcharge: Effective Exploitation of Boot-Time Security Debt | Jon Szymaniak
talks.teaser: Shows how leftover U-Boot debug commands on a speaker expose memory read and write primitives that enable a root shell.
talks.summary:
The talk examines security debt in U-Boot, the bootloader widely used on system-on-a-chip devices. Engineering conveniences such as UART console commands, memory display and modify tools, and environment variables can undermine a secure boot chain when they stay enabled in production builds. The speaker argues that the attack surface reaches beyond the serial console to physical bus interfaces, network boot, and unauthenticated storage.

To demonstrate, the speaker presents Depth Charge, a Python toolkit with a companion microcontroller that operates on I2C buses. Against a consumer Sonos bookshelf speaker, the walkthrough covers initial console inspection and dumping U-Boot from RAM through an I2C command that acts as a read-write primitive. Command tables found in the binary reveal a hidden, more permissive command set. Patching the lock-state checks in memory, without actually unlocking the device, exposes those extra commands. Appending an init argument to the kernel command line then yields a fallback root shell. A deliberate unaligned access triggered a data abort that leaked the global data pointer and its exported jump table.

The closing advice is to expose the minimum by default, remove the command line interface where possible, and use device-unique authentication such as challenge-response for service unlocks instead of shared passwords. Teams should also verify file system and storage contents, since an attacker with physical access can tamper with them. Fault injection and glitching are noted as ways to defeat password checks.

talks.title: Securing CAN bus: augmenting the CAN protocol | Dr. Ken Tindell | Hardwear.io Webinar
talks.teaser: Shows how hardware source tagging and bus guardians can stop CAN bus spoofing and denial-of-service attacks.
talks.summary:
Dr. Ken Tindell opens with why the Controller Area Network in cars, rail, healthcare and factory equipment is hard to secure. Designed in the 1980s before connected vehicles, it has no authentication. Attackers reach it by cutting into exposed wiring, abusing OBD-II dongles, or hijacking an ECU through flaws in infotainment or telematics. He separates frame attacks, which spoof IDs or flood the bus through a normal controller, from protocol attacks that reconfigure the transmit pin and bit-bang the bus.

He then reviews common defences. Intrusion detection spots anomalies but cannot reliably stop a frame. Security gateways filter traffic yet cannot stop a device hijacked through permitted messages. Message authentication adds key-management and replay problems, and shared keys let a compromised node impersonate others. His proposal, CANhg, embeds fast out-of-band bits in standard frames that carry a hardware source address, invisible to ordinary controllers. An IDPS can trigger an error frame before a spoofed frame completes, and a bus guardian disconnects the offending host with overload frames to prevent a bus-off loop.

A bench demo showed a spoofed frame destroyed and the attacking node shut down. Policy stays in software so it can vary per manufacturer, while the hardware supplies mechanisms. Guardians go on the nodes at greatest risk, and FPGA prototypes, a draft specification and formal verification are in progress. The takeaway is that hardware source tagging with software policy can add authentication and denial-of-service protection without rewiring vehicles.

talks.title: Analyzing AMD SEV's Remote Attestation | Robert Buhren | Hardwear.io Webinar
talks.teaser: Shows how firmware bugs in AMD's SEV attestation let a malicious cloud provider extract keys and bypass VM memory protection.
talks.summary:
This talk examines AMD's Secure Encrypted Virtualization (SEV), which encrypts each virtual machine's memory so a malicious hypervisor cannot read it, and its remote attestation protocol on first-generation EPYC Naples processors. Attestation lets a cloud customer verify that SEV is active and deliver secrets through a certificate chain anchored in a chip endorsement key (CEK) derived from a chip-unique secret.

The researchers analyzed the platform security processor firmware, an ARM Cortex-A5 inside the CPU die, whose file system is stored in SPI flash. Firmware directories are unprotected, so an attacker who can edit them can shrink a secondary directory and push entries past the 64-entry limit, overwriting the AMD public key that authenticates later components. With that control, a modified SEV application can read the chip-unique secret and derive the CEK. Because the key is tied to the processor rather than the firmware version, and rollback prevention is absent, a key extracted before patching remains valid afterward. The speaker then showed a migration attack in which a valid CEK lets an attacker start a migration to an unmodified target host, receive the transport key, and decrypt guest memory.

The proposed fix binds the CEK to a chain of intermediate secrets derived per firmware component version, so keys extracted from older firmware stop working. The speaker noted that AMD's SEV-SNP proposal takes a similar direction. In Q&A, the speaker said the boot bug was limited to first-generation Zen hardware, and that Zen 2 systems were not exploitable this way as far as they knew. The main takeaway is that software-only mitigations are not possible on existing Naples CPUs.

talks.title: Building a Repairable Future | Kyle Wiens | Hardwear.io Webinar
talks.teaser: Surveys how software locks and copyright law block device repairs, and the legal fights aimed at restoring access.
talks.summary:
Kyle Wiens, CEO of iFixit, makes the case for a repairable future. He presents iFixit's open repair wiki, which he says reaches about 10 million people a month, and contrasts a linear make-use-discard economy with a circular one where repair extends product life. Software is the main new obstacle: a shut-down cloud service left smart-home owners stranded, and a refrigerator's calendar feature broke after an API change the vendor never patched.

He then surveys the legal ground. Massachusetts' 2012 automotive right-to-repair law standardized car diagnostics, and a newer ballot measure would extend that access to wireless telematics. He describes manufacturer tactics such as takedown notices against laptop service manuals, warranty-void stickers that he argues are unenforceable, and a Microsoft licensing case against a refurbisher that resulted in prison time. The central barrier is Section 1201 of the US DMCA, which makes circumventing access controls on copyrighted software illegal, so jailbreaking depends on exemptions renewed every three years.

He closes with a call to action: join repair.org or securerepairs.org, help write replacement firmware for abandoned devices, and back small repair shops and the EFF. In Q&A he covered rooting versus jailbreaking, proprietary firmware and how to file exemption requests, and urged security experts to counter fear-based arguments against repair laws.
