talks.title: DL-based Denoising of TEMPEST Images for Efficient OCR | Santiago & Juan | Hardwear.io Webinar
talks.teaser: Researchers show how convolutional networks denoise TEMPEST-captured frames so OCR can recover text from display emanations.
talks.summary:
The session opens with electromagnetic side-channel basics: video cables leak emanations that can be received and demodulated into coarse frames. Using an SDR tuned to harmonics of the pixel clock (for example 148.5 MHz at 1080p60), the presenters recover grayscale-like buffers via amplitude demodulation, careful resampling, filtering, and frame sync. Experiments include HDMI capture at about five meters; color is lost, but high-contrast text remains a practical target.

The second segment argues classical denoisers fail because intercepted frames mix unknown distortions, not simple Gaussian noise. The team builds roughly 18,000 aligned pairs of ground-truth monitor images and intercepted counterparts, then trains two convolutional models: a regression network inspired by deep scan-texture deblurring and an encoder–decoder (FC-HarNet) for pixel-level text versus background. Peak SNR rises from about 7.36 on raw intercepts to about 9.7 with the regressor and about 12.4 with FC-HarNet; pixel character detection reaches about 60% before OCR.

Tesseract on denoised frames yields far better precision, recall, F1, and accuracy than on raw intercepts. Q&A notes HackRF-class hardware, shared open tooling, shielding and cable choices as partial mitigations, and that minimum readable font size (about 30 points in their setup) depends more on capture SNR than on the model alone.

talks.title: Analyzing Embedded Systems The Smart Way | Henrik Ferdinand Noelscher | Hardwear.io Webinar
talks.teaser: Explains how to map PCB components, automate part number lookup, and reconstruct a schematic to plan embedded security testing.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this Hardwear.io webinar presentation, Henrik Ferdinand Noelscher discusses efficient methodologies for reverse engineering embedded systems, focusing on printed circuit boards (PCBs). Embedded hardware analysis traditionally begins with tearing down a device and manually inspecting components, tracing connections, and looking up documentation—a process that can be tedious, error-prone, and time-consuming. Noelscher proposes automating component identification, part number recognition, and technical documentation retrieval to reconstruct high-level schematics quickly and accelerate the testing pipeline.

### Key Topics
- **Targeting Active Components**: Prioritizing integrated circuits, microcontrollers, and flash storage over passive parts (such as resistors and capacitors) to identify firmware execution and data storage locations.
- **Optimized PCB Imaging**: Capturing high-resolution images of PCB front and back layers using clean boards, proper lighting, low ISO, long exposure times, and minimal background space to facilitate automated analysis.
- **Automated Component Detection**: Implementing color-based segmentation and rectangular fitting to identify chip packages, paired with template matching to locate repeating components across orientations.
- **OCR and Part Number Resolution**: Extracting text from chip surfaces via optical character recognition, handling noise with character length thresholds, and resolving authentic part numbers using catalog databases and naming schemas.
- **Unlabeled and Rebranded ICs**: Analyzing physical chip package dimensions and power/ground supply pin layouts to identify custom-labeled or scraped chips based on known manufacturer designs.
- **Automated Data Gathering**: Scraping and structuring datasheets, pinout tables, IDE definitions, and reference manuals to surface debugging ports (such as JTAG), communication buses, and architecture details.
- **Hardware Netlist Extraction Techniques**: Comparing low-overhead non-destructive approaches with advanced methods like PCB delayering, X-ray imaging, and automated flying-probe testing.

### Technical Details
To isolate chips on a circuit board, the system blurs high-frequency noise and removes background solder mask colors (such as green) using pixel thresholding. Rectangles are fitted over the remaining segmented blobs to delineate chip boundaries. For passives or missing components, template matching calculates similarity metrics across the board and supports rotation-invariant detection. Extracted chip images are fed into OCR services, filtering out artifacts and matching against catalog patterns (e.g., STM32 naming schemes). For Ball Grid Array (BGA) components, table extraction converts package diagram matrices into structured pinout lists that can be mapped over the PCB layout. When extracting documentation, converting PDFs into HTML, images, and text allows regular expressions on tables of contents and keyword searches (such as targeting JTAG or UART) to automatically segment and index critical chapters.

### Takeaways
Automating the early reconnaissance steps of hardware analysis reduces back-and-forth between the workbench and the computer while minimizing missed attack vectors. Analysts do not need complete physical netlists to begin firmware extraction; partial schematic reconstruction identifying key interfaces (e.g., SPI flash connections, UART lines, debugging interfaces) provides sufficient leverage for penetration testing. High-quality imaging and small, modular automation tools significantly enhance analysis speed and thoroughness.

talks.title: A decade of Machine Learning in Profiled Side-channel Analysis | Stjepan Picek | Hardwear.io Webinar
talks.teaser: Explains how machine learning fits into profiled side-channel attacks and where it still struggles across devices.
talks.summary:
The talk traces profiled side-channel attacks from template attacks, introduced in 2002, through their later variants, and argues that these methods are a form of machine learning even though they are rarely described that way. The attack has two phases: a profiling phase on an identical device the attacker controls, and an attack phase on the target. The speaker notes that many academic results simulate two devices by splitting the measurements from a single device, which hides the difficulty of real portability between devices with different keys.

The middle of the talk covers supervised learning, which the speaker says dominates current work, with most papers framing the task as multi-class classification of S-box or round outputs. Techniques discussed include random forests, support vector machines, multi-layer perceptrons and convolutional neural networks. The speaker reports that convolutional networks perform well on public datasets, including ones with masking and random-delay countermeasures, and that a convolutional autoencoder used as preprocessing can make a hard random-delay case much easier. Recurrent networks were reported to work poorly. Cross-device attacks, where a model trained on one device is applied to another with a different key, often fail.

The closing part addresses open challenges: hyperparameter selection, the lack of public data, metrics such as accuracy that can mislead, and the difficulty of explaining what a network has learned. The speaker suggests that the code needed for such attacks is now short enough that people with little side-channel background can run them, so understanding why an attack works matters. The practical takeaway is to use the results to build more secure designs.

talks.title: Reverse engineering raw firmware: tool to get you started | Guillaume Heilles | Hardwear.io Webinar
talks.teaser: Shows how to recover load addresses and entry points from raw firmware images that have no headers.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from a practical gap: loading a raw firmware dump from an embedded device, such as an automotive ECU or an IP camera, into a disassembler is much harder than opening an ELF binary. An ELF file carries headers with the architecture, load address and symbols, while a raw image has none of that, so the analyst has to guess the processor, the byte order and where the code sits. The speaker walks through the common manual approach of tagging offsets as code, and explains why the disassembler's built-in heuristics often give weak results on these targets.

The core of the method is statistical. The tool reads the whole image as 32-bit words and groups them by prefix, using the size of the memory map to decide how many high bits should match. Clusters of pointer-like values suggest likely base addresses, and comparing big-endian and little-endian readings helps choose the right byte order. The tool then takes candidate function addresses and checks how many of them correlate with pointer tables, which lets the analyst estimate the loading address through an assumption-driven search. For automotive units, it also scans for tables whose first column holds diagnostic service identifiers, since the handler for each service is often found right next to them, including the security access routine.

The demonstrations showed one firmware where the approach worked well and others where the heuristics failed, for example when pointers were not stored as plain words or the image was split into several parts. The speaker argued that the method is architecture-agnostic once a list of candidate functions exists, and said the tool was being prepared for open-source release. The practical takeaway is to use pointer statistics to find the base and load addresses, use protocol tables to locate interesting entry points, and treat every result as a heuristic that needs checking.

talks.title: RF shadow games | Sébastien Dudek | Hardwear.io Webinar
talks.teaser: Walks through software-defined radio basics, signal decoding tools, and real RF targets from remotes and intercoms to cars and RFID.
talks.summary:
The talk is a broad introduction to software-defined radio (SDR) for people new to RF research. It starts with basics such as frequency and wavelength, the legal limits on transmitting in each country, and how analogue signals are sampled and quantised. The speaker explains the Nyquist-Shannon limit and shows how undersampling causes aliasing, then reviews how to choose SDR hardware and antennas based on sample rate, clock stability and the host interface.

The middle of the talk covers tooling and targets. Spectrum analysers help locate active frequencies, a graphical flow-graph builder chains processing blocks, and URH decodes simple on-off keying and FSK signals with automatic parameter detection. For harder signals, the speaker suggests reading chip datasheets and brute-forcing the modulation. Case studies include simple remote controls that often lack rolling codes, intercoms reachable over cellular where a rogue phone number can open a door, and car infotainment systems that expose unencrypted HTTP. Power-line communication, RFID work with Proxmark, and relay attacks that depend on tag timing are also discussed.

The closing Q&A covered learning resources, BladeRF for GSM work, and whether machine learning could help reverse engineer unknown protocols. The main takeaway is that many simple radio links can be captured and replayed, so application-layer encryption is the most practical protection.

talks.title: Hints from Hardware Security for solving real-world challenges | Dr Sergei | Hardwear.io Virtual Con
talks.teaser: Shows how low-cost, chemical-free chip decapsulation and wire repair let hardware researchers keep working during lockdown.
talks.summary:
Hardware security work protects state secrets and intellectual property, and the speaker argues its methods can help with counterfeit detection and supply shortages. Lab access was limited during lockdown, and sample preparation normally involves hazardous chemicals and bulky machinery. The talk reviews a series of attacks from the speaker's research and the lessons each one offers beyond the chip itself.

Earlier techniques covered include fault injection by pushing supply voltage below ground, which erases SRAM data faster than switching power off; optical fault injection with a focused laser; recovery of data remanence from EEPROM and flash; and combined power analysis with fault injection. A device that only returns a yes or no verification result could still leak data by masking bytes and tuning timing for a brute-force search. The speaker also described a passcode-attempt-limit bypass on an iPhone 5c, presented at an earlier conference.

For the lockdown challenge, the speaker mechanically decapsulated a PIC microcontroller with sandpaper and a polishing machine, avoiding chemicals. Because grinding removed the bonding wires, power, ground and programming connections were rebuilt with conductive paint applied through masking tape templates. The repaired chip worked in a programmer and could then be used for UV exposure or optical fault injection. The talk notes limits for ball-grid and very small packages, and suggests that chemistry and out-of-the-box thinking may help solve other real-world problems.

talks.title: Defeating TLS client authentication using fault attack | Nicolas & Sylvain | Hardwear.io Virtual Con
talks.teaser: Shows how a voltage glitch on an ESP32 leaks an ECDSA signing nonce and recovers a device's TLS client private key.
talks.summary:
Many low-cost IoT devices authenticate to a cloud service with a client certificate, keeping an ECDSA private key in firmware. The speakers argue that such devices often have little physical protection, so standard hardware attacks should apply. They walk through the TLS 1.2 handshake used in a major cloud provider's device onboarding, where the device signs the handshake transcript. The key falls if the per-signature random value is reused or reduced.

Their target was the embedded TLS library used on an ESP32. In its code, the nonce buffer was copied into an internal integer one byte at a time, so a glitch that ends the loop early leaves a small, predictable nonce. A precomputed table of small nonces, each multiplied by the generator point, could then match a captured signature, with lookups taking about five seconds after roughly two days of precomputation and 300 GB of storage. A return value initialised to success also meant a skipped check went unnoticed. On the board they removed bypass capacitors, cut a power trace, and drove a crowbar glitcher timed by a GPIO marker. In some runs they obtained a fixed nonce that needed no table.

After disclosure, the library maintainers changed the copy routine and status handling, but the speakers say the signature remained open to fault attacks. Suggested defences include TLS 1.3, which encrypts the handshake, RSA or secure elements with their own trade-offs, and fault detection such as checking loop counts. Q&A covered double-fault attacks, considered feasible but costlier.

talks.title: Reverse engineering of neural network architectures via side-channel | Stjepan Picek | Hardwear.io
talks.teaser: Recovers a neural network's layers, activation functions and weights from power and EM side-channel leakage on microcontrollers.
talks.summary:
Machine learning models are valuable assets, and this talk asks how well a model running on an embedded device resists reverse engineering. The attacker is passive: they only measure power consumption or electromagnetic emissions while the device runs normally, and they can feed it chosen inputs. The work assumes no side-channel countermeasures are present. The targets are feed-forward networks such as multi-layer perceptrons and convolutional networks, implemented on microcontrollers including ATmega and ARM Cortex-M3 parts.

The method works in stages. Timing differences reveal which activation function is in use, since functions such as sigmoid, tanh, softmax and ReLU take different amounts of time to compute. Simple power or EM analysis, read by visual inspection, shows the number of neurons and where layers begin. Correlation power analysis, using a Hamming weight model on the IEEE 754 floating-point multiplication, then recovers each weight to a chosen decimal precision. Comparing hypotheses about which layer a neuron belongs to locates the layer boundaries.

Reconstructed networks were tested against the originals. For a multi-layer perceptron on a common side-channel dataset, accuracy moved from 60.9 percent to 60.87 percent. For a convolutional network on a standard image dataset, accuracy went from 78.47 percent to 78.11 percent, but that attack needed up to 100,000 measurements. The effort grows roughly linearly with network size. The speaker's takeaway is that embedded neural networks need affordable countermeasures, and early experiments on GPUs were noisier but considered feasible.

talks.title: Capturing Mask ROMs | John McMaster | Hardwear.io Virtual Con
talks.teaser: Explains how to image mask ROM chips, turn microscope scans into firmware binaries, and stain implant ROMs.
talks.summary:
Mask ROMs store firmware or data that is built into the chip during fabrication, so the contents are physically encoded in the silicon. The talk explains why someone might need to extract that data, such as checking boot security, keeping an old industrial machine running by moving its firmware to a flash part, or preserving arcade hardware. It suggests trying easier routes first, such as a JTAG or test interface, or code execution that lets the chip read its own memory. Voltage glitching and brute force come after that.

The workflow starts by removing the package with acid and imaging the exposed die under a microscope, with a dedicated image of just the ROM area often giving better contrast. The speaker covers three tools that turn images into bitmaps: ROM Partner, a histogram-based GUI, and a web platform where several people independently type the same region and votes resolve disagreements, reaching near-complete bit accuracy on large ROMs. Converting a bitmap into a usable binary means working out bit order and polarity. Low-entropy regions, recognizable strings and plausible instruction patterns help check whether the result is right.

Implant ROMs do not show up under normal microscopy and need chemical staining. The talk explains why results vary: metal contamination, acid concentration, lighting, temperature and etch time all affect the outcome. Suggested fixes include lapping off metal, using phosphoric acid to strip metal layers, working with roughly 20 percent hydrofluoric acid, keeping the lab warm, and etching in short increments with careful timing. The takeaway is that the process is slow and hazardous, and controlling each variable determines whether the data survives.

talks.title: Hunting UEFI Firmware Implants by Alex Matrosov: hardwear.io Webinar
talks.teaser: Explains why UEFI firmware implants evade endpoint tools and how analysts can approach hunting them.
talks.summary:
This webinar argues that firmware persistence is a major blind spot for endpoint defense. Most security products watch the operating system, while UEFI implants sit below it and can disable agents, survive reinstalls and disk replacement, and hide from standard scans. The talk traces how persistence moved from rootkits to boot kits and then to firmware, as driver signing and Secure Boot raised the cost of earlier approaches.

The middle section focuses on why detection fails and what analysts can do about it. Vendor tools often report only integrity mismatches without explaining impact, and BIOS update paths can be abused or spoofed. Supply chain tampering during shipment, firmware-level controllers such as the BMC, and a DMA-based route into System Management Mode were presented as examples. For analysis, the speaker compared emulation for dynamic work, with its coverage limits, and IDA Pro's EFI-aware pre-analysis against Ghidra for reverse engineering.

The closing points urge practitioners to treat firmware as a critical security asset, to verify update and signing processes, and to account for long vulnerability lifetimes caused by vendor update cycles. The speaker also points to a companion training class that covers boot sequence analysis, firmware reverse engineering, and BMC forensics labs.

talks.title: CXO PANEL: Security Certifications for IoT Devices | hardwear.io Netherlands 2019
talks.teaser: Panelists from Google, Arm, NCC Group and academia debate how security certification should apply to connected devices.
talks.summary:
The panel asks whether security certification should be required for IoT devices, and who should carry responsibility when a flaw sits deep in a multi-tier supply chain. Panelists from a chip designer, a consultancy, a device maker and academia compare the automotive and consumer electronics cases. Several argue that the OEM is the party customers turn to, but that a security requirement only means something once a threat model defines what the product must resist.

The discussion then moved to contracts and threat modelling. Speakers argued that a threat model changes with context: the same microcontroller in a light bulb faces a very different threat from one in a military jet, and the same vehicle sold to a consumer or to a ride-sharing fleet carries a different threat model. They described automotive specifications being passed down as ordinary documents, and suggested that certifying vendor processes, such as patching commitments and security development practices, may be more workable than certifying every product. Opinions differed on government mandates, with European cybersecurity law and US state rules mentioned as early steps toward a minimum floor.

The panel closed with the risk that compliance-driven certification becomes a race to the bottom, as early payment card standards did when they relied on self-attestation. Several panelists saw certification as documenting a baseline rather than defining security itself. Participants agreed that audits should cover the cloud and service layers behind a device as well as the hardware, and that any process should reward good work while penalising deliberate neglect. A show of hands on mandates drew fewer responses than the moderator expected.

talks.title: Electric vehicle CAN man-in-the-middling | Emile Nijssenv | hardwear.io Netherlands 2019
talks.teaser: Explains how a CAN bus man-in-the-middle board lets an old electric car gain range and better regenerative braking.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at upgrading first-generation electric cars, using a 2011 Nissan Leaf as the example. Short range and missing features make these cars hard to keep in service, and the speaker, who runs a small company with a partner, argues that a commercial incentive can turn community fixes that stall partway into a finished product. He explains the CAN bus used inside the vehicle: a shared two-wire bus carrying short messages of up to eight bytes, where an outsider mainly needs the message ID and the data.

To reverse engineer the drivetrain, the speaker places a man-in-the-middle board on the bus and uses its direction of traffic to filter messages going from the vehicle control module toward the inverter. Repeating patterns and an eight-bit checksum-like byte narrow the candidates until the motor control message is identified. Applications shown include changing the reported battery charge so that an added pack gives correct range figures, and altering regenerative braking that a firmware bug had suppressed. A customer's car with a larger pack was described as able to reach an Alpine pass that the stock car could not.

The speaker then describes the replacement battery, higher-performance cells from plug-in hybrids with lower internal resistance, which needed a new battery management approach. The interposing board translates between the new pack and the original computer. Questions covered thermal management, the mechanical brake backup, and cost. The closing message is that security expertise could be directed toward extending the working life of older electric vehicles.

talks.title: Day-1 with a TTIG-868 | Brian Butterly | hardwear.io Netherlands 2019
talks.teaser: Shows how a one-day security review of a LoRa base station uncovers protocol, debug and configuration weaknesses.
talks.summary:
Brian Butterly examines a low-cost LoRa gateway aimed at home users, which joins a Wi-Fi network and forwards LoRa traffic. He asks what a single day of testing can realistically reveal, arguing that basic failures such as exposed services and default credentials matter more for consumer IoT than advanced exploitation. The device implements a newer Basic Station protocol, which he reviews first.

The setup uses a Wi-Fi access point protected by a per-device password printed on the case, and the web interface listens only on port 80. Missing input validation in the Wi-Fi name field was a weakness, and port scanning could crash the device. The configuration and network server channels use TLS, but the configuration path offers a no-authentication option, and whether authentication is active depends on credential files being present, so deleting one could switch it off. On the board, the USB port was dead because of a missing ground resistor and an unpulled reset pin; moving a 10k resistor to pull reset high restored serial debug output. Logic-analyser probing of the flash only worked after a series resistor on the SPI lines was bypassed, and decoding quad SPI remained unfinished. The published firmware source, scanned with Flawfinder, produced 40 to 50 findings that he reviewed by hand, and he found no buffer overflow.

Measured against the UK code of practice, the device passed on default passwords, signed updates and factory reset, but failed on secure storage, since the ESP8266 has no internal memory and keys sit beside the encrypted flash. His conclusion is that the device is not insecure, though not well made, and the review took about ten hours. Next steps include publishing a quad SPI decoder and building a repeatable 24-hour IoT test method with a checklist and test bench.

talks.title: Poking the S in SD cards | Nicolas Oberli | hardwear.io Netherlands 2019
talks.teaser: Low-cost SPI tools uncover SD lock timing leaks and race password erase against flash writes to keep protected data readable.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens by framing SD cards as microcontrollers fronting flash, then walks through the messy command-and-response protocol using SPI, HydraBus, and a homegrown CLI helper that parses identification registers and optional CRC behavior across vendors.

Research focuses on mandatory CMD42 password lock, where processing time on the data line leaks password length and each byte; automating dummy reads after unlock attempts recovers keys on most tested cards, with manufacturer-specific quirks such as Sony’s three-try limit bypassed via CMD0 reset, Kingston checking 32-bit chunks, and SanDisk appearing immune. A second thread abuses erase-on-forgotten-password: specs require wiping data before unlock, yet cutting supply during the charge-pump write spike— sensed through a shunt, STM32 ADC watchdog, and MOSFET—often leaves the card unlocked while user data remains.

Cross-manufacturer testing (~20 cards) shows widespread issues except notable SanDisk behavior; write-protect combinations and ordering of erase versus unlock are validated carefully. The speaker stresses reproducible low-cost lab work, automation for long brute-force runs, and verifying spec claims on real hardware even when OSes ignore SD password features.

talks.title: Roots of Trust and Attestation | Trammell Hudson | Keynote | hardwear.io Netherlands 2019
talks.teaser: Explains how verified boot, TPM attestation and user-owned firmware trade off security, recovery and freedom on modern systems.
talks.summary:
Trammell Hudson opens by questioning whether verified boot alone secures a machine. A firmware signature check that halts the CPU on failure gives no way to tell a failed attack from a hardware fault, and it leaves owners unable to change what runs on their own hardware. He argues that owners should hold the signing keys and documentation, because vendor firmware built from reference implementations often goes unpatched for years.

He then walks through concrete cases. One server board exposed an unauthenticated root shell on its BMC through a serial console, showing how much control that component can have. A boot guard failure on a laptop left the machine looking completely dead, with no way to distinguish an attack from a broken part. Recovery options discussed include a network recovery design at a large internet company that uses a certificate authority in the BMC, and scripted recovery using ordinary Linux tools. He also reviews remote attestation, including Chromebook use of TPM monotonic counters and sealed secrets, a boot-time code check confirmed with a code on a phone, a VPN provider publishing reproducible builds with signed TPM quotes, and enclave and encrypted VM technologies such as SGX and AMD SEV.

He closes by noting that many components in a server, from network cards to power supplies, run their own firmware. His takeaway is that systems should be resilient, recoverable through tools rather than policy, and able to attest their state in ways that protect users instead of locking them out. He sees NIST's platform resiliency guidelines as a strong start, but expects vendor adoption to be slow.

talks.title: Hardware security evaluation of Intel MAX 10 FPGAs | Dr. Sergei Skorobogatov | hardwear.io NL 2019
talks.teaser: Shows how Intel MAX 10 FPGA security fuses can be bypassed with laser, electromagnetic and power glitching attacks.
talks.summary:
This talk evaluates the hardware security of Intel MAX 10 FPGAs, devices marketed for security use because their configuration bitstream sits in on-die flash rather than external memory. The speaker explains the three security fuses (verify protect, encrypted-only and JTAG security) and how the boot logic reads their state from specific byte sequences in system memory. Protection only holds when verify protect and encrypted-only are both set, a point the manufacturer does not clearly document.

The attacks range from invasive to non-invasive. Backside laser fault injection flipped the fuses and gave full access, and timing tests showed the pulse must land close to the TCK edge. Non-invasive methods included searching for undocumented JTAG commands, where none helped, and recovering about 97% of the data through remanence after an interrupted chip erase. Power analysis of boot traces, electromagnetic analysis, which had poor signal-to-noise, and power glitching were also tried, with glitching more effective on dual-supply devices. Electromagnetic pulse injection proved the most practical route, but the flyback voltage from the coil could not be suppressed, as fast, ultrafast and silicon carbide diodes all failed, so the speaker worked with the pulse instead.

The closing section covers dangers to the researcher, including hydrofluoric acid, piranha solution, high-power lasers and charged capacitors or inductors that can produce voltage spikes. The conclusion is that the device was not certified for high security, that newer parts do not necessarily have better protections, and that keys stored in flash remain a weak point. Future work points to reverse engineering and memory extraction on smaller process nodes.

The presenter describes tuning a rare 1985 Honda Civic for more power on E85 without modern OBD or CAN. He sketches PGM-FI basics and why wider injector duty cycles suit ethanol, then turns to goals he cares about: live engine data on track days through an undocumented serial debug port on the P7 ECU, where almost no one has published logging or map work.

He planned to repurpose a Mad Catz gaming keyboard with USB-serial routing and briefly reversed its Qt-based firmware to keep only console and USB services, but set that aside after odd cabling. The main effort became ECU chipping on a non-programmable mask ROM: coordinating with PGM-FI grassroots communities, using a MiniPRO programmer on Linux, reconciling datasheet confusion and address-decoder layout, concatenating dumps correctly, and borrowing a race-team map that already includes datalogging snippets he did not want to reverse on 8051.

Flashing mistakes blanked part of the ROM and silenced the fuel pump until a proper erase and rewrite; UV erasure progressed slowly using a cat toy’s UV LED. A tuner’s E85 map already parses locally—the remaining step is flashing the corrected binary. Practitioners see how legacy automotive controls resist standard tooling and how forum dumps, hardware programmers, and checksum discipline matter as much as exploit flair.

talks.title: It's easier to break than to patch: a stealthy DoS attack on CAN | Stefano Zanero & Stefano Longari
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning It's easier to break than to patch: a stealthy DoS attack on CAN | Stefano Zanero & Stefano Longari.
talks.summary:
### Overview
Stefano Zanero and Stefano Longari present research on inherent design vulnerabilities in the Controller Area Network (CAN) bus, the primary communication standard connecting critical and non-critical Electronic Control Units (ECUs) in vehicles. Unlike attacks that exploit unauthenticated broadcast messages to spoof signals or flood networks, this work demonstrates how standard CAN error-handling and fault-confinement mechanisms can be abused to perform a targeted denial-of-service (DoS) attack that forces a specific ECU off the bus, subsequently allowing stealthy message spoofing.

### Key Topics
- Automotive intrusion detection system (IDS) architectures, including specification-based, frequency-based, and machine learning methods, and their evasion.
- CAN bus electrical properties: dominant (0) vs. recessive (1) bits, arbitration, and bit-level overwriting.
- Abusing CAN protocol fault-confinement rules and Transmit Error Counters (TEC) to induce a "bus-off" state.
- Experimental proof of concept using low-cost hardware against a laboratory testbed and an Alfa Romeo Giulietta.
- Design and evaluation of "CANpy/CopyCAN", a passive state-tracking IDS that monitors ECU error counters directly from bus traffic to detect and mitigate spoofing.

### Technical Details
In a standard CAN network, ECUs arbitrate for bus access. A transmitted 0 (dominant) overrides a 1 (recessive). If an ECU observes a signal on the bus differing from what it transmitted outside arbitration, it flags a bit error and transmits an active error flag (six dominant zero bits). Each transmission error increments the ECU's Transmit Error Counter by 8, whereas successful transmissions decrement it by 1. When the counter exceeds 127, the ECU enters an error-passive state; when it exceeds 255, the ECU enters a bus-off state, disconnecting itself entirely from the bus.

The researchers exploit this behavior through a targeted attack:
1. The attacker monitors the CAN bus for the victim ECU's identifier (ID).
2. Once the victim wins arbitration, the attacker locates a known recessive bit (such as the CRC delimiter, which is always 1).
3. The attacker overwrites this recessive bit with a dominant 0.
4. The victim perceives this discrepancy as a transmission error and increments its error counter by 8.
5. Repeating this sequence 32 consecutive times forces the victim's counter past 255, knocking it completely off the bus.

Because the attacker's hardware must avoid standard automatic error handling, the authors implemented custom software-defined CAN controller logic on an Arduino coupled with a basic CAN transceiver. In experimental trials, they successfully disabled the parking sensor module on an Alfa Romeo Giulietta connected via the OBD-II port, preventing the sensors from functioning.

### Takeaways
The core DoS condition cannot be patched at the CAN protocol level without altering standard fault confinement specifications. However, secondary spoofing—where an attacker impersonates the silenced ECU—can be detected. The authors created a defensive system ("CopyCAN") implementing a finite state machine that observes raw bus bits to track each ECU's error counter. When an ECU enters bus-off, any subsequent frames carrying that ECU's ID are identified as spoofed. The defense can log incidents, alert systems, or actively transmit dominant bits to invalidate unauthorized frames.

talks.title: RIDLed with CPU bugs | Alyssa Milburn & Stephan van Schaik | hardwear.io Netherlands 2019
talks.teaser: Researchers present RIDL, leaking in-flight data from CPU line-fill buffers across kernels, VMs, SGX, and browsers.
talks.summary:
The speakers open by arguing that shared cloud CPUs and virtual machines rest on a fragile assumption: processor pipelines will reliably isolate tenants. They survey errata across vendors, recap speculative execution and cache timing attacks behind Meltdown, Spectre, and Foreshadow, and explain how mitigations mostly hide or segment memory addresses rather than securing microarchitectural state.

The core contribution is RIDL, a microarchitectural data sampling class that exfiltrates stale data from internal buffers such as line-fill buffers instead of caches, evading address-focused defenses. On a mitigated Core i7 system they demonstrate recovering shadow password material locally, co-tenant VM scenarios using SSH-driven confused deputies, and a Spectre-style combination that tricks kernel copy-from-user paths. A Firefox WebAssembly proof shows the primitive without privileged instructions, using huge allocations to provoke page faults where invalid pointers are unavailable.

Practitioners should treat hyper-threading and cheap multi-tenant placement as elevated risk, expect buffer-clearing mitigations to race across sibling threads, and recognize that post-Meltdown patches do not close this channel. The closing emphasis is that many pipeline structures remain poorly documented and under-audited, with more issues likely as researchers map in-flight paths.

talks.teaser: Introduces how machine learning and deep learning are applied to side-channel attacks against hardware implementations.
talks.summary:
The webinar previews a two-day advanced tutorial that combines machine learning with side-channel analysis. The speaker says the course expects prior side-channel knowledge, such as correlation power analysis, but builds the machine learning material from the basics.

The talk traces how profiling attacks such as template and stochastic attacks were recognised as the same train-then-attack paradigm used in supervised machine learning. Researchers then moved to generic machine learning techniques and, from around 2016, to convolutional neural networks, which broke implementations even when countermeasures were present. Because the no free lunch theorem means no single profiling algorithm is best, practitioners must run many experiments and tune hyperparameters, which is costly. Machine learning skills also carry over to data problems outside security.

The course outline moves from basic concepts to preprocessing, feature selection and dimensionality reduction on raw traces, then to classical techniques, multi-layer perceptrons and convolutional networks. It also weighs whether deep learning's extra compute is worth it compared with simpler methods, and it touches on fault injection. The speaker stresses that two days cannot cover everything, so participants should leave able to implement and use several techniques and keep studying on their own.

talks.title: Hack To Discover Weaknesses In A Series Of Smartcards | Christopher Tarnovsky | hardwear.io USA 2019
talks.teaser: Walks through breaking old smartcard chips by imaging their logic and probing buses to extract stored code.
talks.summary:
The talk covers how the speaker reverse engineered a series of older smart card chips, with processes ranging from 350 nanometers down to 65 nanometers. The method starts by polishing a die down layer by layer, imaging each layer under a microscope, and then tracing the logic from the boot ROM outward until the instruction register is found. Some chips also needed a focused ion beam to cut or reroute wires beneath their shields.

Several cases are described. On an ST design, the ROM output passed through two XOR stages, the second scrambling the data bus with a random value generated at each reset, so probing between the stages revealed the executing code. On a 350 nanometer part without a shield, cutting one data line stopped branching, letting the chip be observed passively with needles. For one vendor's chips, strapping the boot ROM to jump straight into flash and cutting the flash output bus exposed the contents, and a one-time programmable area could be overwritten. On an Infineon 66 series part, the speaker bridged shield wires, milled through a metal plate to reach the bus, and glitched the data bus to freeze the instruction register.

The closing advice is to customize the logic of off-the-shelf chips, since standard parts are far easier to break. The speaker argues that a single wire controlling an alarm can defeat most shields, and that even customized hardware blocks can be worked out by loading them with known values.

talks.title: Unique Challenges Of Security Programs For Hardware/IoT Makers | CXO Panel | hardwear.io USA 2019
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Unique Challenges Of Security Programs For Hardware/IoT Makers | CXO Panel | hardwear.io USA 2019.
talks.summary:
### Overview
This panel discussion from hardwear.io USA 2019 features security leaders from hardware manufacturing, product security, and offensive security consulting. The session explores the unique challenges of building and maintaining security programs for hardware and IoT devices compared to traditional web and software environments. Topics include researcher engagement, vulnerability management, secure protocol adoption, user privacy, supply chain risks, and firmware attestation.

### Key Topics
- **External Researcher Engagement:** Engaging hardware security researchers is hindered by high equipment costs, specialized skill sets, tamper-resistant packaging, and locked-down production hardware. Companies navigate this through bug bounties, private programs providing hardware, academic grants, training (such as UEFI education), and open-source tooling (e.g., Chipsec, EDK II/TianoCore initiatives, OpenThread, OpenWeave).
- **Vulnerability Management & Hardware Lifecycle:** Unlike web software where patches deploy in hours, hardware patching involves long validation cycles across OEMs, ODMs, and CSPs, often relying on coordinated embargoes and firmware workarounds. Panelists emphasize secure-by-design principles, robust over-the-air (OTA) update mechanisms, defense-in-depth, and isolating secrets per device.
- **Legacy Protocols & Standards:** Many hardware devices communicate over outdated or plain-text board-level interfaces (such as SPI and I2C) or older wireless standards. Modern microcontrollers and crypto co-processors now enable end-to-end link encryption without substantial overhead. Panelists discussed participating in standards bodies (e.g., Zigbee/Z-Wave, smart metering, PCI) while noting that mixed environments often default to the lowest common denominator of security.
- **Consumer Privacy & Hardware Controls:** User education is often insufficient given pervasive data collection. Proposed solutions include simple hardware-level controls (physical lens covers, mute buttons, hardware kill switches for radios and sensors) alongside strong regulatory baselines and minimized data collection.
- **Supply Chain Security & Manufacturing:** Addressing risks such as hardware implants and untrusted contract manufacturers involves generating cryptographic keys directly on-chip rather than at the factory, utilizing Hardware Security Modules (HSMs) and PKI, exploring blockchain for distributed manufacturing integrity, and performing random sample auditing (such as 3D X-ray inspection).

### Technical Details
- **Per-Device Secrets:** Devices should generate secrets internally and avoid sharing global symmetric keys across product lines, ensuring that key extraction on a single physical unit does not compromise the wider ecosystem.
- **Protocol Decoders and Openness:** Open-sourcing protocol decoders (e.g., Wireshark plugins and Scapy modules for 802.15.4, Thread, and Weave) helps the research community analyze communications without resorting to unnecessary reverse-engineering hurdles.
- **Hardware Defenses:** Panelists highlighted Kerckhoffs's principle, secure elements, and trusted execution environments/enclaves to safeguard key material, while warning that security architectures must assume physical side-channel leakage or extracted secrets over time.

### Takeaways
Hardware must be secure by design; security cannot simply be retrofitted post-production. Organizations must implement automated OTA updates, isolate device secrets, actively train and equip external researchers, and establish rigorous supply-chain verification to manage long-term device risk.

talks.title: Top 10 Secure Boot Mistakes | Jasper Van Woudenberg | hardwear.io USA 2019
talks.teaser: Walks through ten recurring secure boot flaws, from unchecked signatures and timing leaks to fault injection and nonce reuse.
talks.summary:
Secure boot checks that each stage of a platform's startup is signed before it runs, beginning with a boot ROM and moving through bootloaders to the operating system. Privileges usually shrink at each step. Platform initialisation also locks down memory, reads one-time fuses, handles manufacturing and debug modes, and speeds up resume from sleep, and each of these adds room for mistakes.

The talk walks through ten recurring boot mistakes. Examples include unsigned header fields and data used before verification, update paths with buffer overflows reachable over USB, chunked firmware not stitched together safely, and missing anti-rollback that lets an older vulnerable version return. Timing and race issues appear too, such as a byte-by-byte signature comparison that leaked progress and external flash that could be changed after verification. Fault injection with voltage glitches, guided by power traces, can skip a conditional branch. Key handling problems include decryption without authentication, development loaders signed with production keys, and uncleared crypto key slots. A static nonce in ECDSA signing let the private key be computed from two signatures.

Suggested mitigations include signing as much as possible, checking pointers and sizes before use, copying data to internal memory before verifying it, using constant-time comparisons, enforcing monotonic version fuses, keeping update features minimal, fuzzing parsers and drivers, stripping debug functions from production images, and clearing crypto engines. The speaker closes by urging researchers to study hardware attacks and developers to request security assurances from suppliers.

talks.title: Nationally Critical Infrastructure needs Secure Hardware | Dr. Joseph Kiniry | hardwear.io USA 2019
talks.teaser: Argues critical infrastructure needs verifiable secure hardware, and surveys DARPA's open secure CPU program and a voting demo.
talks.summary:
Joseph Kiniry, who works at Galois on national security research, opens by arguing that high-assurance software is undermined by the hardware beneath it. He describes many assurance cases as fragile, since formal proofs of code still assume a CPU that behaves as documented, while hardware and firmware vendors typically make few promises about how their products behave.

He then traces a DARPA program called SIF, which funds six teams building eighteen experimental secure CPUs. The designs are soft cores on RISC-V running on FPGAs, and the goal is to remove whole vulnerability classes in hardware, starting with memory and buffer errors and timing-based information leakage. Galois contributed design tooling that explores variants of a CPU and weighs security against power, performance and area, so designers can pick the trade-off they need.

The talk turns to election technology, which he presents as critical infrastructure with weak security in many deployed systems. He describes his team's open-source, open-hardware ballot demonstrator built around a secure microcontroller, and a planned public red-team exercise at DEF CON where attackers may load their own malware over Ethernet. The practical takeaway is that secure hardware should be shown through open designs and open attack, not simply promised by vendors.

talks.title: Low-Cost IC Emission Reverse Engineering | John McMaster | hardwear.io USA 2019
talks.teaser: Shows how infrared emissions from a running chip can reveal its logic, using inexpensive cameras and microscopes.
talks.summary:
Reverse engineering chips usually means imaging transistors and tracing their structure to infer logic. This talk explores correlating the infrared light that transistors emit while switching with the logic they perform, using a far cheaper setup than a professional failure-analysis lab. The speaker describes sensitive cameras that can capture emission near 1100 nanometers, and the modifications needed, such as removing an infrared filter, adding a 3D-printed adapter, and blocking room light.

To make small changes visible he uses dark frame subtraction and brightness scaling. On a bipolar chip he stimulates inputs and outputs, locates the output stage and ESD diodes by observation, and identifies a two-input NAND gate without tracing its transistors. A 4-bit counter's states were also shown in a video. A floorplanning attempt on another chip did not give a sensitive enough measurement, and CMOS parts were harder to read because of their lower power draw.

The last section covers backside analysis. On a TO-220 voltage regulator he thinned the die by grinding, hand sanding and chemical etching; thinning too far made the chip unreliable, and backside emission at about 30 micrometers was roughly 18 times dimmer than from the front. A photodiode sensor showed no changes, while night-vision optics gave a faint image. The takeaway: low-cost infrared imaging suits simple bipolar logic, while CMOS and backside work need more research.

talks.title: Integrated Circuit Offensive Security | Olivier Thomas from Texplained | hardwear.io USA 2019
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Integrated Circuit Offensive Security | Olivier Thomas from Texplained | hardwear.io USA 2019.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk presented at hardwear.io USA 2019, Olivier Thomas, founder and CTO of Texplained and co-founder of IC's Inside, discusses offensive security and physical reverse engineering of integrated circuits (ICs). Rather than relying solely on black-box attacks or traditional cross-sectional signal tracing, Thomas explains the methodology of deprocessing a silicon die down layer-by-layer to reconstruct a digital netlist and HDL/VHDL model directly from microscopic imagery. He demonstrates how this structural modeling empowers targeted fault injection, code extraction, and security evaluations.

### Key Topics
- **Integrated Circuit Deprocessing:** Combining wet chemicals, plasma etching (dry etching), and mechanical polishing (chemical mechanical polishing/CMP) to cleanly strip passivation, metal interconnect layers, vias, and contacts down to the doped silicon substrate.
- **Imaging and Feature Extraction:** Utilizing Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM) for high-resolution imaging (often generating hundreds of gigabytes per chip) to extract polygons representing metal tracks, vias, contacts, and standard cell footprints.
- **HDL Netlist Reconstruction:** Mapping transistor configurations to standard cell libraries to generate a flat VHDL model that can be simulated in EDA tools.
- **Offensive Analysis and Attack Simulation:** Using the extracted netlist to trace signal paths, locate registers and scan chains (JTAG/debug logic), simulate attacks, and defeat ROM encryption or scrambling.
- **Hardware Trojans and Supply Chain Validation:** Comparing physical layout features against golden models to detect unauthorized modifications or backdoors.
- **Flaws in Hardware Certification Schemes:** Critiquing evaluation frameworks such as Common Criteria, where invasive attacks are often treated as residual risk once high-tier ratings (e.g., AVA_VAN.5 / high rating thresholds) are scored.

### Technical Details
- **Deprocessing Methodology:** Thomas highlights the limitations of using wet chemicals alone, which cause uneven surfaces and holes on modern small nodes. Plasma etching removes oxide and metal selectively based on gas chemistry, but requires combination with mechanical polishing (using diamond-coated discs on a high-precision multi-axis arm) to avoid messy line profiles.
- **Feature Recognition to Netlist:** Deprocessed layers are imaged using an SEM (capable of ~0.7 nm/pixel resolution). Specialized software detects millions of contacts, lines, and standard cells (e.g., multiplexers, flip-flops, combinatorial logic) across multiple metal and poly layers, producing a simulatable VHDL representation in 10–20 minutes once annotated.
- **Interactive Signal Tracing:** In a live demonstration on an 8-bit microcontroller core, Thomas demonstrates tracing memory output lines forward through standard cells to identify 8 flip-flops comprising an 8-bit register. Further tracing reveals scan-chain connections and allows pinpointing the control logic needed to unlock debug interfaces like JTAG.
- **Defeating Complex Memory Protections:** For ROM structures protected by word-line/bit-line scrambling and core-level encryption, Thomas models the address decoders, memory array, and downstream decryption logic in VHDL. By writing a test bench simulating addresses, the model outputs decrypted values without requiring direct microprobing or FIB circuit edits.
- **Precision Fault Injection ("Smart Gun"):** Correlating netlists with physical coordinates enables surgical fault injection. Distinguishing combinatorial cells (where glitches are transient) from sequential cells (registers/flip-flops where fault states latch) allows attackers to construct targeted laser or clock glitching maps rather than blindly testing locations across the die.

### Takeaways
Physical IC reverse engineering to the netlist level shifts the security paradigm from black-box physical testing to structured, simulated attacks. Certification schemes like Common Criteria frequently undervalue these invasive modeling approaches by scoring out earlier in evaluations. Beyond offensive vulnerability assessment, netlist extraction serves critical defensive and engineering use cases, including supply chain Trojan detection, intellectual property (IP) infringement verification, obsolete component reproduction (FPGA replacement), and forensic law enforcement investigation.

talks.title: Bits From The Matrix: Optical ROM Extraction | Chris Gerlinsky | hardwear.io USA 2019
talks.teaser: A walkthrough covers chip decapsulation, optical delayering, and software workflows for extracting boot ROM binary data from silicon.
talks.summary:
Boot ROM executes before user firmware on many chips, so recovering that mask-programmed memory can reveal early boot logic and weaknesses that matter to embedded attackers and researchers. The talk frames ROM as a permanent matrix of ones and zeros in metal or implant structures, notes historical pay-TV, gaming, and archiving motivations, and stresses that the goal is reliable binary extraction rather than mastering every ROM fabrication variant.

The demonstrated pipeline decapsulates packages, delayers with hydrofluoric wet etch or polishing, captures tiled microscope images, and alternates etching until bit contrast appears; dash etch helps implant ROM, while SEM and FIB enter when optical limits bite. Locating the densest memory array, thresholding light versus dark cells, and using tools such as rompar or custom analyzers turn photos into bit matrices, then into bytes checked via ASCII strings, patterns, or disassembly. Walked cases include shielded smartcard silicon, uneven etch pits patched by repeating on a second die, and Motorola set-top ROM where optical reads with scattered bit errors still matched a glitched full-memory dump closely enough to continue exploitation work.

Takeaways emphasize integrated lab and analysis judgment, fume-hood chemistry discipline without turning the session into a safety course, repeated trials to manage dirt and holes, and accepting feature-shrink limits that force electron imaging. ROM encryption is acknowledged as a sometimes weak hurdle. Slides, references, and dated bit-decoding source are offered for those building a home-shop workflow.

talks.title: Exposing The Deep-Secure Elements Of Smartcards | Christopher Tarnovsky | hardwear.io USA 2019
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Exposing The Deep-Secure Elements Of Smartcards | Christopher Tarnovsky | hardwear.io USA 2019.
talks.summary:
Christopher Tarnovsky presents his physical reverse-engineering of a Samsung smartcard IC protecting printer toner cartridges, devices generating millions in monthly revenue for printer manufacturers. The 4-layer metal chip at 130 nanometer aluminum process was systematically stripped using acid polishing and fuming nitric/sulfuric acid, then imaged with a scanning electron microscope at 20,000x magnification, producing composite images up to 150GB in Photoshop.

Using a focused ion beam (FIB) workstation, Tarnovsky attacked the chip's security. The device contained a 24KB executable ROM (encrypted), an EEPROM holding secrets, static RAM, and cryptographic algorithms. The ROM used XOR/XNOR operations with an unusual physical architecture tying left and right memory sides together via output enable lines.

Security features included 200–250 nanometer aluminum shield wires, a parity generator monitoring ROM fetches, and secondary flip-flops ('anti-fly logic') to prevent direct tampering. Tarnovsky used xenon difluoride gas to etch through the shield, creating windows and depositing platinum/tungsten connections to manipulate chip behavior.

A critical flaw emerged: Samsung used the high bit (D15) for branch instructions. By cutting this line or preventing it from toggling to 1, the chip could not branch, forcing sequential execution and revealing ROM code paths. The parity generator and active shielding proved ineffective—neither triggered alarms nor stopped the chip when tampered.

The work consumed ~5–6 hour FIB sessions per attack, destroying approximately 15 chips (~$110 each). While the asymmetric key protecting toner secrets remained inaccessible, Tarnovsky notes that Chinese company Apex and Static Control (North Carolina) somehow obtained it, generating over $1 million monthly from aftermarket toner sales. Samsung responded by switching to a functionally similar chip with different layout, prompting Tarnovsky to abandon the project due to cost and effort. He contrasts Samsung's approach (freeze-on-tamper) with ST Microelectronics (erase-on-tamper), highlighting different defensive philosophies.

talks.title: In conversation with Adam Laurie aka Major Malfunction | hardwear.io
talks.teaser: An insider view of open on-site hardware hacking contests, vendor collaboration, and shifting culture in physical security research.
talks.summary:
The conversation opens with how the presenter chose the handle Major Malfunction, tracing it to Challenger shuttle commentary rather than Full Metal Jacket, and using that understatement as a lens on security hype versus real risk.

Most of the discussion centers on Hardpwn, a live hardware contest where participants need no advance setup: organizers supply targets such as Nest alarms, thermostats, padlocks, and home security gear, plus benches of gear like ChipWhisperer and Saleae logic analyzers and mentors who help with soldering and tooling rather than prescribing exploits. Vendors cooperate through a coordinated disclosure program, pay bounties, and sometimes sit on the floor; one Nest interaction led the vendor to build a Wireshark plugin for the Weave stack atop Thread when decoders were missing. The presenter also describes a prototype RF capture tool meant to complement Wireshark and similar suites for non-ZigBee 802.15.4 traffic.

The middle turns to economics: bug bounties can drain unpaid researcher time while looking efficient for vendors, yet the openness at this event would have been rare a decade ago, with hardware still behind software on sharing. On hardwear.io itself, the presenter praises deeper manufacturer buy-in, inclusive contests, and talks that share full technical detail. The close is lighter—a recurring conference tradition involving elderly monks—before sign-off.

talks.title: In a conversation with Jan Krissler aka starbug | hardwear.io
talks.teaser: The conversation covers consumer fingerprint bypass, fake prints in forensics, and how firms should deploy biometric scanners.
talks.summary:
The exchange opens on roughly fifteen years of work around biometric security, including research on Windows and public demonstrations. On the launch-day iPhone TouchID case, the guest describes receiving the handset in Germany and defeating the sensor the same day, calling the result surprisingly easy given Apple’s market constraints and the difficulty of building durable, affordable consumer fingerprint systems.

The middle turns to cloning politicians’ prints and forensic use. He reports no lasting fallout, aside from a strange home visit after the Schäuble fingerprint episode around 2005. He argues fingerprints are overtrusted in criminalistics because cheap, quick spoofs can plant indistinguishable false marks; prints should be weighed alongside other evidence such as DNA from ridge material.

For organizations weighing scanners, he stresses environment-driven choices (form factor, cost, integration in phones or smartcards), real two-factor designs, and AND-logic when combining biometrics rather than OR-style shortcuts that halve effort for attackers. Injuries and backup paths matter because biometrics can fail and recovery credentials must stay comparably strong. He closes with first impressions of the event’s hands-on atmosphere and a view that Germany’s hardware security community is active, especially around the CCC, with corporate demand outpacing visible supply.

talks.teaser: Explores how open source hardware tools and education can widen access and make the hardware hacking community more inclusive.
talks.summary:
In this interview recorded at hardwear.io, Kate Temkin describes her path into hardware hacking. She explains that she started by building open source educational tools while teaching engineering at a university, frustrated that modern technology was missing from how engineering was taught. Her aim shifted toward making inexpensive versions of costly lab instruments such as oscilloscopes and logic analyzers, so that people without access to a well-funded university could explore the hardware around them.

The conversation then turns to fairness. Temkin argues that many celebrated hackers succeeded because of opportunities others were denied, and that women and other underrepresented people are often just as capable but kept out by barriers to entry. She compares the progress vendors have made in accepting researchers, through bug bounties and in-house security teams, with the slower work still needed on inclusion. She says companies often respond to economic arguments, so the case for diversity has to be made in those terms.

Asked about the conference itself, she notes that events of this size mainly reach people who can afford to attend or whose talks were accepted, and she praises recorded talks and live streams that let remote viewers take part. Her takeaway is that attendees should use the gathering to find ways to benefit people beyond the room, such as improving education for those who cannot attend. The interviewer replied that videos are uploaded quickly and said the team would look at doing more on that front.

talks.teaser: Hands-on automotive security training moves from CAN bus basics to defeating protections and fuzzing connected vehicles.
talks.summary:
Connected and classical vehicles share many of the same weak points, with added attack surface once telematics and remote services enter the picture. The discussion frames car hacking as practical work attackers can use to open doors, interfere with brakes, or cause other harmful effects, including approaches that have appeared in public research on remote compromise. Because flaws can affect people behind the wheel, the goal is to make severity tangible rather than theoretical.

The described course is built for participants without a security or automotive engineering background. It opens with CAN bus mechanics and what practitioners can do on a network, then walks through protections found in modern cars and how those controls fail in realistic scenarios. From there, students experiment with fuzzing and discovery techniques in the spirit of older hands-on security labs, applied to a vehicle context.

Instruction is deliberately structured so automotive engineers see how off-the-shelf attacker methods map to their products, while security specialists who already understand challenge–response schemes and brute forcing learn how those skills transfer once vehicle buses and ECUs are in scope. The expected outcome is sharper awareness of how cheaply some break scenarios reproduce, and stronger motivation to design safer connected platforms.

talks.title: 2018: Black Box Is Dead. Long Live Black Box! by V. Kononovich And A. Stennikov
talks.teaser: Details reverse engineering of an NCR ATM cash dispenser controller's firmware and how its protections were bypassed.
talks.summary:
The talk revisits black box attacks against ATMs, where extra hardware attached to internal buses makes a machine dispense cash without relying on the processing center or the ATM software. The speakers outline the ATM architecture, from the network link and XFS middleware down to device buses, and compare the serial, SDC and USB interfaces used by cash dispensers. They focus on NCR dispensers, recalling an earlier attack that exploited predictable key generation in an encrypted protocol.

The main research targeted the dispenser controller, which can be bought secondhand. The speakers explain how they analysed its unencrypted, unstripped firmware to map its services, classes and command handling. They describe how the initial encryption key is issued after a physical toggle is switched, how the bootloader was reached through a command that is not encrypted, and how the signed firmware upload had to be satisfied. Repeated bricking during firmware uploads is covered as part of the process. Their patched firmware removed the requirement for command encryption, and a demonstration showed a cash withdrawal.

The team reported the issues to NCR, which confirmed them, released fixes in a security update with two CVE identifiers, and published guidance for operators. The practical takeaway is that encrypting bus traffic does not help if firmware can be replaced or its checks patched, so physical access control and firmware integrity verification matter for dispenser hardware.

talks.title: 2018: Z-Shave. Exploiting Z-Wave Downgrade Attacks by Andrew Tierney
talks.teaser: A walkthrough shows how cleartext Z-Wave node-info can be edited during inclusion to pair S2 devices with S0 and recover network keys.
talks.summary:
Home automation gear often links locks, sensors, and hubs over Z-Wave. The talk contrasts legacy S0 pairing, where a well-known temporary key protects the network key exchange, with S2, which adds elliptic-curve Diffie-Hellman and a short device-specific PIN so an eavesdropper at inclusion time should not learn long-term secrets.

The core issue is interoperability: controllers must pair with both S0 and S2 nodes. Before encrypted setup begins, the device sends node information that includes whether it supports S2, and that frame is neither encrypted nor authenticated. An attacker who captures the broadcast can rebroadcast it with S2 capability stripped, then race the legitimate user through inclusion. The presenter pairs an S2-capable lock normally, removes it, and repeats inclusion with a laptop script and an RF dongle so the lock joins at S0 without the PIN step. Sniffing then recovers the network key using the zero temporary key, yielding control comparable to the hub.

Downgrading to S0 is worse than falling back to plaintext on a mixed network because S0 shares one key across many devices, and re-keying often means visiting each gadget. The speaker challenges vendor claims about range, timing windows, and exotic gear, notes weak uptake of mandatory S2, and describes disclosure friction including a pen test finding reclassified as by design. Practitioners should treat inclusion as a sensitive local event, verify the security tier their UI reports, and weigh backwards compatibility against downgrade risk.

talks.title: 2018: TLBleed: When Protecting Your CPU Caches Is Not Enough by B. Gras And K. Razavi
talks.teaser: Shows how a shared TLB leaks cryptographic keys past deployed cache defenses, including hyper-threaded CPUs.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with cache side channels: how a shared hardware resource lets one process infer another process's secret activity without asking for it. The speakers walk through flush-and-reload and table-based AES leakage, then the constant-time rewrites that make such leaks harder to exploit. They then review the cache-level defenses in use, including cache coloring, Intel's Cache Allocation Technology for partitioning, and TSX transactions used to detect eviction-based attacks.

The core finding is that the translation lookaside buffer, which is also shared, sits outside those defenses. Using performance counters and timed eviction sets, the researchers reverse-engineered the TLB structure across several Intel microarchitectures and found the L1 data TLB shared between hyper-threads, observable through timing alone. In a case study against an elliptic-curve point multiplication routine from a cryptographic library, a spy process watching one TLB set classified the secret key bits with a trained support vector machine. Keys were recovered with a high success rate, needing about one millisecond of victim activity and roughly 17 seconds of analysis, and the attack still worked under CAT and TSX protections.

The disclosure drew an initial Intel response that treated the TLB issue as no more serious than existing cache attacks. OpenBSD chose to disable hyper-threading by default, and Red Hat added an option to do the same. For practitioners, the takeaway is that cache isolation alone does not stop leakage: sharing between hyper-threads or between mutually distrusting code on one core needs restricting, or hyper-threading should be disabled where the performance cost is acceptable.

talks.title: 2018: There Goes Your PIN - Exploiting Smartphone Sensor Fusion by David Berend
talks.teaser: Shows how a malicious app can infer PIN digits from smartphone accelerometer and gyroscope readings collected without permission.
talks.summary:
Smartphones give apps access to accelerometer and gyroscope readings, sometimes without any permission prompt and at high sampling rates. The talk argues that a malicious app could record these signals while a user types a PIN, because each digit produces a slightly different hand movement. The speaker frames this as a way to recover a secret from motion data that people do not think of as sensitive.

To test this, three participants each entered many PIN combinations on two phones, a Nexus 5 and a Samsung Galaxy S7, while an app logged sensor data. Instead of classifying whole PINs, the researchers split recordings into single digits, which reduced the problem to ten classes. A neural network performed best among the models tried, and the accelerometer and gyroscope together gave the most stable results. Using accelerometer data alone, about 65% of four-digit PINs were recovered within 20 guesses. Trimming each digit window to 50 milliseconds before the keypress and none after raised that to 83% within 20 guesses. A classifier trained on other people still achieved some success against a person it had not been trained on, which suggested that per-target training is not strictly required.

The speaker also pointed to other uses of motion and device data, such as inferring daily routines, network signal patterns and health-app details, and mentioned early work on battery readings at high polling rates. For countermeasures, the speaker looked at developers, operating system makers, device manufacturers and users. Manufacturers were seen as unlikely to lower sensor rates for commercial reasons, so the operating system was named as the most useful place to act. Suggested controls included limiting high-frequency sensor access to approved apps and disabling background sensor measurement, alongside greater user awareness of permission requests.

talks.title: 2018: Attacking industrial Wireless Mesh Networks by E. Paternotte And M. v Ommeren
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for 2018: Attacking industrial Wireless Mesh Networks by E. Paternotte And M. v Ommeren.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk, Aaron (E. Paternotte) and Matthias (M. van Ommeren) investigate the security of industrial wireless sensor networks, specifically focusing on WirelessHART (released in 2007) and ISA100.11a (released in 2009). Used widely in critical environments like oil fields, refineries, and chemical plants, these systems traditionally measured process parameters (e.g., flow rate, liquid level, pressure) within industrial control loops. While previous research identified theoretical vulnerabilities or relied on expensive, non-injecting hardware, practical tooling has remained virtually nonexistent. The speakers present low-cost, open tooling built on commercial off-the-shelf microcontrollers to inspect, synchronize with, and attack these time-synchronized channel-hopping mesh networks.

### Key Topics
- **Industrial Wireless Mesh Protocols:** Comparison of WirelessHART and ISA100.11a. Both share underlying IEEE 802.15.4 physical and MAC properties and use Time Synchronized Mesh Protocol (TSMP) concepts with channel hopping (hopping up to 100 times per second across channels). ISA100 relies on 6LoWPAN/IPv6/UDP and International Atomic Time (TAI) timestamps, whereas WirelessHART uses sequence-numbered slots and the legacy HART application layer.
- **Cryptographic Management & Weaknesses:** Examination of AES encryption across data link (integrity) and transport (confidentiality) layers. Keys include well-known advertisement keys, network keys, join keys, and session keys. The presenters highlight vulnerabilities such as predictable or hardcoded factory join keys (e.g., Dust Networks default keys, 4-byte weak keys on Emerson devices, or vendor names in ASCII/hex), weak over-the-air provisioning, and exposed debugging interfaces on radio SoCs enabling complete firmware and key extraction from decommissioned hardware.
- **Tooling and Hardware Implementation:** Evaluating hardware platforms including multi-radio OmniSpot/BeamLogic analyzers, Atmel RZ Raven sticks, and NXP development kits. The speakers settled on an active, affordable NXP board (~$50–$60), developing custom firmware integrated into the KillerBee framework along with Scapy and Wireshark dissectors.

### Technical Details
- **Channel Hopping Synchronization:** Because networks hop 100 times per second across 10 ms timeslots within repeating superframe structures (e.g., 512 slots), standard host-to-USB serial control was too slow. The hopping logic had to be executed on the bare-metal microcontroller.
- **Embedded Scheduling Workarounds:** Attempts to use FreeRTOS software timers failed due to timing jitter and serial starvation. The authors instead leveraged NXP's bare-metal scheduler, keeping tasks strictly under 2 milliseconds. Rather than hopping every single 10 ms slot, the firmware calculates the timing of the next designated slot of interest (such as join slots or advertisement slots) from superframe sequence math, jumping precisely when needed.
- **Demonstrated Attacks:** Even without network keys, attackers listening to advertisements signed with well-known keys can target specific communication slots:
  - **Targeted Jamming:** Selectively jamming advertisement slots desynchronizes transmitters until they lose connectivity, blinding the control room and potentially triggering emergency plant shutdowns.
  - **Join-Slot Denial of Service:** Jamming join slots prevents new devices from joining or rejoining.
  - **Rogue Advertisements / Evil Twin:** Transmitting spoofed advertisements using well-known keys to entice transmitters into connecting to a rogue attacker gateway.
  - **Key-Possession Attacks:** With dumped or recovered keys, attackers can inject rogue process values, spoof sensor data, or manipulate counter values to cause legitimate sensor packets to be dropped.

### Takeaways
The lack of offensive and auditing tools previously masked the attack surface of industrial wireless mesh protocols. As industry operators consider expanding wireless networks from passive monitoring to active closed-loop control, the attack surface presents severe operational risks. The speakers announce the open-source release of their KillerBee driver, Wireshark dissectors, and firmware to spur community research, wireless fuzzing, and vendor remediation.
