talks.title: 2018: Spreading The Load: Building A Better Hardware Hacking Community by Kate Temkin
talks.teaser: Traces a Nintendo Switch boot ROM flaw and argues hardware security needs more openness, shared knowledge and accessible tooling.
talks.summary:
This keynote argues that hardware security is about where software security was ten years ago: many vendors either ignore it or hide their implementation details, and the wider community treats hardware hacking as a closed, elite skill. The speaker uses the Nintendo Switch as the main case. The console's software was heavily hardened, but the Tegra X1 boot ROM was deliberately hidden and locked once it finished running. Researchers got the code out using voltage fault injection, and development boards exposed a boot configuration flag that allowed arbitrary memory writes during boot.

Further work showed that USB recovery mode could leak stack contents through a request with a user-controlled length, and that this led to an unbounded memory copy. The flaw affected Nvidia Tegra processors going back about a decade and undermined the chip's root of trust, including key material meant to be inaccessible to software. The speaker describes a coordinated disclosure that was disrupted when someone else published details early, forcing the team to release its tooling sooner than planned. The talk also notes that similar peek-and-poke style commands were found in Qualcomm recovery tools.

The speaker concludes that the problem is cultural as much as technical. Vendors should avoid hiding boot code, since obscurity does not protect devices, and engineers across electrical and software disciplines should stop treating hardware as separate. The community should favour open, inexpensive tools and approachable teaching over secretive exploit showcases. Security also needs to be weighed as a design constraint alongside cost, performance and power, and disclosure timelines for hardware may need negotiating with vendors rather than a fixed 90-day rule.

talks.title: 2018: Bitfi - You Wouldn't Steal My Cloins by Andrew Tierney (@cybergibbons)
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding 2018: Bitfi - You Wouldn't Steal My Cloins by Andrew Tierney (@cybergibbons).
talks.summary:
# Overview
Andrew Tierney discusses comprehensive security vulnerabilities discovered in the Bitfi hardware wallet, which was marketed as "unhackable" by John McAfee. The device claimed to store private keys only in the user's head via a brain wallet model, but security research revealed fundamental design and implementation flaws across multiple attack vectors.

# Key Topics
Bitfi is a WiFi-connected hardware wallet based on a heavily modified MediaTek Android phone. Unlike traditional hardware wallets (Ledger, Trezor) that securely store keys, Bitfi requires users to type their private key every time, supposedly preventing theft if the device is compromised. The team discovered this design is fundamentally flawed.

# Technical Details
**Hardware Contradictions:**
Despite marketing claims of "no memory to hack," the device contains both eMMC flash storage and LPDDR3 RAM. Initial units lacked FCC certification despite containing RF components. Serial numbers on boxes didn't match device internals, suggesting supply chain tampering.

**Vulnerability Categories:**
1. **Touch Input:** Unencrypted I2C capacitive touch panel communication allows attackers to read finger coordinates using logic analyzers
2. **Firmware Access:** SP Flash Tool enables firmware dumping; secure boot is disabled
3. **Memory Extraction:** Private keys remain in RAM long after use (one device retained keys for two weeks); team recovered passphrases from memory dumps
4. **Viewing Angle:** Display visibility claims were false; team recovered a passphrase from an enhanced image posted by a Bitfi defender
5. **Cold Boot Attack:** Specialized tools allowed complete memory extraction in under 2 minutes after device restart, recovering keys and passphrases before they degrade
6. **Runtime Hooking:** Using Frida to intercept Java layer secrets; arbitrary transaction messages could be injected after routing the device
7. **WiFi Credential Recovery:** Recovered CEO's WiFi SSID and PSK from bounty devices via cold boot attacks

**Root Causes:**
No secure boot implementation, brain wallet model fundamentally incompatible with secure key handling, lack of memory scrubbing, unencrypted internal communications, and core reliance on an unsuitable Android phone platform.

# Bounty Program Failures
Bitfi offered $400,000 (later $10,000) bounties with restrictive rules requiring attacks on their supplied wallets. The research team successfully demonstrated multiple vulnerabilities meeting all bounty criteria. Bitfi discontinued the bounty program immediately after vulnerabilities were disclosed and refused to pay out.

# Social and Marketing Issues
John McAfee claimed to have invented cybersecurity and heavily promoted Bitfi despite clear vulnerabilities. Marketing claims included "unhackable," "no RAM," "not a phone," and "narrow viewing angle prevents shoulder surfing"—all proven false. McAfee made threatening statements when challenged, invited the researcher to his house, and posted edited fake news articles attacking them.

# Takeaways
The research demonstrates that hardware wallet security depends entirely on proper implementation. "Unhackable" claims are red flags. Even conceptually sound designs fail with poor engineering (no secure boot, inadequate memory handling). Supply chain security remains a critical unsolved problem. The brain wallet model is fundamentally problematic for daily use. Ultimate trust in hardware wallets rests on manufacturer integrity, making Bitfi's marketing deception particularly damaging. Cold boot and data remanence attacks remain viable threats that are difficult to fix remotely.

talks.title: Car Hacking | Gabriel Cirlig & Stefan Tanase | hardwear.io
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Car Hacking | Gabriel Cirlig & Stefan Tanase | hardwear.io.
talks.summary:
Overview

This talk explores automotive cybersecurity, arguing that modern cars are essentially computers on wheels and therefore inherently vulnerable to hacking attacks. The speakers emphasize the importance of hardware security conferences in fostering dialogue between security researchers and the automotive industry to prevent future compromises of connected vehicles.

Attack Vectors

The speakers categorize attacks into two main types: those requiring physical access and those requiring remote access. Their proof-of-concept demonstration combines both approaches, leveraging physical USB port access paired with remote hacking techniques. They note that current vulnerabilities are amplified by increasing wireless connectivity in vehicles, including Bluetooth and other communication interfaces.

Technical Details

A critical vulnerability example discussed is the RDS (Radio Data System), which transmits data packets over airwaves decoded by in-car radio units. Malicious actors can craft malformed data packets to crash radio units or establish entry points for remote code execution exploits. The speakers stress that comprehensive input sanitization across all system layers is essential but frequently absent in current automotive system design. They note that vulnerabilities from older exploits, such as Bluebugging, may resurface in modern embedded systems.

Industry Challenges

Automotive engineers are highly skilled but typically designed isolated infotainment systems not intended for external connectivity. As vehicles become connected, this legacy approach creates security gaps. The industry lacks sufficient understanding of how cyber attacks translate into physical threats to passengers, creating cultural resistance to prioritizing cybersecurity measures.

Key Takeaways

The speakers advocate for automotive manufacturers to implement cybersecurity with the same rigor applied to physical safety features such as airbags and seatbelts. They stress that conferences like hardwear.io are essential platforms for bridging the gap between security researchers and hardware vendors. They also call for teaching developers secure coding practices from an attacker's perspective, not merely to prevent system crashes. Active engagement between security researchers and automotive vendors is presented as critical to establishing security-first development in the automotive industry.

talks.title: 2017:- CXO Panel: UnDependable Dependencies In Safety Critical Infrastructure
talks.teaser: Panelists from health tech, rail and energy debate disclosure, policy gaps and dependable critical infrastructure.
talks.summary:
The panel opened from the premise that dependence on connected technology is growing faster than the ability to secure it, with consequences reaching public safety, national security and trust in institutions. Panelists spoke from medical devices, a Dutch railway, a former member of parliament and an energy network, and framed the problem as dependable infrastructure rather than isolated vulnerabilities.

Much of the discussion asked who should act. Speakers said policymakers tend to respond only after incidents and need people who understand the technology to write workable law. One rail speaker noted that a new European signalling standard had no policy or assurance behind it, so building that capability would take years of collaboration. The energy architect described security-by-design and asked how far end users could isolate themselves from grid risk, noting that costs are shared equally across customers. Responsible disclosure drew the most debate. Panelists recalled a December 2015 Chaos Computer Club hack of European train components with no channel back to the group, said coordinated disclosure policies are spreading in US and European bodies, and described how a US researcher's arrest had a chilling effect on the community.

In closing, panelists asked where the line on acceptable risk should sit and what fixing field issues might cost against new projects. They argued for teaching children how software works from an early age and for risk-management literacy in schools, parliaments and companies. The host ended with a challenge: find someone who does not yet care about security and connect with their motivations.

talks.title: 2017: The RTOS Exploit Mitigation Blues by Jos Wetzels
talks.teaser: Surveys exploit mitigation adoption in tiny RTOSes and presents micro Armour, a mitigation baseline for deeply embedded devices.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at exploit mitigations for tiny real-time operating systems, the kind found in radios, smart locks, vehicle ECUs and industrial controllers. It argues that memory corruption bugs are especially dangerous in these devices because patching is slow, privilege separation is often missing, and unsafe languages still dominate firmware work. The speaker surveyed 45 embedded operating systems and 78 core families for a minimal baseline of non-executable memory, address space layout randomization and stack canaries. Support was sparse, and almost none of the deeply embedded operating systems offered any of the three.

The talk then explains why adoption lags. Mitigations depend on memory protection hardware, virtual memory, secure random number generators and advanced CPU features that many chips lack, and boot-time entropy is often scarce. Examples from Sapphire and a Google RTOS show partial implementations, including canaries seeded from weak timestamp-based randomness, a static fallback canary value, and kernel panics on canary failure. Two academic AVR schemes that re-randomize code by reflashing the chip were also shown to let an attacker wear out flash by forcing repeated resets.

From these lessons the speaker proposes criteria for deeply embedded mitigations: low overhead, hardware independence, modular responses to attacks and lightweight entropy handling. The prototype, micro Armour, combines MPU-based execution protection, a compile-time per-device diversification tool, a modified stack canary component and a random number generator seeded from SRAM startup values. Reported code size overhead stays at or below 5 percent. The talk closes with its limitations, such as the narrow attacker model and limited hardware support, and with future work on safer languages and control-flow integrity.

talks.title: 2017:- TEMPEST Attacks Against AES by Craig Ramsay
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of 2017:- TEMPEST Attacks Against AES by Craig Ramsay.
talks.summary:
### Overview
Craig Ramsay presents research conducted at Fox-IT alongside Jasper van Woudenberg (and in collaboration with Riscure) examining TEMPEST (electromagnetic side-channel) attacks against AES implementations from a distance. While past TEMPEST research largely focused on asymmetric cryptography and most symmetric cryptographic side-channel analysis was restricted to "on-package" probing with direct physical access, this project demonstrates that AES-256 keys can be fully recovered from a distance using low-cost, off-the-shelf software-defined radio (SDR) hardware.

### Key Topics
- **EM Side-Channel vs. TEMPEST**: Distinguishing near-field, on-chip surface measurements from distance-based TEMPEST/EMSEC attacks on symmetric crypto.
- **SDR vs. Oscilloscopes**: Replacing traditional, expensive oscilloscopes (which sample wide frequency bands from DC up and generate massive datasets) with a cheap RTL-SDR dongle tuned down to a narrow band centered around the device clock frequency.
- **Signal Capture and Pre-Processing**: Stream-recording analog electromagnetic radiation, filtering and amplifying it, and splitting continuous captures into individual AES execution blocks.
- **Correlation Power Analysis (CPA)**: Modeling power consumption and bus switching via Hamming weights on intermediate values (T-table lookups) to brute-force AES key bytes individually.
- **Distance Progression**: Scaling the physical attack distance from contact-level EM probes to 30 cm using a log-periodic antenna in a DIY shielded box, and finally to 1 meter in an anechoic chamber.

### Technical Details
- **Target Platform**: An ARM development board running an unhardened OpenSSL-style software AES-256 implementation (utilizing standard 32-bit T-table lookups). The researchers initially tested an ARM Cortex-M3 (clocked up to 140 MHz) before moving to an ARM Cortex-A9 to achieve higher clock frequencies, which allowed using smaller, practical antennas matched to the electromagnetic wavelength.
- **Hardware & Tooling**: The capture pipeline utilized a 20-euro RTL-SDR USB dongle, Mini-Circuits RF amplifiers, and bandpass filters. Software analysis relied on custom MATLAB scripts for alignment/slicing and Riscure Inspector for correlation analysis.
- **Leakage Modeling**: Correlation analysis targeted intermediate values immediately following the initial round key addition and T-table lookup. By analyzing the switching power of the address lines across consecutive load-word instructions (`LDR`), the researchers observed consistent polarity correlation spikes across all bits.
- **Attack Milestones**:
  - *Contact Probe*: Verified the 14-round key schedule and execution rounds with an EM loop probe.
  - *30 cm Distance*: Using a printed log-periodic antenna and a DIY foil-lined cardboard enclosure to block ambient interference, the attack extracted the AES key in 50 seconds after capturing ~500,000 encryption blocks (total hardware cost ~200 USD).
  - *1 Meter Distance*: Tested inside an anechoic chamber at OSPL with full electrical isolation (the target was powered via an isolated USB battery pack under foil, encrypting in an autonomous loop without Ethernet/data cables). Using a discone antenna, the full key was recovered from ~2.5 million encryption blocks in roughly 5 minutes of streaming recording.

### Takeaways
- Software-defined radios drastically accelerate side-channel attacks compared to oscilloscopes by eliminating arm/trigger/copy latency and reducing data bandwidth via analog down-mixing.
- Standard unhardened AES implementations running on general-purpose ARM microprocessors leak sufficient electromagnetic radiation to be vulnerable to TEMPEST attacks up to a meter away using budget hardware.
- Moving to longer distances requires directional antennas and careful noise suppression or shielding, but the digital signal analysis methodology remains identical to standard contact-level side-channel attacks.

talks.title: 2017:- KERNELFAULT by Niek Timmers & Cristofaro Mune
talks.teaser: Shows how voltage glitching on an ARM Linux system can bypass kernel checks and redirect program control flow.
talks.summary:
The talk explains how voltage fault injection can be used against a Linux system running on an ARM-based embedded target. It starts with background on glitching: a workstation drives a glitch generator, a trigger signal from the target marks the attack window, and the glitch timing and shape are randomized until the software misbehaves. The speakers note that fault injection has previously been used to pull keys from smart cards and to bypass protections on game consoles, and that finding exploitable kernel bugs has become harder, which makes hardware-assisted attacks attractive.

To tune the attack, the team built a test setup in which a user-space application talks to a kernel module that updates a counter while it runs. Plotting the results across glitch length and intensity showed a narrow band where the counter was skipped without the target crashing. They then applied the technique to a kernel check on a user-supplied length value, which let them load more data into memory than the check should allow. A second case used glitching to corrupt instructions so the program counter jumped to unintended addresses, giving control over execution. They report a success rate of roughly one percent, or about one successful bypass every 15 minutes, and they also show a variant driven from user space.

The main takeaway is that a single well-timed glitch can break software security boundaries, and that the search for working parameters can be narrowed to speed up results. The speakers argue that checks tied to one point in time are weak, because a glitch can land at many different places in the code.

talks.title: 2017:- Hardware Root Of Mistrust by Joe FitzPatrick
talks.teaser: Walks through five hardware security devices, from RSA tokens to YubiKeys, and shows how each can be sniffed, cloned or bypassed.
talks.summary:
The talk examines hardware security devices as people actually use them, not as their designs promise, and asks whether the trust placed in them holds up. It covers five case studies. For an RSA SecurID token, a logic analyzer read the LCD segments without touching the crypto, and a small Bluetooth module tapping the token's battery broadcast the displayed six-digit code to anyone nearby. For secure boot, the chain runs from a Microsoft-signed shim to a GRUB bootloader signed by Ubuntu, and when no signed kernel is found, GRUB can load an unsigned one. The speaker argues that GRUB's size and parsing code make it a likely weak point.

The middle of the talk looks at TPMs and YubiKeys. Cheap TPMs bought from unvetted sellers could in principle be built from the open specification, and a malicious one could leak keys, although the standard connector lacks the pin needed for DMA attacks. A YubiKey's one-time-password check was defeated with an Arduino that emulated the device, after a real key was reprogrammed with a copied AES key. A second device then leaked keys by sending simulated mouse input that a web page could collect. The final case is a stateless design built from an EEPROM and a quad XOR chip, where a counterfeit XOR gate made from a microcontroller quietly recorded the key while it worked.

The takeaway is that hardware is not a fixed trust anchor. Supply chain tampering, end-user modification, counterfeit parts and intrusive chip work all belong in a threat model, and a few dollars of microcontroller can defeat protections that once required large budgets.

talks.title: 2017 - Shaking trust in hardware by Ben Gras&Kaveh Razavi
talks.teaser: Shows how cache side channels and Rowhammer bit flips let software attackers break ASLR and compromise VMs through hardware flaws.
talks.summary:
The talk challenges the assumption that hardware can be trusted as a stable foundation for software. The presenters argue that flaws in hardware can be triggered entirely from software, without any bug in the software itself. They cover two attacks built on hardware behaviour.

The first is a side channel on the memory management unit. When the CPU translates a virtual address to a physical one, the page table walk leaves traces in the CPU cache. By timing cache accesses from JavaScript, the presenters recovered the virtual addresses of data and code, which undermines address space layout randomization. They reported working proofs of concept in Firefox and Chrome, and said a unique high-confidence solution took about 40 seconds. The technique worked on 22 microarchitectures from Intel, AMD and Arm, and the presenters noted that Apple later shipped a mitigation.

The second is Rowhammer, a DRAM fault that lets repeated reads from aggressor rows flip bits in nearby victim rows. Combined with memory deduplication on a cloud host, a malicious virtual machine could place data where a flip would land in a neighbouring VM. In one case the flip corrupted an RSA public key so it could be factored, which allowed access to a victim's OpenSSH server. In another, a flip altered the signing key or a package repository domain used by apt, so a malicious coreutils package was installed on the victim. The takeaway is that hardware can leak secrets and be corrupted, so software-level trust assumptions do not always hold.

talks.title: 2017:- Flip A Bit, Grab A Key: Symbolic Execution Edition by Jasper van Woudenberg
talks.teaser: Shows how symbolic execution can automate differential fault analysis to recover DES and AES keys from faulted ciphers.
talks.summary:
Symbolic execution models a program as a set of equations that a solver can work through, including working backwards from a result to the inputs that produce it. Fault injection takes a different route: it disturbs a device while it runs, for example by skipping an instruction or changing a register value. The talk surveys how this is done with power, clock, electromagnetic and laser techniques, and how software-driven methods such as DRAM row hammering and a published attack on a mobile trusted execution environment can cause faults too. These faults can undermine checks such as signature verification in secure boot.

The speaker then turns to differential fault analysis, which recovers keys by comparing correct and faulted cipher outputs. Its usual drawback is that a researcher must study each cipher and fault model by hand. The idea presented was to combine a symbolic engine with fault injection so the solver derives the equations and the key. The first attempt on AES failed because lookup tables produce large numbers of branches and the engine ran out of memory. Switching to bit-sliced implementations that use only boolean operations made it work. A tool built on the angr engine recovered a DES key in a toy example, and for AES it recovered the key for one four-byte mix-column with about two faults. Runtime rises quickly as equations accumulate, and the talk compared different fault models, including how many bits flip on each half of DES.

The main takeaway is that the approach can automate fault analysis for software ciphers with few assumptions about the fault, provided the faults fit the chosen model. Ciphers that rely on lookup tables need conversion first. Future work includes unknown ciphers and white-box cryptography, and the speaker said the code and paper would be released later.

talks.title: 2017: Ghost in your Transmitter by Emmanuel Cottais, Chaouki Kasmi, José Lopes Esteves
talks.teaser: Covers polyglot RF waveforms that smuggle covert bits through legitimate QPSK links and how defenders can surface them.
talks.summary:
The session opens by placing covert channels in a three-part taxonomy—host, network, and air-gap—and narrows in on physical-layer, network-style channels built from polyglot signals, where one waveform is parsed differently by a legitimate receiver and a covert peer. It revisits the idea that radio receivers act like parsers whose modulation and error-correction steps discard information the upper layers never see, then asks whether hidden traffic must use complementary dimensions such as phase versus amplitude or can stack similar modulations, including QPSK carried inside QPSK.

Against a simplified QPSK transmitter model, the work maps attacker entry points at software (IQ sample tampering, FPGA or front-end configuration) and hardware (local oscillator manipulation, unintended EMC coupling from nearby buses). Simulations implement amplitude-style riding on legitimate QPSK and a QPSK-over-QPSK scheme using controlled alpha and beta offsets that stay inside quadrants so correction treats them as benign noise while a covert receiver recovers the hidden symbols.

For defense, the speakers propose reusing existing receiver correction blocks: extract correction factors, watch their spectra for periodic structure when covert traffic is active, and note follow-on ideas such as wavelet or blind modulation classification plus FPGA integrity and PCB isolation practices. They close by stressing that capacity and stealth trade off with legitimate link parameters, that both software and hardware compromise paths matter, and that richer RF monitoring may be needed even when no extra on-air emitter appears.

talks.title: 2017: Hardware Trojans And The Internet Of Things by Dr. Christof Paar
talks.teaser: Shows how a hardware trojan slipped in during chip manufacturing could expose plaintext data in IoT devices.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at hardware trojans, malicious changes made to a chip's circuitry during design or manufacturing. Integrated circuits are often designed and built by third-party vendors and foundries outside the buyer's control, and the speaker presents this as the core trust problem. The framing extends to Internet of Things products, where connected devices, smart grid equipment and hardware tokens depend on such chips, along with concerns about tampering by intelligence agencies.

The middle of the talk moves to a case study of a cryptographic chip. The speaker describes how a lookup table, a small component that maps inputs to outputs inside the circuit, can be altered so that secret text is exposed to an attacker. The analysis involves opening up a device and examining its structure to understand how such a modification would work and where it would sit within the logic.

The closing part draws the practical lesson that hardware cannot be trusted simply because it came from a reputable supply chain. Security teams buying or deploying connected devices should consider how components were sourced, and how they might verify hardware behaviour rather than relying only on software controls.

talks.title: 2017: Reverse Engineering Of Programmable Logic Bitstreams by Andrew Zonenberg
talks.teaser: Explains how to lift gate-level netlists from GreenPAK and CoolRunner devices into higher-level circuit structures.
talks.summary:
Andrew Zonenberg's talk looks past recovering bitstreams and photographing chips, and asks how to turn the cell-level netlists of programmable logic into something a designer can actually read. He argues that hardware lacks the per-architecture decompiler pipeline that software has, and proposes separate front ends for each device family that lift netlists into a shared intermediate representation, with the goal of eventually producing behavioral Verilog.

Prototype front ends covered Silego GreenPAK4 parts, the Xilinx CoolRunner-II CPLD, and the Lattice iCE40, where existing open tooling had already done much of the work. Once netlists reach the intermediate form, the flow runs technology mapping in reverse and then de-synthesis, recovering shift registers, adders, toggle flip-flops, counters and multi-bit gates. Examples included an LED chaser and a 10BaseT autonegotiation circuit. Graph rendering tools struggled with high fan-out nets such as clocks and resets, which pushed the speaker toward better visualization work.

The talk also touched on extracting bitstreams from locked devices, including differential power analysis against encrypted bitstreams. Future work includes an interactive GUI, tracing signals back to physical layout, and recognising physical IP blocks. The Yosys extensions and device front ends have been released as open source. The talk closed with an account of a CoolRunner device destroyed by shorting its switch boxes, where failure analysis was still inconclusive.

talks.title: 2017:- Challenging Real World Targets by Dr Sergei Skorobogatov
talks.teaser: Covers iPhone 5c NAND mirroring, Audi key EEPROM imaging, and invasive firmware pull from a wireless insulin pod.
talks.summary:
The presentation walks through three hardware security engagements driven by strong vendor or agency claims. On the iPhone 5c, the work responds to FBI assertions that only a software update could enable unlimited passcode tries. The speaker removes and rewires the glued NAND flash, solves boot and iTunes trust problems with delay tricks and serial-number copying, decodes proprietary NAND commands, and demonstrates mirroring that restores state after several PIN attempts—work shown on video but limited mainly to the 4 and 5c generation.

A second thread starts from a dealership insisting a spare Audi key was mere plastic while the car reported three programmed keys. Teardown shows the spare holds the same transponder silicon as the full remote key. Using scanning electron microscopy on legacy EEPROM in Philips-family PCF transponders, the talk explains how permutation of data lines—not encryption—stores keys and how imaging can recover contents when invasive lab methods are required.

The third project supports an artificial-pancreas community that needed to talk to an FDA-approved tubeless insulin pod. After mechanical teardown and schematic capture around an HCS08-class MCU, secured flash blocks SEM-based passive voltage contrast, MATLAB image processing, and disassembly with vendor tool data. The speaker stresses that older, poorly documented devices often fall to invasive failure-analysis techniques, while shrink and memory encryption on modern parts demand new collaboration and funding.

talks.title: 2016:- CXO Panel: The Path Toward IoT Security
talks.teaser: Panelists from disclosure, trusted hardware, telecoms and regulation debate how to secure IoT devices across the supply chain.
talks.summary:
The panel asked what a secure path for IoT would require, bringing together a vulnerability disclosure specialist, a company that builds trusted execution software for handsets and connected devices, and the chief information security officer of a Dutch telecom operator. The discussion framed the problem as a fragmented ecosystem with many protocols, uneven standardization and components that vendors often cannot fully list. Security was described as depending on every party from chip makers to carriers.

The operator described rolling out a long-range radio network used for street lighting, waste sensing and industrial cooling, and said its security team had to push for testing before launch. The disclosure specialist pointed to medical device guidance that asks manufacturers to process incoming vulnerability reports, and to EU data rules with fines of up to 4 percent of global turnover. Another speaker warned that very small device makers would struggle with added liability and cited Dutch duty-of-care rules for vital infrastructure. Several panelists doubted that regulation alone would work, and some said a catastrophic event may be needed to force change, recalling a 2003 worm that took down half of the US power grid.

The trusted-execution representative said the isolated environment used in phones is now being offered to microcontrollers. The panel also agreed that device identity and software bills of materials matter, since many vendors cannot say whether a product includes a vulnerable library. Detection across heterogeneous IoT networks was called an open problem, with a honeypot project mentioned as a starting point. The closing advice was for buyers to ask vendors whether they are affected by a named component, and for researchers to share the tools they build for testing these devices.

talks.title: 2016: Tower defense for hackers: Layered (in-)security for microcontrollers by Milosch
talks.teaser: Frames microcontroller security as layered defenses, spanning physical protections and firmware updates, in a tower defense analogy.
talks.summary:
The talk uses the idea of a tower defense game to look at security for microcontrollers, the small processors inside embedded and wireless devices. It contrasts these chips with high-end systems such as mobile phones and notes that many of these devices are now reachable over the internet, so their protections have to be arranged in layers. The speaker moves through physical security, the system-on-chip and the update path of a device, treating each as a ring of defense that an attacker may have to get past.

The middle section moves to hands-on analysis of an embedded device. The speaker describes starting from the data a chip processes and watching its operations, and mentions measuring the power the device draws while it runs. Wireless controllers and a Bluetooth device come up as examples, and the discussion returns several times to firmware updates and how the update process can open or close access to the hardware.

The closing part looks ahead to how these layers hold up over the life of a product. The main takeaway is that a device's security depends on how its layers work together, since one weak protection can undo the others.

talks.title: 2016: Self driving cars and not so autonomous security by Nicolas Massaviol
talks.teaser: Walks through attacking car ECUs via debug ports, firmware and diagnostic backdoors, and questions trust in self-driving cars.
talks.summary:
The talk treats modern cars as networks of roughly 30 electronic control units joined by CAN buses. These networks were shaped by features rather than security, and CAN messages carry proprietary bit fields that change between manufacturers and models. Gateways between buses offer some protection, but the speaker notes that compromising a multimedia unit can still reach braking and engine messages.

For finding vulnerabilities, the speaker starts with hardware: open serial consoles and JTAG ports, dumping EEPROM, eMMC and flash chips, and extracting firmware from update packages that were sometimes only weakly obfuscated. ARM and embedded Linux images are approachable, while older automotive microcontrollers are slow to reverse. One telematics unit was found shipping an outdated OpenSSL release. The team's own mistakes highlighted risks: blind fuzzing and some diagnostic routines can wipe an ECU, mismatched multimedia versions broke work, and JTAG probes were costly. Backdoors covered hidden developer menus, a USB mode giving a passwordless SSH shell, UDS seed-and-key checks using a short shared key, and supplier routines that allowed raw memory access after the manufacturer had disabled it.

Remote risks included an anti-theft feature in Brazil that accepted SMS commands without authentication, with the same software shipped elsewhere and only configuration differing. Emergency call units that relay cabin audio were also raised as a privacy concern. Looking ahead, development cycles freeze technology years before launch, so today's security practices would shape future vehicles. Because self-driving systems depend on constant connectivity and many parties, the air-gap approach used for other critical systems does not fit, and more research is needed.

talks.title: 2016 :- Reverse Engineering vehicles Burpsuite Style by Javier & Ferdinand
talks.teaser: Shows an open-source CAN bus tool that logs, rewrites, and hijacks UDS and TP 2.0 diagnostic sessions in cars.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the diagnostic protocols that run over a vehicle's CAN bus. The speakers explain that UDS and TP 2.0 are transport layers that split payloads larger than a single CAN frame, and they describe the main UDS services that matter to an attacker: security access, reading memory by address, reading data by identifier, and requesting firmware uploads. They note that TP 2.0 is a close relative of UDS with different service codes and frame sizes.

They then introduce the Cam Badger, a low-cost board built around an LPC1769 microcontroller with two CAN interfaces, an SD card for logs and rule files, and standalone, USB serial, and network modes. Its firmware parses UDS and TP 2.0 traffic in real time and can run as a man-in-the-middle that rewrites specific bytes or masks on the fly. In a live demo, a speed-related byte was halved on the way through with no visible added latency. The talk also covers recording traffic with timestamps for later playback and capturing firmware transfers from the bus to the SD card.

The final section covers security access hijacking. A bridge device watches for another tester completing a successful security access exchange, then takes over that diagnostic session without knowing the key or algorithm. The demo shows that the session type must match the target module before the hijack works, and that memory can then be read without authentication. The takeaway is that a session authenticated for one tool can be reused by another device on the bus. The speakers publish the tool and its documentation on GitHub and offered a booth demo afterward.

talks.title: 2016 :- Keynote by SERGEY BRATUS
talks.teaser: Argues that hardware buses lacking tools for injecting crafted inputs are insecure, illustrated with Wi-Fi, Zigbee and USB cases.
talks.summary:
The keynote argues that a bus or component shipped without practical tools for injecting crafted inputs and states should be treated as insecure, and that its exposure grows the longer those tools are missing. The speaker traces this through networking history: raw sockets let researchers craft packets, which helped TCP/IP stacks harden, while SCADA systems stayed fragile because few people could test them.

The middle of the talk moves to parsers and dialects. Early Wi-Fi injection tools and frame-handling firmware showed that some chipsets and drivers accepted nonsensical flag combinations that others rejected, so two devices could read the same frame differently. A Zigbee experiment with custom radio hardware showed that changing the preamble length altered which receivers heard a frame, and that an application-layer payload could be interpreted as a valid frame. For USB and storage, the speaker described devices that set up a transaction to expect one thing and then supply another, and warned that a hard drive backdoor could be woken by a pattern of block reads.

The closing argument is that operating systems trust lower layers to keep their state unchanged, which makes time-of-check and time-of-use gaps and weird machines possible. The speaker urged researchers to build tools for exploring buses and OS components, and to make data conform to types that limit computation. In the Q&A the speaker noted that relocation tables can act as code. The talk also raised concern that export and intrusion-software rules could restrict the injection tools researchers need.
